cards.title: Candy, Dish and Shell Game
case: A man lies bleeding on the pavement. Near his body are a mint, a plate and a spent .45 caliber shell.
cards.mystery: Why was the man shot?
clues: Coincidentally, the man's name was Bill.
The mint was not the kind you can eat.
story: The man was a bold thief who had entered a U.S. Mint, grabbed a currency printing plate, and attempted to dash out the door with it. A federal security guard shot him, and he collapsed just outside the building.
cards.specialInformation: Because currency printing plates are now much larger than in the 19th century, this scenario would be more likely in the late 1800s. However, a fearless felon with track training might be foolish enough to attempt it today!
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the man was shot while trying to steal a currency printing plate from a U.S. Mint.

cards.title: Death Begins at Forty
case: Morton dies on his 40th birthday shortly after receiving a gift. He was a partner in a small, very lucrative oil business. The company has survivor rights, which means that the partners will inherit Morton's share. Therefore, all three partners are suspects.

An astute detective investigates. Two of the partners live within ten miles of Morton's home; one has known him for three months, the other for six months. The third partner was a childhood friend of the same age, who lives 850 miles away in Morton's hometown. "That's the man I want," said the detective. "Extradite him and charge him with murder."
cards.mystery: Why did the detective zero in on Morton's childhood friend?
clues: The gift came in a bunch, but was not floral.
Morton's last words sounded strange.
story: Morton's secretary, who had known him only a short time, told the detective that when Morton's gift of balloons arrived (without a card), he smiled as if he knew who had sent them. Taking one of the balloons, Morton went straight to the phone. He dialed a number, then opened the balloon and inhaled its contents.
The balloon contained potassium cyanide powder along with the helium. Death was almost instantaneous.

Only an old friend could have known about Morton's life-long habit of breathing in the helium from his birthday balloons and singing "Happy Birthday to Me" in a chipmunk voice. Morton had dialed this "friend's" number — a friend for whom a life sentence began at forty.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the childhood friend anonymously sent Morton helium balloons containing poison, knowing that Morton would inhale the contents and die.

cards.title: Sweet Revenge
case: A man is found dead on the linoleum floor of his kitchen. Near his body is a jar partially full of candy. His wife has been out of town for days; nevertheless, she is arrested and charged with her husband's murder.
cards.mystery: How did the wife kill her husband?
clues: Usually, the man appreciated candy for its "shock" value.
The candy was not what it seemed.
story: The man was a lazy spendthrift who had finally managed to fritter away the last of his wife's fairly sizeable inheritance. She was mad enough to kill him, and set out to do just that.

Her husband was an acute diabetic who took daily injections of insulin. Before she went away, she secretly boosted the concentration of his insulin so that his daily shot would send him into insulin shock. When this happened the next day, he reached for the candy which he always kept on hand. But his wife had switched his usual candy with artificially-sweetened candy, and he became comatose and died. Police discovered the substituted candy and proved that the man's wife had bought it just before her trip. Her sweet murder plan ended on a very sour note.
cards.specialInformation: A diabetic needs daily insulin injections to maintain the proper blood sugar level. Injecting too much insulin can cause insulin shock, coma, and eventually death. The diabetic can fend off insulin shock by eating sugar immediately. Artificial sweetener, of course, will have no effect.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the wife boosted her diabetic husband's insulin concentration, substituted artificially-sweetened candy for his real candy, and that her husband went into a coma and died as a result.

cards.title: Close Call
case: Sally answers the telephone in her living room. The conversation goes like this:
Sally: "Hello?"
Caller: "Hi, Sally. Are you coming in to work today?"
Sally: "No, I'm afraid not. I've got the flu or something."
Caller: "Oh, I'm sorry. Do you think you'll be in tomorrow?"
Sally: "I can't tell yet. Can you make my excuses to the boss?"
Caller: "Sure. Anything else I can do for you?"
Sally: "No, thanks. Maybe I'll see you tomorrow. 'Bye."
The caller immediately notified the police, who surrounded Sally's house, broke in and arrested the man who was holding her hostage.
cards.mystery: How was Sally's caller tipped off to her plight?
clues: Sally was in the communications business.
As Sally talked into the phone, she "spoke" another language.
story: Sally was being held hostage by an escapee from a nearby maximum-security prison. When her telephone rang, the man ordered her to answer it but not to arouse any suspicion.

Sally worked for Western Union, where employees are still required to know Morse Code. Relieved that the caller was a colleague, Sally turned away from the intruder and rested her thumb on the pound key of her touch-tone phone. As she spoke, she secretly tapped on the pound key in Morse Code: S-O-S ... S-E-N-D P-O-L-I-C-E. With the phone close to her ear, Sally muffled the sound so that the intruder could not hear her message.
Luckily for Sally, her caller kept cool, and the police were quickly able to "reach out and touch" the bad guy.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Sally secretly tapped out S-O-S ... S-E-N-D P-O-L-I-C-E in Morse Code to her Western Union colleague on her touch-tone phone.

cards.title: Music to Kill By
case: A man dies during a performance of Gershwin's Concerto in F# at Symphony Hall.
cards.mystery: Who killed him, how, and why?
clues: The dead man was a violinist in the orchestra.
The Gershwin Concerto begins and ends with loud kettle drums.
story: The victim was a married violinist in the orchestra, who had gotten the oboist's daughter pregnant. Crazed with hatred, the oboist made a small dart from a fishing lure and dipped the tip in poison. At the end of the concerto, when the kettle drums pounded and the woodwinds were silent, he inserted the dart into the end of his oboe, unscrewed the reed and, pretending to "blow out" his instrument, instead blew the tiny poisoned dart into the violinist's neck.

Because the oboist was at the end of the woodwind row, next to the violins, no one noticed anything out of the ordinary. And because of the loud drums, no one heard the violinist scream in pain. His death wasn't discovered until he failed to stand during the applause. In the confusion that followed, the oboist sneaked to the airport and hopped a plane, which crashed upon landing in Lima, Peru. No one figured out that it was an ill woodwind that blew no good.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that a married violinist had gotten the oboist's daughter pregnant, and that the oboist killed the violinist with a poison dart that he blew out of his instrument.

cards.title: Smash Hit
case: A car driven by a drunken man collides with a limo on a busy street. Miraculously, the limo driver and his passenger are not critically injured, and the driver of the car walks away unhurt. Nevertheless, the drunken man is later arrested for negligent homicide.
cards.mystery: On what grounds was the drunken driver arrested?
clues: The limo was speeding to save a life.
Something was smashed, besides the drunken driver.
story: It was an emergency. The limo's passenger was a medical technician, rushing a liver from the airport to the hospital for a life-saving transplant. But the crash smashed the liver to smithereens, making the transplant impossible.
Though the two men in the limo lived, the unlucky patient died in the hospital, waiting in vain for her new liver to arrive. By his negligence, the drunken driver caused the patient's death.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the limo was rushing a liver to the hospital for an emergency transplant. The crash, caused by the drunken driver, smashed the liver and caused the patient to die.

cards.title: Don't Shoot!
case: A group of people are sitting around a card table at Nick's house. Suddenly a man appears at the door with a pistol in hand. He enters the house and fires two bullets at Boris, who falls to the floor mortally wounded. As the gun-wielding stranger stares at the body, Nick reaches into a drawer, pulls out a gun and shoots him. On the way to the hospital the intruder dies. Days later, Nick is arrested for both murders.
cards.mystery: Why was Nick charged with murder?
clues: What the victims didn't know hurt them.
Both Boris and the intruder had "blank" looks on their faces.
story: Nick and Boris were practical jokers, always playing wacky pranks on their friends. But when Nick found out that his wife and Boris were fooling around, it was no joke. He carefully plotted his revenge.

Nick and Boris had planned a special prank for poker night. They hired an actor to rush into Nick's house at midnight, draw a gun and shoot two blanks at Boris, who would fall over and pretend to die. Nick would then draw a gun from a nearby drawer, shoot blanks at the intruder and give everybody a double scare. But Nick placed real bullets in the gun that he gave to the actor, and in his own gun. At midnight, the actor showed up and shot Boris. As real blood spurted from Boris's heaving chest, the stunned actor stood transfixed by the horrible sight. Nick then reached into the drawer, pulled out his gun and fired real bullets into the frightened actor.

An ambulance came for the mortally wounded victims. Nick might have gotten away with his dastardly deed, if the dying actor hadn't regained consciousness for a final curtain call. With his last breath, the actor mentioned something about shooting blanks. Nick's trick was discovered, and now he plays practical jokes behind bars.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Boris and Nick planned a gag for their friends. They hired an actor to appear at their poker party and shoot blanks at Boris. But a vengeful Nick put real bullets in the gun, and the actor unknowingly killed Boris. Nick, pretending to protect his guests, silenced the actor by shooting him.

cards.title: Bye-Bye Bertie
case: Bert's wife Wanda works at a real estate office. She returns home one night from showing a house, and begins to undress as her husband watches from the bed. Suddenly he gets up, grabs his suitcase and starts packing. Wanda asks, "Where are you going?" Bert replies, "I'm leaving you, Wanda — this time for good!"
"But why?" whines Wanda.
cards.mystery: What is the answer to Wanda's question?
clues: Wanda's luck had "run" out.
Bert "left" Wanda for the "right" reason.
story: Bert and Wanda would have had the perfect marriage, if only Wanda could resist the occasional fling with a client. Finally, Bert had had enough. Next time Wanda wandered, Bert would desert, he decided. And Bert began to keep close tabs on his wayward wife.

When Wanda dressed for her appointment that night, Bert noticed a small run in the left leg of her pantyhose. When Wanda returned home, the same run was on her right leg, suggesting that she had shown a little something besides a house. Thus, Bert's no-nonsense decision to run for the hills.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Bert left Wanda because she was cheating on him. He noticed that she had a run in her pantyhose that moved from one leg to the other when she took them off and put them back on — obviously during a romantic tryst.

cards.title: Reno No No
case: Sam is found dead in the back alley of the Reno casino where he worked as a croupier. Police bring in Paula, his singer girlfriend, for questioning. "You got nothin' on me," she indignantly tells the officer. "I was singin' at a private party when Sam was killed. I got witnesses."
"I know," replied the officer, "but we found this in your garbage."
cards.mystery: What was the "this" the officer held in his hand? Who killed Sam, and how?
clues: Sam gambled with characters of questionable morals.
Sam thought he was on a roll, until his gambling buddies discovered his secret.
story: Sam dumped Paula for a younger model, and Paula swore revenge. She knew that each night after hours, Sam hosted a private gambling party for several underworld characters. Paula purchased a pair of loaded dice at a local magic shop, and secretly switched them for Sam's legitimate dice one evening just before his guests arrived.

Just as Paula had planned, the shady characters accused Sam of cheating, discovered the loaded dice, and beat the "craps" out of him. What Paula's arresting officer held in his hand was her sales receipt for the dice, which police had discovered to be bogus. Paula had lost her gamble to get away with murder.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Paula secretly slipped Sam loaded dice, causing his unscrupulous customers to accuse him of cheating and beat him to death.

cards.title: A Clue Before Dying
case: A trail of blood leads from the locker room through the open door of the office. Leon had probably tried to get to the phone, but didn't make it. His body lies beside the coach's desk, near a paperback edition of Frankenstein.

Captain Grayson of the police notices that Leon is clutching the last page of the book in his hand. He removes the crumpled page and reads it carefully several times. "Oh, yes," he finally mumbles. "I get what he was trying to say. Well, this certainly narrows it down."
cards.mystery: What had Leon meant by his final act? Who killed him, and why?
clues: The suspects were all members of a college football team.
A great many books have the same ending.
story: Leon Reece was a notorious gambler. His presence in a college locker room in late November could mean only one thing: Leon was trying to fix the football games.

Since Leon was not known as the literary type, Captain Grayson was at first confused by the clue. Nothing on the page seemed significant — until Grayson suddenly realized that "THE END" might mean a position on the football team.

Grayson then reviewed some recent game tapes. He noticed that Ted Binky, the tight end, fumbled or missed several easy passes. Under intense questioning, Ted confessed that he had been "throwing" games for Leon's syndicate. When the athlete later had a change of heart and wanted to call it quits, Leon threatened to expose him. Ted countered with a knife — and Leon got the point.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Leon was a gambler who was stabbed to death. The key words on the page were "THE END." The killer was the football team's tight end, who had been "throwing" games for Leon.

cards.title: Laddy Goes Home
case: Laddy, a five-year-old miniature poodle, has just died. At the dog's memorial service, his owner, Mr. Driscoll, says the following words: "This animal gave his life to protect his humans from a deplorable, premeditated crime. We will always be grateful for Laddy's noble sacrifice."
cards.mystery: How did Laddy die, and what crime did his death prevent?
clues: No one was meant to be seriously hurt.
Laddy's heroism was performed under the table.
story: Annie Carver's plan was simple: get a job as a cook for a rich family, slip a dose of sleeping powder into their food, then rob them blind and disappear as they slept. The fatal flaw in Annie's plan was that she was a rotten cook — especially when it came to desserts. In fact, the Driscoll family had already given her notice.

On the evening in question, the family suffered through another of Annie's culinary curiosities. Dessert was eclairs, heavily laced with enough sleeping powder to bring on a long, deep sleep. As usual, however, the desserts were all sneaked under the table to an eager Laddy, the only family member who didn't complain about Annie's cooking.
Laddy quickly died of an overdose of sleeping powder, which the Driscolls discovered from the autopsy. Annie was arrested, and the porky poodle was buried with full honors under his favorite tree.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the Driscolls fed Laddy food that the cook had laced with sleeping powder, and that his resulting death from an overdose of drugs prevented the cook from robbing the family.

cards.title: Gym Nasty
case: Mary Webster, a recently unemployed advertising copywriter, is found dead in the women's shower at her gym. The police correctly assume that Mary slipped and died of a head injury.
cards.mystery: Why, then, was another patron of the gym, Mrs. Eden Hershey, arrested for Mary's murder?
clues: Mary needed fast cash to pay her bills.
Mary could keep a secret if the price was right.
story: Early one morning at the gym, Mary walked into what she thought was an empty dressing room, and discovered that Mrs. Hershey was really a man. Seizing a golden opportunity, Mary told the wealthy transvestite that $100,000 in small bills would keep "her" secret safe. "Mrs." Hershey agreed to get the money the next day.

But instead of paying up, "Mrs." Hershey struck back. The next morning "she" got to the gym early. First, "she" entered the shower that Mary always used after her early workouts, and slathered the floor with "her" moisturizer. Next "she" waited, with a 10-pound weight in hand, until Mary went in, slipped and fell. Then, "she" entered the shower and finished Mary off with a well-placed blow to the skull.
"Mrs." Hershey was booked for murder when police found the 10-pound weight and matching moisturizer in "her" locker. "She" had slipped up by not getting rid of the evidence. What a dumbbell!
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Mary tried to blackmail "Mrs." Hershey when she found that "she" was a man. "Mrs." Hershey killed Mary by spreading moisturizer on the shower floor, then hitting her with a dumbbell when she slipped and fell.

cards.title: A Drop of Schnapps
case: A man's body floats ashore on a New Jersey beach. No one ever identifies it.
cards.mystery: How and why did he die?
clues: The man was German.
The victim's demise occurred just before World War II.
story: The date was May 6, 1937. Dietrich Von Schnapps was traveling to Lakehurst, New Jersey, on the Hindenburg. While in the U.S., Dietrich planned to sell stolen U-boat plans to the American government.

His traveling companion, Hans Gundlach, had discovered Dietrich's treachery, and did what he considered to be his patriotic duty. First he stole Dietrich's wallet so that he could not be identified. Then, shortly before the men reached their destination, Hans pushed Dietrich out the window of the airship. Dietrich fell into the Atlantic and drowned.
Minutes later the Hindenburg exploded, and both men were listed as dying in the disaster. No one ever knew that the spy in the sky had been murdered.
cards.specialInformation: For the purposes of this game, the Hindenburg can be described as an airship, zeppelin, dirigible or blimp.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the victim was a German spy, traveling to the U.S. on the Hindenburg. He was pushed out of a window and drowned in the Atlantic by his colleague, who had discovered he was a traitor. Moments later the Hindenburg exploded, and both men were listed as casualties.

cards.title: Open and Clothes Case
case: A woman suddenly disappears from her home, leaving all of her clothes behind — even the ones she was wearing!
cards.mystery: What became of the woman?
clues: The woman was from the west.
There is a puddle of water where the woman was last seen.
story: The Land is Oz, and the woman is the Wicked Witch of the West. Dorothy melted her with a bucket of water, and Ding Dong — the witch was dead, leaving only a puddle of water and the clothes she was wearing.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the woman was the Wicked Witch of the West from The Wizard of Oz, and that Dorothy had melted her with water.

cards.title: Fish Story
case: Rick and Roy own a small fishing boat. They are spending a weekend at the shore, fishing by day and drinking in their motel by night. Saturday Rick returns alone in the boat, phones the police and reports that Roy lost his balance, fell overboard and drowned.
On Sunday, Roy's body washes ashore and is taken to the coroner for examination. Police later find Rick by the motel pool and arrest him for Roy's murder.
cards.mystery: How did Roy die, and why was Rick arrested?
clues: Rick and Roy had an argument on Friday night.
The coroner did some "fresh" thinking on this case.
story: Late Friday evening, Rick and Roy were drinking alone by the motel pool, and arguing over who was the better athlete. They angrily agreed to settle the matter with a lap around the pool. Roy finished well ahead of Rick, and proceeded to boast as the men finished off a few more beers. Rick's anger turned to rage, and he proceeded to prove that Roy could not hold his breath underwater for ten minutes. Before Rick realized what he was doing, Roy had drowned.

Desperate to camouflage his crime, Rick loaded Roy's body into the boat and dumped it overboard at sea. During the coroner's autopsy, fresh water and chlorine were found in Roy's lungs, proving that Rick's fishy story was all wet.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Rick drowned Roy in the motel swimming pool and dumped his body into the ocean. Rick was arrested when the coroner discovered fresh water in Roy's lungs.

cards.title: Pillow Talk
case: A man and a woman are lying in bed together. The woman says, "I think Richard is onto us. He threw a tantrum last night and accused me of having an affair with you. I told him he was crazy — I'm just extra-nice to you because he's your best friend. Anyway, I've decided that when Missy goes off to college, I'm telling Richard to hit the road..."
Before the woman can say more, the man picks up his pillow and smothers her to death with it.
cards.mystery: What made the man murder the woman?
clues: This scenario took place very late at night.
The woman could not have seen the man reach for the pillow.
story: The man was Richard, the woman's husband. The woman was talking in her sleep, obviously to her lover. Richard's worst nightmare was realized in her dream — a dream from which he made sure she would never awaken.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the woman and the man were married, and that the woman was talking to her lover in her sleep.

cards.title: Two Sloppy Spies
case: It had been a long day. The spy sat in his room and opened his briefcase. As he looked at an envelope of secret documents, he knew immediately that someone had tampered with it.
The spy mentally retraced his day's activities. Suddenly he exclaimed, "I know where it happened!"
cards.mystery: Where did the breach occur, and how did the spy deduce it?
clues: When the breach occurred, the spy's face was covered.
National security had been compromised by a scallop.
story: The sealed, padded envelope had been opened with the help of a small pair of scissors with scalloped edges. The spy recognized the cuts as the work of a pair of cuticle scissors, the kind used by the pretty manicurist at the barbershop he had visited that afternoon.

The briefcase, he recalled now, had been out of his sight for a full minute while the barber had placed a hot towel over his head and massaged his temples. That's when he realized that this particular "clip joint" clipped not only his hair, but his secrets as well.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the envelope containing secret papers had been cut open with cuticle scissors, implicating the barbershop's manicurist.

cards.title: A Chinese Folk Tale
case: The Emperor's jade cricket box had been stolen from the imperial bedchamber. The chief of guards had narrowed the suspects down to two palace servants. Because neither would confess, the Emperor had decided to execute them both.

Then the court magician intervened. Through his magic arts, he would identify the true thief so that the innocent man could live. The emperor consented to this plan, and gathered both suspects into his courtyard.

The magician asked each servant to cut a stalk of bamboo. He then shoved the two bamboo stalks into the ground, exposing only the upper foot of each stalk. He then said, "Each bamboo now holds the spirit of the man who cut it. At dawn, when we return to this spot, we will know which man stole the box." He then explained how his magic would work.
cards.mystery: What was the magician's explanation of his magic plan? And how did he identify the guilty servant at dawn?
clues: This might have been the original Pinocchio story.
The courtyard was left unguarded that night.
story: The magician told the servants that the bamboo stalks were bewitched. The stalk cut by the guilty man would magically grow during the night. When they returned at dawn, his stalk would be exactly one inch longer than the stalk of the innocent man.
At dawn, everyone gathered again and were amazed to see that one stalk was two inches longer. The magician smiled, and said, "The man with the shorter stalk is your thief."
The chief of guards protested: "No, no. You said the man with the longer stalk."

The magician shook his head. "My magic was not needed. The thief was afraid his stalk would grow and reveal his guilt. So he sneaked into the courtyard during the night and cut two inches off his own stalk: one inch to compensate for the magic, and one inch to implicate his fellow servant. By trying to hide his guilt, he had proven it."
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the magician explained that the guilty man's stalk would magically grow before dawn, and that the thief secretly cut his own stalk during the night, proving his guilt.

cards.title: All Wet
case: Wayne lies dead in the water, wearing a plastic raincoat.
cards.mystery: Who killed Wayne, how, and why? How did his murderer get caught?
clues: Wayne was married.
Wayne's girlfriend was a little over-the-edge.
story: The plan started off well enough. Wayne told his wife he was traveling on business. Then he and his sweetie-on-the-side, Greta, drove to Niagara Falls for a getaway weekend.

Greta was hoping that Wayne would finally promise to dump his wife and marry her. So she was shocked when Wayne told her over dinner that he thought their relationship was going nowhere. Greta reacted calmly, but secretly plotted to pay back the insensitive slob for the pain and suffering he had inflicted upon her.

The next day, the two visited a deserted area near the falls, wearing their raincoats in the mist. Greta asked Wayne to pose for a snapshot. As he stood facing the camera, Greta kept saying, "Move back a little...just a l-i-t-t-l-e more." Wayne's final step backward was off the riverbank. As Greta gleefully clicked the shutter, Wayne went over the falls, then drowned in the water below.

Greta spent the rest of the day at the tourist traps, then drove home. When Wayne didn't return from his "business trip," his wife reported him missing. Police got the picture when the alert developer of Greta's snapshots phoned in with irrefutable evidence: a snapshot of a panicked Wayne flailing his arms as he went over the falls.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the married Wayne had tried to break up with his girlfriend. For revenge, she took a snapshot of him, telling him to step back until he accidentally went over a waterfall and drowned. She was caught when the snapshot was developed.

cards.title: Ship Gyp
case: After saving for years, Oscar purchases a 40-foot cabin cruiser at a bargain price. Then, a week later he wins a contest for an all-expense-paid stay at a luxury resort on the island nation of St. Aretha. Oscar immediately takes some time off from work and heads for the Caribbean paradise. He is thrilled with his good fortune, but slightly puzzled because he can't recall entering the contest.
cards.mystery: How did Oscar win a contest he never entered? What crime was involved, and who was behind it?
clues: Oscar got a government deal.
Beware of phony "free" vacations with hidden costs.
story: Oscar loved the sea and finally saved up enough money to buy a cabin cruiser at a government auction. The boat had recently been confiscated from a drug smuggler. The smuggler had several silent partners in crime, but refused to implicate them.

Before his arrest, the smuggler had stashed a fortune in drugs in a special hidden compartment on the boat that narcotics officers failed to find. The smuggler's partners didn't dare come forward and bid on the boat because they knew they were under surveillance by the authorities. Instead, they found out who bought the boat and sent him a phony first prize vacation notice. They hoped to lure the unsuspecting Oscar to the "friendly" waters of St. Aretha, a place where U.S. officials had no authority and were not welcome. Once Oscar arrived, it would be a simple matter for the smugglers to sneak on board and unload the drugs.
Unfortunately, Oscar was not a skillful skipper and his boat sank in a storm. The smuggler's stash, as well as Oscar, went down with the ship.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Oscar bought a boat at a government auction and that drugs had been hidden on board by smugglers. The drug smugglers planned to lure Oscar to an island where the narcotics could be safely retrieved.

cards.title: Jack Knifed
case: A teenager is taking her regular shortcut to school when she comes upon a gruesome sight in the woods. Lying on the path is the body of her neighbor, Jack Cutnick, with a bloody knife protruding from his chest. The girl runs away in fear, but returns to the site with the police. Jack's body has disappeared and all that remains are a few drops of his blood.

The police never find the body. A month later, however, they serve a search warrant on Archie Gore, a traveling salesman who lives 50 miles away. Hidden in his garage are Jack's bloody clothing, his wedding ring, and a photo of Jack with his arms around Archie's wife. The police arrest Archie, but not for murder.
cards.mystery: What happened to Jack and why did the police arrest Archie?
clues: Archie was trying to simplify his life.
There was no corpse for the police to find.
story: The police didn't arrest Archie for murder because Archie and Jack were the same person. Archie was leading a double life, with two wives who were completely unaware of each other's existence. Archie was a traveling salesman, giving the bigamist husband the perfect excuse for his periodic absences.

Archie decided to simplify his life and do away with his alter ego. He staged the fake murder so that "Jack's" wife could collect on his life insurance policy. Archie knew that his young neighbor was the only one who walked through the woods at that time of day, and correctly assumed that she would run to get help.

When Jack's photo appeared on the news, a neighbor of Archie's noticed the resemblance and called the police. They couldn't arrest Archie for murder, but they did arrest him for insurance fraud and bigamy.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Archie and Jack were the same person and that he faked his death so that "Jack's" wife could collect on his life insurance policy.

cards.title: Seoul Food
case: A woman is found dead on the streets of Seoul, the South Korean capital. Beside her lies a basket.
cards.mystery: Who killed the woman, how, and why?
clues: The woman was betrayed by someone she knew.
Too late, something in the basket "struck" the woman as odd.
story: The killer was a Korean political activist who worked as a meat vendor in the local market. His victim was a member of the ruling regime, who bought snake meat for dinner each Tuesday. It was easy for the vendor to plan her murder by performing a sneaky snake switcheroo.

When the woman arrived at the vendor's booth that Tuesday, he slipped a sedated, highly-venomous cobra into her shopping basket, instead of the non-poisonous snake he usually sold her. Halfway home the snake awakened and bit the unsuspecting woman, poisoning her to death almost instantly.
The local police found the cobra, wormed the story out of the vendor, and arrested him.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the woman was sold a sedated cobra by her political-activist vendor, and that the snake awoke and poisoned her to death.

cards.title: Initial Amnesia
case: A young man wakes up on the side of a desert road with a nasty bruise on his temple. He has no car, no possessions, and no clothes to his name. In fact, he can't even remember his name, since the blow to his head has left him with amnesia.
Desperately, he looks around in search of a clue that might tell him who he is. That's when he notices a tattoo on his left arm. There are three short rows of letters:
Eb - Ob
wsn
SWIS S
cards.mystery: Who is the young man? What happened to him, and what does the tattoo mean?
clues: The young man was dizzy and not thinking clearly.
He was looking down at the tattoo when he read it.
story: Scott Sims had been a U.S. Marine. After his discharge in 1993, he had bought a new sports car and was now taking a leisurely cross-country tour. On that fateful day, Scott picked up a hitchhiker along an empty stretch of road. The hitchhiker mugged the ex-Marine, stripping him of everything and leaving him to die.
After a minute of confusion, Scott realized he was reading his tattoo upside-down. What it really said was:
S SIMS
usm
The highway patrol soon came to his rescue, contacted the Marine Corps and had Scott identified. A week later, he recovered his memory and picked his hitch-and-run assailant out of a line-up.
cards.specialInformation: After reading The Case, ask the Investigators to write down the three short rows of letters as follows: On the first line, capital E, small b, dash, capital O, small b. On the second line, small w s n. On the third line, capital S W I S, space, capital S.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Scott Sims was an ex-Marine who was mugged by a hitchhiker, and that the tattoo meant S SIMS, U.S. Marine, 90 - 93.

cards.title: Stain Power
case: Her coat was ruined — spattered indelibly with an ugly purple stain. Although it was a cold winter and the coat was the only one she owned, she never had greater cause for celebration. Very possibly, a life had been saved.
cards.mystery: What was the cause for celebration?
clues: Her stainer was her savior.
Her coat was not available at any store.
story: She was a baby seal whose coat had just been sprayed with purple stain by a Greenpeace helicopter. The ugly purple stain would prevent fur merchants from slaughtering her for her beautiful coat.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that she was a baby seal who had been sprayed to protect her from being slaughtered.

cards.title: Deadpan
case: A woman in a white dress is found dead. Near her body is a broken teacup.
cards.mystery: Who was the woman? Who killed her, how, and why?
clues: The white dress was not a pretty gown.
The woman had an unfortunate personality.
story: Thaddeus Twiddle, a bedridden 92-year-old stroke victim, lived in his mansion with his sister, staff and private nurse. Because of his incapacities he could neither talk nor write. So he had no way to tell his sister that he hated his dour, fussy, malicious, sadistic nurse, Miss Prout, and wanted her dismissed at once.

One day, when Miss Prout brought him a cup of bitter tea, which always burned his throat and made him nauseous, he looked for something with which to strike her. Spotting the glass he kept his false teeth in, he smashed the top of it and held the weapon under the covers.

As Miss Prout leaned over to force the bitter brew down his throat, he jabbed the jagged glass into her throat, killing her instantly as she dropped the teacup. Twiddle died in his sleep before he could be prosecuted. As for the late Miss Prout, a little TLC would have prevented her premature RIP.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the woman was a nurse whose patient, unable to communicate that he hated her, stabbed her in the throat with a broken glass.

cards.title: In a Fix
case: Harvey Gearhead is in the federal witness protection program. He now works incognito as a car mechanic in his own small auto repair shop. One morning Harvey drops dead while working on a car.
cards.mystery: How and why was Harvey killed?
clues: There was a lot of wheeling and dealing going on at the garage.
Harvey was thinking about "retiring."
story: Several years ago, Harvey Gearhead testified against his boss, a mobster named Willie Getem. In exchange for his testimony, Harvey was given a new identity and a new job in another city. Willie was furious with Harvey and swore he'd get even. After he beat the rap on a technicality, Willie planned his revenge.

When Willie learned that Harvey owned his own auto repair shop, the mobster decided to give him some business. Willie filled the tires of an old car with poisonous gas and ordered one of his new henchmen to bring the car into Harvey's garage for new tires. When Harvey drained the "air" from the old tires, he was killed by a blast of deadly gas.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that when Harvey let the "air" out of the tires on a mobster's car, he was killed by poisonous gas that had been pumped into the tires.

cards.title: A Fast Kill
case: Swami Morishi was on a hunger strike until his followers could raise two million dollars to pay off the mortgage on their cult compound.

Even into the third week of his fast, the Swami kept to his routine. He would meditate in the mornings, then meet privately with Michelle, his second-in-command, to work on any business. He would then teach in the afternoons and in the evenings tour the compound.
One night, right after his tour of the kitchen, the Swami collapsed. Michelle was called from her cabin and rushed to the scene. By the time the ambulance arrived, the Swami was already dead.
Michelle took over the cult leadership until a week later when she was arrested for murder. The Swami had been poisoned with cyanide.
cards.mystery: How did Michelle poison a man who had sworn not to eat anything?
clues: The Swami followed a deadly routine.
In some cases, the cure is worse than the disease.
story: Driven by ambition, Michelle wanted to take over the cult. She knew that Rusty Morishi, otherwise known as the Swami, would sooner or later faint from hunger. When that finally happened, Michelle was ready.

When she heard of his collapse, Michelle took a vial of liquid smelling salts and dropped in a cyanide pellet. While she pretended to revive him, she was really sticking the vial under his nose and making him inhale the fatal gas.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that instead of reviving the Swami, Michelle was killing him with poisoned smelling salts.

cards.title: Caribou Mating Season
case: There weren't many females living in Caribou, Alaska, so Biff felt really lucky when Eileen, the woman at the bar, fell for his corny come-on lines. She and Biff left the bar together and dove into a whirlwind romance. A month later, Biff's oil company sent him on a trip to their headquarters in Texas.
At the end of two weeks, Biff returned to Alaska. On that same night, his body was found less than a mile from the airfield. His head was bashed in.
Eileen eventually confessed to the murder, but refused to explain why she did it.
cards.mystery: Reconstruct that fateful night. Why did Eileen kill Biff?
clues: The sun shines brighter in Texas than in Alaska.
Eileen noticed something about one of Biff's lines — and it wasn't a come-on.
story: During their month-long romance, Biff had neglected to tell Eileen about his wife and kids back in Dallas.

On his return flight to Caribou, the married man once again removed his wedding band. What he couldn't remove, however, was the 1/4-inch pale line around his finger where his wedding band had been. The hot Texas sun had given him a very noticeable tan line.

When Eileen picked him up at the airfield, she noticed the tan line and immediately knew the truth. She then grabbed the baseball bat she always kept in the back seat for protection. She didn't have a lot of swinging room, but it was enough.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that when Eileen noticed the tan line around Biff's ring finger, she realized that he was a married man and killed him.

cards.title: Dirty Politics
case: A controversial, ambitious senator is murdered in a public place.
cards.mystery: Who was the man? Who killed him, and why?
clues: The victim had been a war hero.
It was a mid-month murder.
story: On March 15, 44 B.C., Julius Caesar was stabbed to death in the senate house by his friend and protégé, Marcus Junius Brutus, and several others. Despite Caesar's heroism and reforms, his power as dictator for life caused great resentment among his enemies and even some of his friends. It was an early, and very famous case of political back-stabbing.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the dead man was Julius Caesar, stabbed to death in a political conspiracy by Brutus and several others.

cards.title: A Time to Die
case: Three people are murdered in neighboring towns, all by the same method. Near each body is a stopped clock. When the police investigate the scenes, they happen to notice that each clock is set at exactly the same time.
cards.mystery: Why were the clocks set at the same time? How were the three victims killed?
clues: The police had trouble "producing" the criminal.
Each clock was set at 12:00 — 12:00 — 12:00.
story: Rob Doyle was a TV producer with a grudge. His prime time special had just received disastrous reviews from the three most influential critics in town, making him the laughing-stock of L.A. Rob swore revenge. In his basement, he rigged up a special videocassette tape that was capable of short-circuiting an electrical system.

A few days later, when the critics came home and opened their mail, they found a package supposedly from a network head's office. The enclosed letter read: "You are my favorite critic. Please review the enclosed tape. It's our newest project and I would love to hear your opinion."

Eagerly, each critic slipped the cassette into his VCR. But something went wrong — the tapes got stuck and wouldn't play. They ejected their tapes to examine them. But as they touched the tapes to pull them out, they completed the circuit, electrocuting themselves and causing a power surge. Each body was found lying in front of the VCR — each machine's clock flashing 12:00.
cards.specialInformation: The clocks stopped at the time of the murders, but the murders were not committed at the same time. There was no power failure, just a power surge.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the three victims were electrocuted by a specially rigged videocassette, causing a power surge which reset the clocks on their VCRs to 12:00.

cards.title: Greetings, Adios!
case: Suddenly, and without warning, hundreds of people over a multi-state area are dead from cyanide poisoning. Many of the deaths occur simultaneously. After much investigation, the case is solved by a deputy sheriff in central Alabama who arrests a local female clerical worker for the mass murders.
cards.mystery: What did the victims have in common? Who killed them, how, and why?
clues: All of the victims were members of a group.
The victims were planning a get-together.
story: All of the victims were members of a Southern televangelist's church. An inside job was immediately suspected, because the Tuscaloosa headquarters had recently sent out mailings to all church members announcing an upcoming revival meeting.

Angela, a disgruntled follower of the flock, had been jilted by one of its more insensitive members. In her irrational rage, she blamed not only him, but the whole church-going "family," and swore revenge on them all.

Since Angela worked as a filing clerk at the headquarters, it was relatively simple for her to sprinkle cyanide dust on the gummed edge of the RSVP return envelopes enclosed with the invitations. With deadly consistency, the recipients discovered too late that just one lick did the trick. All those who RSVP'd quickly RIP'd.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the murderer was a disgruntled member of a televangelist's church who worked at their headquarters. She sent out invitations to church members and dusted the gummed edge of the RSVP return envelopes with cyanide.

cards.title: Show Off
case: Despite the fact that his wife Ruby has been missing for two weeks, abstract artist Hugh Brown is hosting an art show in his studio. Suddenly a police officer enters the studio, conducts a brief investigation, and places Hugh under arrest for Ruby's murder.
cards.mystery: On what evidence was Hugh arrested for polishing Ruby off?
clues: Hugh was handy with his sculpting tools.
The officer brought a friend of Ruby's with him.
story: Hugh, a sculptor, had discovered that Ruby was secretly posing nude for several of his professional rivals. A bitter argument ensued in Hugh's studio, during which he stabbed Ruby to death with a chisel. As her final resting place, Hugh chose the piece he was finishing for his upcoming show: an abstract bronze cube. Hugh squeezed Ruby into his cube and welded it shut, figuring his secret was eternally safe.

The police officer arrived with Ruby's dog. After Ruby's disappearance, the dog wouldn't go near Hugh. A sympathetic and suspicious neighbor took the dog in, and reported its strange behavior to the police. On a hunch, the officer brought the dog to the studio and coaxed him inside. After some sniffing, the dog stopped at the cube and barked loudly. The cube was pried open and Ruby's remains were revealed, proving that all is not well that ends weld.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Hugh stabbed Ruby, then welded her into his sculpted cube, where her dog sniffed her out.

cards.title: Nobody Loses Her Head
case: At the No-Thrills Sideshow, Thelma Nobody, "The Woman Without a Body," was a popular draw. The trick was done with mirrors, of course — until that fateful morning when she was actually found without a body. Her head was discovered first, cut off with an ax belonging to Tony the Knife Thrower.

The police later found other parts of Thelma's corpse spread out around the sideshow grounds, all except for one piece. It seems that the killer purposely hid or destroyed one particular part of Thelma's body.
cards.mystery: Who dismembered the body? What part of Thelma was missing, and why?
clues: Thelma was buried without that favorite necklace of hers.
Some sideshow performers have unique physical attributes.
story: Jerry Twelvefingers, the sideshow piano player, was desperately in love with Thelma. She was a flirt and enjoyed the attention, but she had no plans to get involved with the ugly, twelve-fingered fellow.

Jerry didn't take Thelma's rejection of him well. After he finished strangling her, Jerry saw that he had left bruises on her throat — 12 telltale bruises that could only be from his distinctive hands. He had to get rid of that neck!
By cutting up the body and spreading around the pieces, Jerry hoped to draw attention away from the missing neck. That way, maybe he could save his own!
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that a man with extra fingers dismembered Thelma's body in order to draw attention away from her missing neck. The neck had to be destroyed because it held the imprint of his extra digits which would "finger" him as the killer.

cards.title: The Awesome Arson
case: Awesome Imports has gone bankrupt. The company's warehouse is padlocked until the inventory can be sold at auction. Only the court-appointed receiver has the keys. But Eric, the owner, gets lucky. A fire starts in the securely locked warehouse, burning down the building and all of its contents. The insurance money will pay off the company's debts and leave a tidy profit, too.
The police are sure that Eric torched his business for the insurance money. What they can't figure out is how he got inside the warehouse to do it.
cards.mystery: How did Eric Awesome torch his padlocked warehouse?
clues: Eric suddenly got interested in astronomy.
A pile of grass skirts was near a window.
story: Eric never entered the warehouse to burn it down, but he did buy a large telescope and removed its biconvex lens used to focus light.

Shortly before the courts padlocked the building, the diabolical Eric uncrated a shipment of Hawaiian grass skirts and placed them near a rear window. Then a week later, on a sunny day, he stood outside the warehouse window and used the lens to focus sunlight onto the highly flammable grass skirts. The window glass cut much of the intensity, but it was still enough to set the skirts on fire. Aloha, Awesome Imports!
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Eric did not enter the padlocked warehouse to burn it down. He stood outside the building's window and set highly flammable material inside on fire by focusing sunlight through a powerful telescope lens.

cards.title: Color Me Dead
case: During the trial, two key pieces of evidence are a can of black paint and a can of white paint.
cards.mystery: Who's on trial? What was the crime? How and why was it committed?
clues: The people on trial are a band of eco-terrorists.
The crime scene was on the newly-opened Foggy Bend road.
story: The Green Guerrillas were a band of eco-terrorists that sought revenge from the county that had built a new road through a wetlands area.

At four a.m., the terrorists blocked off the new section of Foggy Bend road from traffic with detour signs. At the road's hairpin turn, they used black paint to eliminate the white lines down the center of the road; with the white paint they redrew the center line, aiming it straight off the edge of the road and into the soggy wetlands below.
After the detour signs were removed, traffic began to move on the sabotaged road. As always, there was a thick fog on the road and the drivers had to follow the white line.

By the time the police arrived, a total of 33 vehicles had piled up in the worst traffic disaster in state history. The accident also resulted in two deaths and charges of murder to the band of terrorists.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that eco-terrorists are on trial for murder. They sabotaged a foggy road's white lines with paint, thereby luring cars over an embankment and causing a disastrous traffic accident that resulted in two deaths.

cards.title: A Crime of Fashion
case: Petite Missy Clark, a wedding consultant at a chic department store, is found dead and hanging from a hook.
cards.mystery: Who killed Missy, how, and why?
clues: Missy needed all the commissions she could get.
The bride-to-be had three parents.
story: Ginny Malcolm, the bride-to-be, had two mothers: her biological mother and her stepmother. Greedy little Missy had knowingly sold both the ex-Mrs. Malcolm, mother of the bride, and the new Mrs. Malcolm, stepmother of the bride, the same $4,000 original designer dress for the wedding. Her motive was the huge commission on a quick $8,000 sale.

The local newspaper crucified the ex-Mrs. Malcolm, a size 14 going on 20, labeling her a "fashion victim." They called the new Mrs. Malcolm, ten years younger and four sizes smaller, a "fashion sensation."

Disgraced and humiliated, Mrs. "ex" went to the department store just before closing time on the following Saturday, to wreak revenge on Missy. Feigning friendliness, Mrs. "ex" picked out an expensive dress, knowing Missy would accompany her into the fitting room. Once there, Mrs. "ex" pulled the protective plastic clothing bag over Missy's head, tied it tightly, and hung Missy on a clothes hook by the back of her bra. Missy suffocated, then hung around through the weekend until she surprised an unsuspecting shopper on Monday morning.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the ex-Mrs. Malcolm suffocated Missy in the dressing room because Missy had humiliated her by selling her and the new Mrs. Malcolm the same dress for their daughter's wedding.

cards.title: An Alarming Experience
case: A neighbor finds Mr. and Mrs. Cranlon, a security-obsessed suburban couple, tied up in their living room in the middle of the afternoon. They had been robbed.
cards.mystery: How did the thieves get past the Cranlons' state-of-the-art security system?
clues: The Cranlons were retired and living on a fixed income.
Mildred Cranlon got lots of junk mail.
story: Mildred Cranlon entered every sweepstakes that came in the mail — so many that she could never remember the particulars of each. Her husband, Robert, was aware only that the pile of junk mail got higher and higher each month.

One afternoon, when the doorbell rang, Mildred peeked through the viewer in the door and saw two respectable-looking young men with a placard that read: "Congratulations! You've just won $10,000,000!" She then looked out the window and saw a van, with "Money Mobile" painted on the side, parked in front of the house. Thinking she had finally hit the jackpot, Mildred and Robert turned off the security system and opened the front door. Once inside, the men held them up at gunpoint, then tied them up and cleaned them out.

Although they later painted their van and changed the license plates, the crooks were caught when an ear-splitting high-tech alarm they had stolen from the Cranlons went off accidentally and could not be shut off. When the police told them they had a right to remain silent, they shouted, "Wha-a-a-t?"
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the robbers posed as sweepstakes people who had come to award the Cranlons a big cash prize, and gained entrance to the house when the Cranlons shut off their alarm.

cards.title: Oxford Don
case: Donald Cartwright, arrogant lawyer, is found dead in a store. The murder weapon, in plain sight, is never discovered.
cards.mystery: Who killed Donald, and how?
clues: Cartwright's body was sitting in a chair.
Cartwright had been a prosecuting attorney.
story: Jeff Dandridge, unjustly convicted of manslaughter, had left prison after serving ten years, changed his name and found a job selling shoes. One night while Jeff was alone in the store, Donald Cartwright, the prosecuting attorney who had put him away, came in for a pair of Oxfords.
Cartwright obviously didn't recognize Jeff, so he couldn't have suspected that he was about to pay the steepest possible price for sending Jeff up the river.

While getting Cartwright's shoes in the stockroom, Jeff removed the leather lace from one shoe and palmed it. As Cartwright donned the new Oxfords, Jeff moved behind Cartwright and strangled him with the lace. Satisfied that justice had finally been served, Jeff put the lace back into the shoe on Cartwright's foot and tied it. He then left the store and the city, never to be heard from again. The shoe was now on the other foot.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Cartwright was strangled with a leather shoelace by the innocent man he had sent to prison.

cards.title: Down and Out
case: A man is found unconscious on the floor. His clothing is scorched.
cards.mystery: What happened to the man?
clues: There are many little footprints outside the house.
The man is near the fireplace.
story: T'was the night before Christmas, and all through the house was the strong, smoky odor of Santa's red blouse.

Tired after a long journey, Santa forgot to check a chimney before climbing in. A fire was going and Santa was overcome by the smoke. Upstairs, little Justin and Katie heard a strange "thud." They quietly sneaked downstairs and peeked into the living room. Much to their surprise, they spotted Santa "asleep" on the floor.

Unsure of what to do, they finally began tugging on his fluffy white beard. Santa awoke with a start, then managed to cough up a hoarse "Ho-ho-ho!" After some milk and cookies, Santa felt better. He thanked the children and then magically disappeared — through the front door!
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the unconscious man was Santa Claus, who had fainted from fireplace fumes as he climbed down a chimney.

cards.title: Crossing to the Other Side
case: Senator Sherman's car had just pulled onto the long suspension bridge when it went wildly out of control. The car careened across the divider and slammed into oncoming traffic. The bulletproof windows were up and the doors locked. Inside was the Senator, dead — shot once through the head. No gun was found in the car.
cards.mystery: Who killed the Senator? What was the motive? And how could he have been shot in a locked car?
clues: Crossing the bridge took its toll on the Senator.
The Senator was a driven man.
story: It wasn't Senator Sherman who was the target. It was his chauffeur, Rocko.
Rocko was a heavy gambler who was behind in his payments to a local loan shark. After weeks of excuses, the greedy moneylender decided Rocko must pay — with his life!

The assassin-to-be was disguised as a tollbooth attendant when the limousine approached the bridge. Rocko was just about to pay the toll when the killer pulled the gun. Rocko quickly pressed the button to close the electric window and floored the accelerator, causing the killer to misfire into the back seat — and unfortunately into the Senator. Rocko, who lost control of the car, was knocked out in the accident, but when he regained consciousness, he told the police everything!
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the chauffeur was the target, not the Senator. The killer was a loan shark disguised as a tollbooth attendant who was "paying back" the chauffeur for not paying him back! The killer fired through the open electric window just as it was automatically closing.

cards.title: Screaming Mimi
case: Mimi McKay, a cut-throat Hollywood gossip columnist, is found dead in the water.
cards.mystery: Who murdered Mimi, how, and why?
clues: Mimi had made a late appointment for a massage and whirlpool.
The whirlpool attendant was found unconscious.
story: Mimi McKay had recently called actor Hamilton Alexander a has-been in her much-read column. The column had cost him the lead in a hot new film, and Hamilton wanted to kill her. But it was his wife Stephanie who shut Mimi up for good.

Stephanie, a chemist, went to the same health spa as Mimi. She knew Mimi, but Mimi didn't know her. When Stephanie overheard the columnist making a late appointment for a massage and whirlpool, she went to her lab, then returned to the spa. First, she knocked the whirlpool attendant unconscious from behind, and hid her in the towel closet. Then she dumped a large container of hydrochloric acid into the whirlpool.

When Mimi arrived, Stephanie pushed her into the whirlpool and quickly ran out the back door. Mimi was instantly burned to death by the searing acid. Never again would she call anyone "all washed up."
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Mimi wrote a degrading article about an actor. For revenge, the actor's chemist wife burned Mimi to death by dumping acid into the whirlpool at their health spa, and pushing Mimi in.

cards.title: The Lead Anniversary
case: Eileen was happy! Today was her wedding anniversary. To celebrate, she and her husband Bobby went for a long ride in the country, followed by a picnic on a secluded riverbank. Sometime during the meal, Eileen returned to the car, retrieved Bobby's revolver from the glove compartment and fired four slugs into her startled husband.
cards.mystery: What made Eileen kill her husband?
clues: Eileen smelled a rat.
The blanket couldn't quite "cover up" Bobby's activities.
story: One of Bobby's favorite pastimes was getting romantic on a blanket outdoors in the fresh summer air. Eileen, herself, was looking forward to this sweet ending to their picnic. But as soon as Bobby took the blanket from the car trunk and spread it on the grass, Eileen smelled her sister's distinctive perfume. It was coming from the blanket! This could mean only one thing: her sister Della had been on this blanket with Bobby!
When the insanely jealous Eileen questioned Bobby about Della, she could tell he was lying. She had forgotten to bring a carving knife to the picnic, so she had to make do with a Colt .45.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Eileen killed her husband because she smelled her sister's distinctive perfume on the picnic blanket and knew that he had had a romantic interlude on it with her sister.

cards.title: Beach Bummer
case: Bonnie is found dead on a beach. Upon investigating a nearby motel room, police arrest Clyde, its occupant, for her murder. Among the incriminating evidence are a partially-used bottle of sleeping pills, white paint and a brush.
cards.mystery: How was Bonnie murdered?
clues: Clyde took liberties with a label.
Clyde was burned up at Bonnie; his revenge burned Bonnie up, too.
story: Bonnie and her husband Clyde were vacationing in Myrtle Beach while Bonnie participated in yet another beauty contest. The night before, while Bonnie was in for a facial, Clyde visited the motel bar. There he overheard the upcoming contest's emcee reciting the names of contestants who were trying to influence him with sexual favors. Near the top of the list was (you guessed it) Clyde's wife, Bonnie!
Seething with anger, Clyde returned to the motel room with a tube of white acrylic paint and a bottle of #2 sunscreen. He then secretly painted a "0" after the "2" on the sunscreen's label.

The next morning, before Bonnie left for her first sunbathing session on the beach, Clyde slipped three sleeping pills into her coffee. He then convinced her to use the "20" sunscreen "to protect her skin." Bonnie drank the coffee, slathered on the sunscreen and hit the beach, where she immediately fell fast asleep for several hours. Bonnie died of a third-degree sunburn — and Clyde took the heat.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Bonnie died from an acute sunburn prompted by Clyde's tampering with the sunscreen label and her coffee.

cards.title: Pushing the Envelope
case: Violet is found dead in her home with an envelope in her hand. During their investigation, police discover a bottle at the home of her boyfriend, Dusty. On this and other evidence, they arrest Dusty for Violet's murder.
cards.mystery: How did Dusty "dust" Violet?
clues: What killed Violet was her oversensitivity.
The buzz was that Dusty stole the bottle.
story: Finally fed up with Dusty's rotten temper, Violet was cutting him loose. During their final argument, Dusty swore he'd make her pay — and he meant it.

After the argument, just before leaving Violet's house, Dusty secretly transferred her bottle of bee-sting antidote from her purse to his pocket. (Violet had a severe allergy to bees.) He then picked up a dozen roses from the local flower shop — and several bees from his garden. Dusty hid the bees in the box with the roses, attached an envelope with an unsigned card, and sent the "farewell gift" to Violet's home.

When Violet opened the box, she was immediately stung by the bees. She died of shock and respiratory failure while searching desperately for her missing antidote, the card and envelope still in her hand. Police found the bees in her house, then dusted the box for fingerprints and discovered Dusty's. Finding Violet's antidote in Dusty's home gave police the evidence they needed. Dusty was clever but careless, and had pushed the envelope a bit too far.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Dusty stole Violet's bottle of bee sting antidote, and caused her death by sending her a box of flowers with bees hidden inside.

cards.title: Gorgeous George
case: The officer serving the search warrant found the metal rectangle he was looking for, and arrested Mike for George's murder.
cards.mystery: What was the metal rectangle?
clues: George "fell" for Mike's clever switch.
Mike was at the end of his rope when he hatched his plot.
story: Each year, George challenged Mike to join him in another brainless, daredevil adventure. Last year it was bullfighting; the year before it was hang gliding. This year, George announced that the two of them would bungee jump off the bridge at Gruesome Gorge. Fed up with these reckless adventures, Mike said "No way."

George replied that if Mike backed out, he'd tell Mike's wife about Mike's fling with a chambermaid in Tijuana the year before. The threat sent Mike off the deep end. Desperate and angry, he visited the bridge at Gruesome Gorge. A popular place for bungee jumping, the bridge sported a rectangular metal marker which read "777 FEET ABOVE RIVER." He then replaced it with a marker that read "888 FEET ABOVE RIVER."

When the day arrived, Mike dared George to jump first. George obliged, and learned the hard way that his jump was over 100 feet too long. The officer discovered the original metal marker in Mike's house, and jumped to the right conclusion.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Mike caused George's death by switching elevation markers before his bungee jump. The officer found the original marker in Mike's house.

cards.title: Sock It to Me
case: Willie is found dead in a field. His wife is arrested when a sock belonging to Willie is examined, along with a container of starch belonging to his wife.
cards.mystery: How did Willie's wife waste him?
clues: The sock was not part of a pair.
Willie's last landing wasn't exactly a breeze.
story: Willie was an airplane pilot who spent lots of time towing advertising banners. His jealous wife had recently learned that while Willie winged it with a banner touting a local beauty contest, he was also taking several of the contestants for joy rides.

Willie took off and landed on a narrow asphalt strip bounded on each side by a treacherously steep gorge. Essential to safe maneuvering was his wind direction indicator, a windsock. After Willie took off on his next flight, his wife used cornstarch to convert the limp windsock into a stiff triangle, indicating a wind direction 90 degrees off actual bearing. Willie missed the strip on his landing, and plunged to his death in a field below.

Officials became suspicious when they spotted the windsock standing at attention in the absence of any wind. When they traced the cornstarch to an empty box in Willie's widow's wastebasket, it was "plane" that she was the culprit.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Willie was a pilot whose wife starched his windsock, causing him to misread the wind direction and to crash his plane.

cards.title: Cold Clash
case: Captain William Fremont, a handsome 20-year-old, is found dead in the snow. His murder is never detected.
cards.mystery: How was Fremont killed? And why was his murder undetected?
clues: William came from a wealthy family.
History has recorded it as a particularly bitter winter.
story: William Fremont was a captain in George Washington's Continental Army, stationed at Valley Forge during the bitter winter of 1778. Like many other southern gentlemen, when William joined the fight he brought along his indentured servant. Joe, the servant, hated his master and yearned for a better life. Joe figured that if the war didn't kill William, the winter would. And then Joe would be free.

But as the war and the winter lived on, so did William, and Joe decided to take matters into his own hands. Joe found some wild oleander, which he knew was poisonous. That evening, Joe brought William his meager dinner, garnished with plenty of the poison. William ate heartily and died quickly. The murder was never detected because so many soldiers died of exposure that winter at Valley Forge. In the meantime, Joe slyly worked his way up north and became a free man.
cards.specialInformation: Oleander is an evergreen with poisonous sap and leaves.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that William's indentured servant poisoned his food at Valley Forge during the winter of 1778, to gain his freedom. The murder was undetected because so many soldiers died of exposure that winter.

cards.title: The Crime Wave
case: Union Camp has always been a peaceful town, with no crime other than the occasional stolen library book. But recently, strange things have been happening. Last week, the town clerk's office was broken into. Two days ago, a dog was shot and killed for no apparent reason. And today Jim, the local mail carrier, was attacked with a baseball bat and wound up in the hospital with 20 stitches.
"We got us a regular crime wave," the neighbors complained. "What's going on here?"
cards.mystery: What is going on in Union Camp?
clues: The murdered dog had belonged to the mail carrier.
Unknowingly, Jim was hiding something that someone wanted.
story: The Taggert brothers were local boys with a passion for Civil War history. In the library's document collection, they came across an old diary that mentioned a buried cache of gold bullion. According to the diary, retreating Union soldiers had buried the gold in a nearby field to prevent it from falling into Confederate hands.

To pinpoint the location, the Taggerts broke into the clerk's office and stole a 130-year-old property map. From this, they deduced that the gold was buried on the mail carrier's property. They then killed Jim's dog so it wouldn't alert the neighbors by barking. Finally, they put on ski masks and attacked the mail carrier with baseball bats.
With Jim in the hospital and his dog out of the way, the Taggerts were confident of being able to sneak onto his land undisturbed, and dig for the buried gold.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that two men looking for buried treasure stole a map from the town clerk's office. Deducing that the treasure was on the mail carrier's property, they killed his dog so it wouldn't bark, then beat up the mail carrier to send him to the hospital, so that they could dig for the treasure undisturbed.

cards.title: Mind Bender
case: Jacques dies in the hospital. The doctor who treats him notices something unusual, and reports it to the police. Later, Jacques' partner Cal is arrested for murder.
cards.mystery: How did Jacques die? What did the doctor notice, and why was Cal arrested?
clues: Jacques and Cal had been searching for treasure.
The doctor made a "timely" discovery.
story: The victim, Jacques Gusto, and his partner Cal Ipso were diving together far offshore at a depth of 200 feet, looking for sunken treasure. Cal had spotted the gold — but instead of telling Jacques, he planned an "accident" for him so he could keep the loot for himself.

Before their next dive, Cal tinkered with Jacques' diving watch to slow its movement. Then Cal feigned illness, knowing that daredevil Jacques would foolishly dive alone. Because his watch was slow, Jacques stayed down much longer than he should have for a safe dive. Not realizing the length of his dive would require him to decompress as he ascended, Jacques came up too fast and developed a severe case of the bends. By the time the boat docked and Jacques was rushed to the hospital, it was too late.
What the alert doctor noticed was that Jacques' watch was running more slowly than his own. Police found Cal's fingerprints inside the watch, and it was only a matter of time before Cal confessed.
cards.specialInformation: Divers can contract the bends when they stay down longer than safe limits allow, and ascend to the surface without decompressing. Nitrogen bubbles form in the bloodstream, joints and tissues, which is excruciating and can be fatal. The immediate cause of death is cardiac arrest or stroke.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the doctor noticed that Jacques' diving watch was running slowly. Cal had slowed its movement, resulting in Jacques' death from a severe case of the bends.

cards.title: Track Attack
case: A man lies dead on a track. Near his body is a shard of glass.
cards.mystery: Who murdered the man, and how?
clues: Tracks can be tricky, depending on how you look at them.
Upon reflection, the driver should have seen the problem.
story: The track is the Indianapolis 500, and the man was the number-one pole-positioned driver, Mario Confetti. Mario's wife and the lead pit-crewman were having an affair, and contrived an "accident" to take Mario out of the picture permanently.

As the race began, spectators noticed that Mario was coming treacherously close to other cars during passing maneuvers. When Mario attempted a tricky inside pass, he sideswiped a third car and slammed into the wall at terminal speed. Among pieces recovered from the accident were shards of glass from Mario's side-view mirrors.

Mario's wife and her lover had secretly replaced the flat side-view mirrors with convex ones, so that Mario's opponents would seem much farther away than they really were. They used carbolic acid to burn off the notice: "Objects are closer than they appear." Mario didn't notice the switch, though he was starting to wonder — too late — why passing was the pits.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Mario's wife and her lover replaced the flat glass in his car's side-view mirrors with convex ones, causing Mario to sideswipe a car fatally that appeared to be safely to his rear.

cards.title: Class Act
case: Buzzy's body is found near his dormitory on a prep school campus. His roommate, Chip, is arrested for the murder.
cards.mystery: How and why did Chip bump Buzzy off?
clues: Chip had a "relatively" good reason to resent his roommate.
Buzzy had the right time, but the wrong story.
story: Chip knew that Buzzy was having a very secretive affair with someone. Each Tuesday, Buzzy's alarm clock would ring at 1:45 a.m., whereupon Buzzy would sneak out of the dorm by backing out of the window of their first-story room. Chip did not know that the someone was his own mother, until he spotted her name on a credit card that Buzzy had begun using.

The shock of Buzzy's betrayal, and of Chip's mother's unfaithfulness to his father, made Chip wild with thoughts of revenge. The next Tuesday, Chip slipped a mild sedative into Buzzy's bedtime soda. It was just enough to keep Buzzy asleep as Chip later carried him (and his alarm clock) up to an unoccupied sixth-story dorm room and into a similarly-situated bed.

When the alarm clock rang at 1:45, a fuzzy Buzzy backed out of the window and dropped six stories to his death. The sedative in Buzzy's soda was traced to Chip through his fingerprints, telling the true story of the "switched stories."
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Buzzy was having an affair with Chip's mother. Seeking revenge, Chip drugged Buzzy and moved him to the sixth story of their dorm, and Buzzy fell to his death when he backed out of the window.

cards.title: The Crafty Klepto of Central Park
case: For weeks, visitors to New York City's Central Park have been attacked and their jewelry stolen. The mugger's method is to knock out the victim from behind, then make off with all of his or her valuables. Searches of exiting park patrons turn up nothing. After much head-scratching, the investigating officer makes a brilliant deduction, and the crook is finally arrested.
cards.mystery: Who was the crook? On what evidence was the crook finally caught?
clues: The officer's inspiration came to him out of the blue.
The crook worked in the park.
story: The crook was one of the park's hot dog vendors. Concealed in his pushcart was a small flock of well-trained homing pigeons, each with a little bag strapped to its feet. After robbing each victim, the hot dog vendor would slip the booty into a bag, then send the pigeon back to its cage on the roof of his home.

Hoping for a break, the officer decided to check people entering the park as well as leaving it. The man's pigeons were seen hidden in the pushcart, bags and all. The man's house was searched, and the stolen jewelry inside the bird bags bagged the cagey thief.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the thief was a hot dog vendor, who placed the stolen jewelry in bags attached to his homing pigeons' feet.

cards.title: Dead Ringer
case: A man is dead in a ring on a sunny afternoon. The man responsible for his death is arrested nearby with a small object in his hand.
cards.mystery: Who killed the man? What was the object, and what part did it play in his death?
clues: The man was killed in an act of blind rage.
Police made a bull's-eye by arresting the perpetrator immediately.
story: The dead man was a bullfighter, and his killer was the bull he was fighting. The man responsible was a professional adversary who aimed to stage an "accident" that would permanently knock the bullfighter out of the ring.

The man sat in the stands as his victim performed, aiming a small mirror at the bull's eyes. The reflection from the sun temporarily blinded and confused the bull. The bullfighter, unaware of the bull's plight, continued to yell, "Toro! Toro!" Finally, the enraged bull made a "dead run" toward the bullfighter's voice, goring him in a fatal finish.
A spectator reported the man with the mirror to the police, who "took the bull by the horns" and arrested him before he could escape.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that a rival in the stands used a mirror to blind and confuse the bull, causing it to charge in the direction of the bullfighter's voice and gore him to death.

cards.title: Marbelous Marvin
case: Marvin is found dead near a bicycle surrounded by marbles.
cards.mystery: Who killed Marvin, and how?
clues: Too late, Marvin realized the gravity of the situation.
Marvin had a rival who was a little off-balance.
story: Tip Moore had been famous for his circus high-wire act until Marvin Lee joined the troupe. Marvin's balancing bicycle feats on a higher wire had made him a headliner, and Tip a has-been. But Tip had a plan to recapture the spotlight.

After dark, Tip sneaked under the big top and removed the special non-rolling lead ballast that weighted the ends of Marvin's balance bar. He then replaced the ballast with four pounds of marbles, and returned the bar to the rafters where it was stored.

During Marvin's next performance, Tip tossed the bar to him as always, after Marvin mounted the bike on the wire. Marvin tilted in vain to stabilize his balance, while the marbles rolled wildly in his bar. Finally, Marvin plummeted to the concrete floor below, losing not only his marbles, but his life as well. Matching marbles found in Tip's trailer tipped off the police, who promptly put Tip behind bars.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Marvin's rival planted marbles in the balancing bar Marvin used in his high-wire bicycle act, causing his death by throwing him off-balance.

cards.title: Goodbye, Dolly!
case: Aging millionaire Elmore Channing III hobbles out to the front lawn of his elegant mansion. Dolly, his beautiful young mistress, is walking toward her car. "Please come back, Dolly," the sick old man pleads. "I'll do anything. I'll even marry you!"
Dolly stops and turns toward Elmore. "Well, it's about time!" she says as she follows him back to the mansion. "I want to get married soon!"
That night the millionaire dies in his library. Days later, Dolly is found in a distant motel with $50,000 hidden in a sack. She is arrested for murder.
