cards.mystery: How and why did Dolly kill the rich old codger?
clues: The millionaire's library was a "safe" place.
Dolly wanted to give back a little to gain a lot.
story: Elderly tycoon Elmore Channing III had been promising to marry mistress Dolly Dollerz for two years. Tired of waiting, she stole $50,000 from Elmore's library safe, and was making her getaway when Elmore stopped her with his sudden marriage proposal. Dolly realized that instead of a mere $50,000, she'd have access to millions by marrying Elmore and waiting for him to die. She accepted.

That night, Dolly crept down to the library to return Elmore's money before he discovered it missing. But Elmore was a light sleeper and caught Dolly as she was putting back the cash. Ironically, he assumed she was stealing from him and threatened to have her arrested. Dolly grabbed the fireplace poker and used it to change his mind with a sharp blow to the head. Unfortunately, the poker was too persuasive and Elmore dropped to the floor — dead! Since marriage was then out of the question, Dolly again took the $50,000 and fled.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Dolly had stolen $50,000 from Elmore, then secretly tried to return it after Elmore promised to marry her. Ironically, Elmore caught Dolly putting back the cash and threatened to have her arrested, so she killed him.

cards.title: The Master Plan
case: Late one evening, Lord Flauntit is in his study watching television. He rings a little bell and Jasper, his butler, enters the room. The master and servant have a brief conversation, at the end of which Jasper gives his notice.

At midnight, a fire breaks out at Flauntit Hall. When the firefighters arrive, they find Jasper's body spread-eagle on the gravel driveway. He is quite dead. The firefighters assume that in his panic to escape the fire, Jasper jumped out of his third story bedroom window and broke his neck in the fall.
The firefighters easily put out the small blaze and then call the constable. The entire county is shocked when respectable Lord Flauntit is later arrested for arson and murder.
cards.mystery: Why did Lord Flauntit kill Jasper and set the fire?
clues: It was Jasper's lucky day, and his unlucky day!
In case of fire, find your most valuable possession.
story: Lord Flauntit knew that Jasper, his loyal servant, always played the same numbers in the lottery. That night on the news, the winning numbers were announced and the master knew immediately that Jasper had won ten million pounds. He rang for his servant and when the excited lottery winner entered the room, the two of them discussed Jasper's plans for a life of leisure. But Lord Flauntit had other plans for Jasper's winnings. Flauntit was on the verge of bankruptcy and desperately needed to acquire the winning lottery ticket. But how? Jasper had hidden the ticket well until he could cash it in.

Lord Flauntit reasoned that a small fire would serve two purposes. It would scare Jasper into retrieving his ticket and would also make Jasper's "fall" from the window more plausible. The master started the fire in a hall wastebasket. When he heard Jasper rummaging around in his room, Flauntit burst in on his servant, clubbed him senseless, stole his ticket and pushed him headfirst out of the window.
A local barmaid also knew of Jasper's winning numbers. When Lord Flauntit tried to cash in the ticket, she went straight to the coppers.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Lord Flauntit killed Jasper to obtain his lottery ticket. The fire was set to scare Jasper into retrieving the ticket and to help disguise the murder.

cards.title: Card Sharks
case: Ralph wants to visit a psychic, but he doesn't know any good ones, so he visits a Psychic Referral Counselor. The counselor charges Ralph $100, then recommends Madame Zuzu. The counselor then proceeds to offer proof of Madame Zuzu's talent.

The counselor pulls out a deck of cards and asks Ralph to pick a card at random. The counselor then looks at Ralph's card and tells Ralph to concentrate mentally on that card. She then dials a long-distance number and says, "I'd like to speak with Madame Zuzu please." After a pause, the counselor says, "Madame Zuzu, please tell the gentleman what card he has picked." The counselor hands Ralph the phone and Madame Zuzu tells him "the four of diamonds," which is correct.
cards.mystery: Madame Zuzu is not really a psychic and the Psychic Referral Counselor is a fraud. Explain their trick.
clues: Madame Zuzu spoke to the counselor before the counselor spoke to Madame Zuzu.
It's not what the counselor said, but when she said it.
story: Madame Zuzu and the Psychic Referral Counselor are con artists. After Ralph picked the four of diamonds at random from the card deck, the counselor called her associate, Madame Zuzu, on the phone. As soon as Madame Zuzu picked up the phone — but before the counselor said a word — Madame Zuzu began calling out the card suits. When she said "diamonds," the counselor interrupted her by saying, "I'd like to speak with Madame Zuzu please." Madame Zuzu then knew that the correct suit was "diamonds."

Madame Zuzu immediately began calling out card numbers from Ace to King. When she reached the number "four," the counselor interrupted her again by saying, "Madame Zuzu, please tell the gentleman what card he has picked." Madame Zuzu then knew that the correct card number was "four."

Using this verbal code, the crafty counselor and the sneaky psychic cheated their clients out of considerable cash. If Madame Zuzu had been psychic, she might have known that Ralph was an undercover cop and that her clever con was kaput!
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Madame Zuzu and the Psychic Referral Counselor used a verbal code to trick Ralph. While on the phone, Madame Zuzu quickly called out card suits, and the counselor interrupted her when she reached the chosen suit. The same code was used to determine the chosen card number.

cards.title: Lights Out!
case: A woman lies dead in a room. The room has a window, but there is no light. She has been murdered.
cards.mystery: Where is she and why was she killed?
clues: The room once had a view, but not always the same one.
The killer needed a quick change.
story: The murder took place on the Titanic. The dead woman is in her cabin, inside the ship at the bottom of the ocean. When the ship began sinking, it was announced that women and children would be first to board the lifeboats. This didn't sit well with a cowering creep named Kurt. Determined to stay alive, Kurt decided to disguise himself as a woman.

Feverishly searching the slanted deck for a lady his own size, Kurt spotted a large chorus girl wearing a blonde wig. He cornered the woman in her cabin and insisted that she disrobe and de-wig. When she resisted, he persisted and crowned her with a "bon voyage" champagne bottle. He then dressed in drag and headed for the lifeboats. The murdered woman went down with the ship. The murderer escaped, but was later consumed with guilt and flipped his wig.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that a cowardly male passenger aboard the Titanic killed a female passenger, then used her wig and clothes to impersonate her and secure a place in the lifeboat.

cards.title: Keep Smiling
case: Hank walks into a bank and hands a teller a bag. The teller opens the bag, reads the note and smiles. Then she hands the note to a nearby bank guard. The guard draws his gun, points it toward Hank and approaches him. As Hank raises his hands, the guard immediately shoots and kills him. A few days later, a female clerical worker in a neighboring office building is charged with murder.
cards.mystery: What did the note say and why was the murder committed?
clues: Sometimes a surrender signals an attack.
Hank didn't know what he was doing.
story: Hank handed a deposit bag to the teller thinking that all it contained were deposits from the office where he worked. Hank was unaware of a note in the bag written by Eunice, an office clerk whom Hank had been sexually harassing for many months. Eunice wanted Hank out of her life — permanently. The note read as follows:
Keep smiling. This is a bank robbery. Fill this bag with money and then give this note to the bank guard. Keep smiling.

Attention bank guard! Do not say anything. I have a bomb. You are to be my hostage. Careful! Don't try anything funny. I just have to raise my hands above my head and a remote control device will set off the bomb. So do the following, exactly like it says —
Draw your gun, keep it pointed in front of you and walk towards me.

As the note requested, the guard approached Hank with his gun drawn. Hank was naturally frightened and instinctively began to raise his hands. The guard, fearing that a bomb would explode, immediately shot Hank before he could fully raise his hands over his head.
Unfortunately for Eunice, the typewriter she used to type the robbery note had a broken letter "K" on it. When police traced the note to her machine, Eunice confessed to the crime.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Hank was unaware of the note placed in the deposit bag by a clerk whom he was sexually harassing. The note indicated that Hank was robbing the bank, that the guard should surrender his gun to Hank and that if Hank raised his hands above his head, a bomb would go off.

cards.title: Book Ends
case: Three senior editors of a book publishing company are found dead in a hotel room on an October weekend.
cards.mystery: Who killed them, how, and why?
clues: The victims and the killer had been business associates.
The victims wore costumes.
story: After many years as an editor at Ratz & Finx Publishing, Briggs Danford was fired by the three senior editors. His severance pay was a pittance, and his pension too paltry to allow his family to live well. He had nothing to live for but revenge.

Briggs sent invitations to a Halloween costume party to the three senior editors, forging the signature of Harvey Ratz, the publisher. The party would take place at a swanky hotel. Everyone was ordered to keep the event secret, and to arrive in costume. The editors, who had no reason to doubt that the invitation had come from their boss, obeyed on both counts.

Briggs, decked out in his desert camouflage uniform complete with gas mask, greeted his guests as they entered the hotel room. They, of course, all thought that Ratz was behind the mask. Then Briggs lit candles in several jack-o'-lanterns — special candles made of toxaphene, a waxy-smelling industrial material that gives off deadly fumes when heated. Soon, all three editors were dead from breathing the poison. Briggs, protected by his mask, lived on to gloat secretly about his clever revenge.

Police mistakenly arrested Ratz, who was then subjected to a lengthy and humiliating investigation. Briggs was finally apprehended, but the publishing company went under, and Ratz left the sinking ship.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the killer, who had been fired by the three editors, gathered them at a Halloween party and killed them by lighting poison candles. The fumes killed all but himself, who was protected by a gas mask.

cards.title: Last Night
case: A man is found dead in the night air.
cards.mystery: Who murdered the man, how, and why?
clues: The man's getaway was his downfall.
He died because he had too much power.
story: The victim, Geronimo Jones, and his partner Buck were a notorious skyjacking duo. Posing as a plane passenger, Geronimo would fleece his fellow fliers of their valuables at gunpoint. Then he would disable the radio and force the pilot to fly toward a rendezvous spot where Buck waited on the ground. An expert parachutist, Geronimo would jump out of the plane and glide inside the circle of flares set up by his partner. Just before landing, he would toss the bag of baubles clear of the flares. The partners would then split the spoils, with Geronimo grabbing the lion's share.

Buck had grown weary of forking over most of their fortunes to Geronimo, and secretly vowed that the next big night would be Geronimo's last. On the appointed evening, Buck set up the flares under the power lines of a huge hydroelectric transmission station. Geronimo's jump gave him a lethal jolt, and Buck a booty he didn't have to share.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the skyjacker's partner set up flares under power lines to electrocute his parachuting partner, so that he could keep the stolen valuables for himself.

cards.title: Learning the Hard Way
case: "I didn't mean to kill him," Dennis Twitchell moaned. "It was an accident. I just wanted to teach him a lesson."
The young man was on trial for murdering his friend Arnie. Although the jury believed him and was sympathetic, they still felt obligated to return a verdict of involuntary manslaughter.
cards.mystery: How did Dennis kill his friend? And what lesson had he been trying to teach?
clues: Dennis studied harder, but Arnie got better grades.
Cheaters never prosper.
story: Arnie was cheating on his high school tests. His method was to write out a tiny crib sheet and hide it in his palm during a test; when he was through using it, he would slip it into his mouth, chew it up and swallow it. Without success, Dennis had often warned Arnie that cheating was wrong.

One night before a test, Dennis secretly wet Arnie's crib sheet and rubbed white pepper into it, hoping that Arnie would finally develop a bad taste for cheating. Next day, when Arnie stuffed the peppered paper into his mouth, he had a severe allergic reaction to the pepper. He lost consciousness and was rushed to the hospital, but was dead on arrival. Dennis, who couldn't lie any more than he could cheat, confessed immediately.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Arnie cheated on tests, and that Dennis rubbed white pepper into Arnie's crib sheet. Arnie died from a severe allergic reaction after he put the sheet into his mouth.

cards.title: Lord Love a Duke
case: Just seconds after they heard the gunshot, the butler and young Lord Michael came running into the hall together from the library. They raced up the staircase, only to find the old Duke lying dead in his room, the gun still clutched in his hand. "He's killed himself," Lord Michael cried, his eyes welling up with tears. "Poor old Uncle Humbert."
During the course of the investigation, the police came across a feather and a tiny piece of metal. Then they knew it was murder.
cards.mystery: What was the significance of the feather and the piece of metal? Who killed the Duke, and how?
clues: The feather once belonged to a goose.
The piece of metal was a charred bullet shell.
story: Young Lord Michael was desperate for his inheritance, so he arranged his uncle's murder to look like suicide. That evening, while the butler was downstairs in the library, Michael visited his uncle in his bedroom. He shot the old Duke through a pillow, to muffle the sound of the gunshot. He then placed the gun in Uncle Humbert's hand, tossed the pillow into the fireplace along with a fresh bullet, and quickly ran downstairs. A few minutes later, when the bullet exploded from the heat of the fire, Michael was in the library with the butler, his alibi firmly established.

Scotland Yard became suspicious when they found a feather from the pillow next to the body. In the fireplace ashes, they discovered the burnt remains of the pillow and the second bullet shell — and Michael's inheritance went up in smoke.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Lord Michael shot his uncle earlier in the evening, using a pillow to muffle the sound. To create an alibi, Michael then placed a bullet in the fireplace which exploded later from the heat.

cards.title: Tune in for Murder
case: Elderly Nigel Harper-Smith is found dead of a heart attack in front of his TV set.
cards.mystery: Who killed Nigel, and how?
clues: Nigel's own TV was at the repair shop.
Nigel and his wife had eyeglasses with identical frames, but opposite prescriptions.
story: Thirty-year-old Christina Poore had married the wealthy Nigel, expecting him to drop dead from a bad heart any minute. But the curmudgeonly old man lived on, with the help of his pacemaker, to criticize her every move.

When Nigel's TV set went on the blink, Christina told him the repair shop had loaned them a small TV so that he could watch his Saturday football game. Then she swung into action. First, she secretly switched his eyeglasses for hers — they had identical frames but opposite prescriptions. Then she switched the TV for a microwave oven, and put his radio next to it. Finally, she tuned in the game on the radio, then placed a frozen turkey into the microwave and set it for three hours.

Unable to see (but too vain to admit it), Nigel believed that the microwave was the loaner TV. He immediately fell asleep, and when the microwave signaled "done," so was Nigel — his pacemaker had become erratic, and his heart had stopped.

Christina switched the microwave and the TV, figuring she had committed the perfect crime. But she was arrested when police discovered that Nigel was wearing her glasses. She just wasn't farsighted enough to remove them.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Nigel's wife switched his glasses for hers, then placed a microwave and a radio in his room and turned them both on. Unable to see and thinking he was watching TV, Nigel fell asleep. The microwaves caused his pacemaker to become erratic, and his heart stopped.

cards.title: Three's a Crowd
case: After a horrible plane crash, Roger Rector's remains are returned home. Soon afterward, Roger's wife Dodie remarries. A few weeks after her honeymoon, Dodie dies and is buried next to Roger. Then a flood devastates the graveyard and washes open many of the graves. In addition to Roger and Dodie, there is a third body in the Rectors' grave!
cards.mystery: Who was the third person, and why was the body in the Rectors' grave?
clues: The unidentified body had been there the longest.
Dodie's second husband was an undertaker.
story: During a late-night flight on Rickety Airlines, Roger realized he was tired of his dead-end job and his sickly wife, Dodie. Suddenly the plane took a nosedive and crashed. Roger was the only survivor and miraculously walked away unscathed. Amazed at his good fortune, he impulsively decided to start a new life. He left his wallet beside a badly burned corpse and disappeared into the darkness. The corpse, mistakenly identified as Roger's, was returned to Dodie for burial.

During funeral preparations, Dodie fell in love with Harvey, the attentive and charming undertaker. Harvey fell in love with the hefty life insurance payment Dodie received after Roger's demise. After six months of mourning and courting, Dodie married Harvey.

Meanwhile, Roger desperately needed money. He secretly approached Harvey and demanded 50% of the insurance payment. Harvey threatened to turn Roger in, but Roger reminded him that if his secret was revealed, the insurance company would demand return of the entire payment. Not willing to give up his newfound fortune, Harvey decided to kill Roger. After all, everyone thought he was dead anyway! A carefully aimed shot to the head with a bottle of embalming fluid rendered Roger quite dead but well-preserved.

Shortly thereafter, Dodie died. Harvey dumped Roger's body into a large coffin with his dearly departed wife. After a quick burial, Harvey departed for parts unknown with a suitcase full of cash! The police blamed the graveside threesome on the flood, so Harvey's illicit undertaking was never discovered.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Roger survived the plane crash and that another body from the crash was buried in his grave. Roger demanded insurance money from Dodie's new husband. The husband killed Roger and later buried him in the same casket with his recently departed wife.

cards.title: Sweet Charity
case: On a southern plantation in the year 1840, an engagement party was in progress for Charity Merriweather and Dr. Ambrose Washburn. In the receiving line, ravishing Jasmine McDrew suddenly said, "Ouch!", crumpled to the floor, and died moments later.
cards.mystery: What happened to Jasmine, and why?
clues: Jasmine was a man-stealer.
Charity's maid was a dwarf.
story: Charity knew that her pending marriage was in jeopardy, because Jasmine was seducing Ambrose. The day of the party, Charity dipped a hat pin into curare, a quick-acting poison, from Ambrose's dispensary. She gave the poisoned pin to her Venezuelan dwarf maid, who then cleverly hid with it under Charity's huge hoop skirt.

During the party, the dwarf adroitly moved with Charity while hiding under her skirt. As Charity talked to Jasmine in the receiving line, she signaled the dwarf by tapping her on the head. The dwarf then bent down, lifted Charity's skirt a little, and jabbed Jasmine in the ankle with the poisoned hat pin.
Within minutes, Jasmine was gone with the pin, and so were Charity's worries about losing her beloved Ambrose.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the jealous Charity hid her dwarf maid under her hoop skirt with a poisoned hat pin. The maid jabbed Jasmine in the ankle with the pin, causing her death.

cards.title: Rubble Trouble
case: Truck driver Moose Morgan is reported missing by his company, TransAm Trucking. His mangled body is later found in a heap of rubble.
cards.mystery: Who murdered Moose, how, and why?
clues: Moose, a married man, had a girl in every truck stop.
Moose's wife knew that they had to move out of their apartment.
story: Moose was on a month-long trucking trip when his wife Flo learned that their apartment building was going to be torn down. Flo phoned TransAm Trucking to find out where Moose would be staying that night, so she could tell him the news. When Flo called the motel, a woman answered the phone and the flummoxed Flo immediately hung up. The next night, in a different motel, a different woman answered, and again Flo hung up. When this continued for several nights, Flo finally got the picture. Her no-good, two-timing husband was going to get his.

Flo moved to a new apartment without telling Moose. Just before he was due home, Flo found out exactly when their old building was going to be razed. Then she sent a fax to his motel saying: "Meet me at the apartment at 3:00 p.m. Tuesday. Urgent!"

Flo entered the empty apartment, unscrewed a doorknob and hid it behind her back. Soon after, Moose, surprised to see a "Condemned" sign on their building, walked in. Flo knocked him out with the doorknob and ran out of the building shortly before the wrecking crew smashed it to bits. Moose was killed by the collapsing walls and flying bricks. The only thing not mangled was the fax in his pocket, which led the police straight to Flo. For once in his life, Moose was on the ball.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that while the unfaithful Moose was away, his wife did not tell him that their apartment building was going to be razed. She lured him to the old building and knocked him out just before the wrecking crew smashed the building, killing Moose.

cards.title: House Trap
case: Harold reads the morning paper, then looks in the phone book and drives to a residence. He rings the bell, pulls a gun on the man who answers the door and says: "I want $100,000 — now — or you're dead!"
Two police officers then suddenly appear from the next room and arrest Harold.
cards.mystery: Who was Harold, and what had he read in the paper?
clues: The two men had met the day before.
Harold had been reading about a crime.
story: Harold had held up a bank the previous day, and the teller had quietly filled the bag with $50,000. What Harold read in the paper the next morning was that the bank had been robbed of $150,000. Figuring the teller had pulled a fast one by keeping $100,000 for himself, he looked up the man's address in the phone book and hightailed it over there to collect the missing money. But the teller wasn't hiding anything except a couple of crafty cops. They had planted the phony news story, hoping to lure the greedy crook into their trap. It worked.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Harold was a bank robber who was tricked into believing the bank teller was hiding extra money from his heist the day before.

cards.title: Window Pain
case: Mason, a performer, is found dead on the floor of a locked room with a triple-glazed blood-stained window. His head is bashed in, and blood is running out of his ears.
cards.mystery: Who killed Mason, how, and why?
clues: A colleague "engineered" Mason's death.
Mason had been a radio announcer.
story: Mason Brooks, a radio announcer, was having an affair with the wife of Adam Singleton, the recording studio sound engineer. One evening, Mason had a late recording date at the studio, working with Adam. What Mason didn't know was that Adam knew all about the affair, and had found his chance for revenge.

When the last employee left at 2:00 a.m., Adam locked the door of the soundproof booth where Mason was recording, went back to his controls and piped an ear-splitting, high-pitched feedback into the booth. Mason was trapped in the locked room with no way to stop the torturous sound. As Adam left the studio, Mason, crazed with pain, was beating his head against the booth's window, trying to knock himself out. By the time he was found, at 7:00 a.m., Mason was dead from the effects of the ear-splitting sound. Adam was convicted of the crime, his pleas of innocence falling on deaf ears.
cards.specialInformation: A person can indeed die from the effects of extremely loud, high-pitched sounds.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that radio announcer Mason was having an affair with a sound engineer's wife, and that the engineer caused Mason's death by locking him in a soundproof booth with ultra-loud feedback.

cards.title: The Last Frat Boy
case: The Kappa Delta fraternity of '55 had organized a tontine.* Each frat brother contributed $100 and the money was invested into stocks, with the agreement that all proceeds would go to the last surviving member of the group. When Bill stayed overnight at the house of his old roommate Greg, the fund was well over $1,000,000, and they were among the three surviving members. Late that night, a car plummeted to the bottom of a ravine. The bodies of both Bill and Greg were found inside. Aside from being dead, Bill had a nasty bruise on his left temple.
*A tontine is a financial agreement in which the participants contribute equally to a joint fund that is awarded entirely to the surviving participant.
cards.mystery: What happened that night? Was it murder, an accident, or something else?
clues: The police were fascinated by the guest bathroom.
Greg didn't get the "brake" he was expecting.
story: The police found blood matching Bill's type on the floor of Greg's guest bathroom. They also discovered that the brakes of Greg's car had been tampered with. From this and other evidence, the police reconstructed the following:

Bill was a debt-ridden gambler who wanted to get one step closer to the fortune. So earlier that fateful night, he tampered with the brakes on Greg's car. Later, before Greg could use his car, Bill slipped and fell as he stepped out of Greg's shower, hitting his head and knocking himself out. Greg bundled his unconscious friend into his car and headed for the hospital — but halfway there, Greg's brakes failed. The car skidded around a sharp curve and plunged into a ravine.
Nathaniel, the last frat boy, ended up with the whole fortune, which he promptly lost in bad investments.
cards.specialInformation: This is a combination murder and accidental death. The fact that Bill accidentally died during the commission of his crime does not make his death a suicide.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Bill tampered with Greg's car brakes, then later injured himself in a household accident and was an unconscious passenger at the time of the car accident. Greg was not out to kill Bill.

cards.title: The Widow Wendy
case: Wendy Wegman waits the required 48 hours before filing a missing persons report. "My husband has run off before," she tells the sergeant. "Usually when we're fighting. But he's never been gone this long. Something awful must have happened."

The police are at the Wegman home three days later, when they get a call. "I'm sorry," the sergeant tells Wendy. "Your husband's body has just washed up near his family's beach cottage. His sister was there and she identified him."
"No! It can't be!" Wendy exclaims. She becomes distraught and takes to her bed. At three o'clock the next morning, Wendy Wegman is arrested for her husband's murder.
cards.mystery: On what evidence did the police arrest Wendy?
clues: The police had suspected Wendy all along.
The police had found the body two days before telling Wendy.
story: Wendy had often publicly threatened to murder her husband, so the police suspected her from the start. When an officer found the body at the bottom of a wooded cliff with a bullet wound to the head, it all fit. She must have shot him during a fight, then transported his corpse to the nearby hills and dumped him out of her station wagon.

After two days of forensic testing, the police could find nothing to incriminate Wendy. Since they could no longer keep the body's discovery a secret, they devised a plan to lie about where the body had been found. The false report that her husband was found miles away from where she dumped him both frightened and confused the murderess. In the wee hours, Wendy drove to the spot where she had really disposed of the body. The police were waiting for the wily widow, and arrested her on the spot.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the police found Wendy's husband's body where she had dumped it, then falsely told her that it was found elsewhere. She incriminated herself by visiting the spot where she had dumped the body.

cards.title: Melvin Plays the Ponies
case: The first phone call came on Saturday at 5:30 p.m. "First race at Aqueduct," the mysterious voice whispered. "Bet on Leapin' Lana to win." At 6 p.m. Melvin watched the race on TV and, sure enough, Leapin' Lana won the first race by two lengths.

The next week the call came again at 5:30, and once again, the mysterious voice had correctly predicted the winner in the first race. On the third Saturday, Melvin was ready. As soon as the voice hung up, he phoned a bookie. Just as before, the predicted horse came through and Melvin won several thousand dollars.

On week four, the call came early, on Wednesday. "I've given you three winners," the voice said. "If you want the horse for Saturday's race, it'll cost you $10,000. If you're interested, we can arrange a drop-off point."
cards.mystery: How did the voice consistently pick winners for Melvin?
clues: On weeks one, two and three, the voice also called other people.
On his previous wins, Melvin had just been lucky.
story: It was just luck. This is an old con game that can be performed by any criminal willing to make several hundred phone calls. On the first Saturday, the con man picked a race with seven horses running. Then he called 343 people, divided into groups of 49, and told each group to bet on a different horse. The second week, he called only the 49 people he had told to bet on Leapin' Lana the week before. This time he told each group of seven people to bet on a different horse for that week's race.

By the fourth week, only Melvin was left, and by that time he was convinced that the voice had a foolproof system. Luckily, Melvin didn't have the $10,000 and tried to borrow money from his brother, an officer on the bunco squad. The con man was arrested that Friday when he went to pick up the money.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the con man began by calling hundreds of people. Each week he called only those who had won the previous week, until only Melvin remained.

cards.title: The Efficiency Apartment
case: The nosy neighbor finally called the police. "The Ryans across the hall had this awful fight. They were both screaming and throwing things. Then all of a sudden it got quiet. That was two days ago and no one has left the apartment since. I'd know if anyone went out. My dog would have heard them and barked up a storm. I think he killed her!"

The police knock on the Ryans' door. Mr. Ryan answers. His wife, he claims, walked out two days ago and didn't say where she was going. The police search the modern gadget-filled apartment but find no trace of the missing woman.
cards.mystery: What happened to Mrs. Ryan?
clues: Mrs. Ryan often went to pieces during a fight.
The Ryans' fancy oven was immaculately clean.
story: Ryan killed his wife during their domestic dispute. He knew he could never move the body without being observed. So he disposed of it in the apartment.

He cut the body up in the bathtub, placed the pieces in the oven, and turned on the self-cleaning function. With a few repetitions, the oven heated up to between 800 and 900 degrees — cremation temperature. Eventually the entire body was reduced to ashes and bone fragments, which he vacuumed up.

Luckily, the nosy neighbor didn't give up. She urged the police to make a second search of the Ryans' apartment. Eureka! In the hall closet they found a vacuum cleaner bag full of dark, chunky dust. A lab analysis confirmed this was all that remained of poor Mrs. Ryan.
cards.specialInformation: If the Investigators ask if Mrs. Ryan is still in the apartment, the answer is "yes." (Her remains are in a vacuum cleaner bag in the hall closet.)
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Ryan disposed of his wife's body by cutting it up, reducing it to ash in a self-cleaning oven, and vacuuming up the remains.

cards.title: Murder Must Detour
case: Mr. Basil was a methodical man who liked to plan things down to the smallest detail. This evening's schedule, for instance, included murdering his shrew of a wife. He would do it as soon as they got home.

While driving back to their house, Mr. Basil made a slight alteration to his plan. He dropped off his wife at the front door, then drove across town to the home of Dean Archway. After killing Archway, Basil returned to his own house and proceeded to go through with the scheduled murder of his wife.
cards.mystery: Why did Basil alter his plan and make the detour to kill Archway?
clues: Mrs. Basil had her last meal at her favorite restaurant.
Basil and Archway had similar tastes in clothing.
story: Mr. Basil made lists for everything, including every detail of his wife's upcoming murder. The deadly plan was neatly written on his personalized stationery, with every "t" crossed and every "i" dotted.

Unfortunately for Archway, Basil and his soon-to-be-murdered wife were dining at the same restaurant as he that fateful night. And even more unfortunately, Basil had left the list in his coat pocket and had hung up his coat in the restaurant's lobby.

Upon exiting the restaurant, Basil realized he had the wrong coat. Someone else had already left with his coat — and the incriminating list. Basil searched through the stranger's pockets and found a dry cleaning receipt that contained Archway's name and address.
When Basil knocked on Archway's door, he had no intention of killing the man. But Archway had already gone through Basil's pockets and read the list. Basil felt that he had no choice but to kill him.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Basil left an incriminating list in his coat pocket and that he and Archway had accidentally switched coats at the restaurant. Archway was murdered because he had read the list and knew of Basil's plan to murder his wife.

cards.title: The Timely Intruder
case: Something strange was happening on Elm Street. Every day, for three days straight, between 11:30 a.m. and noon, someone broke into the same empty townhouse, triggering a silent alarm. Each time, the police responded quickly, finding no evidence of theft or vandalism. On the fourth day, at 11:30 a.m., a police officer was lying in wait, hoping to catch the intruder when he or she struck — but no one came on that day, or any day after that.
cards.mystery: Who was triggering the alarm? Why did it happen at approximately the same time for three days running?
clues: The house belonged to a recently-murdered man.
The mail carrier regularly arrived between 11:00 and 11:30 a.m.
story: Kirk Weaver was an investigative journalist. He was in New York, working on an exposé connecting a union official to a pair of unsolved murders. When the official got wind of Kirk's investigation, he tried to stop it with bribery, then threats. Kirk was not intimidated. He told the official, "I mailed all my notes and information to my house in Baltimore, addressed to my cleaning lady. If anything happens to me, Doris will take that envelope straight to the police." Impulsively, the desperate official killed Kirk on the spot.

The next day in Baltimore, the official was in front of Kirk's house. For three days he followed the same routine, waiting for the mail carrier to arrive, then breaking into the house and checking the pile of newly-delivered mail on the hall floor. On the third day, the incriminating packet finally came. The killer took the evidence, burned it and returned to New York.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the house belonged to a murder victim who mailed a critical piece of evidence to his home. His killer broke into the house each day for three days right after the mail delivery, to retrieve the incriminating envelope.

cards.title: Road Kill
case: Ron is found dead in the street three miles from his home. After a police investigation, his wife Rhonda is charged with murder.
cards.mystery: How and why did Rhonda kill Ron?
clues: Ron's death was kind of a drag.
Surgeons generally give warnings.
story: Rhonda was a health nut who continually nagged Ron to quit smoking and start jogging. Ron began running and after months of effort, had reduced his habit to a single "after-sex" cigarette.

Ron remained faithful to his jogging routine, but not to Rhonda. Rhonda's suspicions were aroused when Ron's 45-minute jaunts turned into 2½-hour marathons. She also noticed that Ron always brought along his cigarettes when he jogged.

Rhonda followed Ron one day, and discovered that his daily run involved some extra-curricular heavy breathing at the home of his girlfriend, Babette. Rhonda sought revenge! Before Ron's next run, she secretly injected the filter tips of his cigarettes with a slow-acting, but deadly neurotoxin. Ron took the bait and lit up his last cigarette after a fateful frolic with Babette. On his return jog home, Ron collapsed and died in the street. Too late, he discovered that the Surgeon General was right — cigarettes were hazardous to his health!
An autopsy matched the poison in runner Ron's system with that in his cigarettes. A police search of the house turned up a jar of the same poison — with Rhonda's fingerprints on it.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Rhonda killed Ron by secretly poisoning his cigarettes after discovering that Ron was unfaithful during his jogging jaunts.

cards.title: Gone Fishing
case: Bob and Linc operate an oceanside marina. It is widely known how tired Bob has grown of Linc's long-winded fish stories, and that Bob would like to run the marina by himself. One day Linc goes fishing in his boat and doesn't return. The next morning, the Coast Guard finds the boat 12 miles out at sea. It has major structural damage but is still floating. Linc is gone. The boat is towed to shore and police investigate. Bob is charged with murder.
cards.mystery: What happened to the missing Linc?
clues: Linc always had a "flare" for fishing.
Bob had an explosive temper.
story: Bob knew that Linc was going fishing and that his favorite spot was about 12 miles out to sea. Bob decided to send Linc on a one-way trip. He siphoned gas out of the boat's tank and then tampered with the gas gauge so it read "full." He then disabled the boat's two-way radio.

After a successful day of fishing, Linc began his return to port. Shortly thereafter he ran out of gas. After unsuccessfully attempting to radio for help, he remembered the signal flares. The flares were his only hope for rescue as darkness set in. Unknown to Linc, Bob had spliced the top of the signal flares onto sticks of dynamite! Surrounded by darkness, Linc unraveled the strike cap and ignited it. Seconds later the phosphorus of the flare reached the explosive. Linc was blown out to sea in bits, a mere midnight snack for some hungry sharks.

But Linc's sturdy craft didn't sink. Police found bits of Linc about the boat and Bob's fingerprints on the gas gauge. The remaining dynamite flares provided proof of foul play. Obviously Bob assumed that the evidence would go down with the ship. Instead it was used to send him up the river.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Bob sabotaged Linc's boat and replaced his signal flares with dynamite sticks. When Bob signaled for help, he was blown out to sea.

cards.title: Field of Nightmares
case: "I didn't kill him," Mr. Weebol wailed. The nervous, precise man certainly didn't look like the type who would be involved in murder. But the evidence was overwhelming.

Little Louie the Lip, the local bookie, was dead. Earlier that night, an alert police officer had noticed movement in an overgrown field. There Weebol was spotted, dragging Louie's body through the brush. His car was parked at the roadside with a shovel still in the back seat.
When Weebol was further questioned about what he was doing with the body, he merely stammered, "I want a lawyer."
cards.mystery: What was Weebol hiding, and what really happened?
clues: The field was behind Weebol's house.
Weebol's wife had disappeared two months ago.
story: Mr. Weebol saw a car stop by the field behind his house. Horrified, he saw the driver open the trunk and drag a man's body into the field.

Weebol knew it was just a matter of time before the body was found. Police would scour the field, looking for clues — and maybe even for more dead bodies. They were sure to notice that plot of ground he had dug up two months ago. It was where he had buried his wife after he had murdered her!

He had no choice. He had to move the man's body to another location. After the killer left, Weebol put a shovel in his car, parked by the field and started to drag the body towards his car. That's when he was spotted by the cop.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Weebol was innocent of killing Louie. When he was caught with the corpse, he was in the process of moving it to another location to keep the police from finding his murdered wife's burial spot.

cards.title: Death's a Beach
case: Movie star Tad Oliver's marriage was on the rocks and his agent was worried about his mental health. When Tad didn't answer his phone one day, the agent called the police and they sped to Tad's beach house. The doors and windows were all locked from the inside.

The police broke in and found the leading man on his bedroom floor, barely clinging to life. A gun was in his hand and a bullet hole in his chest. The distraught agent bent over his dying client. "Why'd you do it, Babe? Why? I just got you a four-picture deal with Metro!"
The star's dying word was whispered, but both the agent and an officer heard it: "Jealousy."
cards.mystery: Tad's death was murder. What did he mean by "jealousy"? And how did the killer get out of the house that was bolted from the inside?
clues: Tad never said "jealousy."
Tad's last look was glassy-eyed.
story: Tad and his estranged wife, Marie, had a horrible fight at the beach house that day. She settled the argument decisively by taking the gun from the nightstand and shooting Tad. Knowing that she would be a suspect, she made his murder look like suicide.

She put the gun in Tad's hand, bolted every door and window, and left the house by sliding the glass slats out of the bathroom's jalousie window. She crawled through the narrow opening, then from the outside she carefully replaced the panes of glass — all except for the top one, which wouldn't fit in with the window closed.

Tad saw her escape and his dying word, "jalousie" — not jealousy — alerted the police. They noticed the missing slat and dusted for prints. That evening, Marie was called out of her step aerobics class and arrested.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Tad's last word was "jalousie," not "jealousy." He was murdered by his wife who tried to make it look like suicide by leaving the bolted beach house through a jalousie window. She dismantled the window, crawled through, and reassembled its glass slats from the outside.

cards.title: Double Shot
case: Trixie Bell has been at the beauty salon for two hours when she gets the phone call from a worried neighbor. "I knew you'd be there. I just heard a gunshot coming from your house. I've called the police!"

When Trixie races home, she finds the police wheeling out the body of her wealthy, elderly husband Alex Bell. An officer tells her that the house has been ransacked and it looks like a botched burglary has turned into murder.
That same night, Buddy, a gardener, is found dead in his apartment, an apparent suicide. The same gun that shot Alex is clutched in his hand.
cards.mystery: How did the two men die? And what part, if any, did Buddy play in Alex Bell's death?
clues: Buddy was in love, but Trixie wasn't.
Alex didn't die from a gunshot wound.
story: Buddy was the Bell's gardener. He was madly in love with the flirtatious Trixie. One morning, Buddy arrived at the Bell house and found Alex's body in the kitchen, with a half-eaten muffin in his hand. Before dying, Alex had managed to write the word "poison" on his morning paper. Buddy immediately knew that Trixie had killed Alex; he also knew that the police would come to this same conclusion.

To save the woman he loved, he destroyed the newspaper, shot Alex's body with a gun he had in his glove compartment and ransacked the house. The police would think that Alex had been shot during a botched robbery. It would give Trixie the alibi that she needed!

That evening, Buddy telephoned Trixie and told her of his heroic deed. She went to his apartment. Although grateful, she honestly told him she could never love him. Buddy grew angry and threatened to tell the police. She spotted the gun. After one quick shot, Buddy became a convenient "suicide."
cards.specialInformation: Trixie and Buddy were not in cahoots. Buddy did not kill Alex. He is guilty, however, of being an accessory after the fact.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Trixie poisoned Alex. To give her an alibi, Buddy shot the already-dead Alex, disguising the time and manner of his death. To keep Buddy quiet, Trixie shot him with the same gun and made it look like suicide.

cards.title: Hot Cash
case: Inside the charred remains of an old, dilapidated boarding house is a grisly sight. The burned bodies of three elderly men and one middle-aged man are in the parlor. The middle-aged man has a bullet hole in his head, but none of the other bodies show any apparent signs of foul play.
cards.mystery: Who was the middle-aged man and why was he killed? And what role did the other three men play in the story?
clues: The boarding house had a freezer in the basement.
The elderly men were all receiving retirement checks.
story: Jake ran a boarding house. One day, his oldest tenant died just as he was signing his two retirement checks. After Jake cashed the man's checks, a brilliant scheme popped into his head. He would put the old man's body in his freezer and continue to pretend he was alive, forging his name to cash his checks every month. If investigated, Jake could thaw out the body and say that the old man had recently died.

Before long, Jake was doing this for three deceased tenants, all of whom had died of natural causes and were preserved in the basement freezer. Then disaster struck. The son of one of the old men arrived on the scene. When the middle-aged son insisted on seeing his father, Jake panicked and shot him. His scam was over.
Hoping to hide his crime, Jake placed the three frozen corpses in the parlor with the man he had just shot. Then he set the whole place on fire, counting on the fire to thaw out the bodies.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the owner of the boarding house froze three of his elderly dead tenants and pretended they were alive, cashing their retirement checks for himself. When one of the tenant's sons came to see his father, the owner shot him, then set the boarding house on fire to hide his crime.

cards.title: The Sparkled Band
case: Connie lies dead in a ring with Sheila. Police arrest Tanya for Connie's murder, and Sheila goes free.
cards.mystery: How did Tanya kill Connie? What role did Sheila play?
clues: The classic love triangle started it all.
Of the three females, one is not human.
story: Tanya the tightrope walker and Connie the cat lady were both in love with Clyde Batty, the circus ringmaster. When Connie caught Clyde's eye, Tanya took offense and plotted revenge.

Just before showtime the next night, Tanya pulled a switcheroo. She placed the identifying sparkling collar of Connie's prized tigress on Sheila, a look-alike cat who had just begun training. Instead of Connie's tigress, Sheila was brought out for the grand finale. Seeing the familiar collar, Connie didn't realize she'd been conned as she performed her final trick: opening the cat's jaws and sticking her head inside. The hungry Sheila, who didn't know any better, thought dinner was served. When she took a bite, poor Connie lost her head. Police investigated, found sequins from Tanya's costume in Sheila's cage, and quickly collared Tanya.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the jealous Tanya replaced Connie's tigress with Sheila, an untrained look-alike cat, who killed Connie during the grand finale of her circus performance.

cards.title: Derailed
case: Two men are seated side by side in a commuter train, one dressed in gray and the other in black. The man in gray hands something to the man in black. At the next stop, the man in black pulls out a gun with a silencer, shoots the man in gray dead, and leaves the train.
cards.mystery: What did the man in gray hand to the man in black? Why did the man in black kill the man in gray?
clues: The man in black was looking for evidence.
The man in gray was European.
story: It was a contract hit, and the hit man was the man in black. He was hired by a jealous husband who wanted his wife's lover identified and executed.

The husband had arrived home from a business trip unexpectedly, to discover that his wild wife had been partying at their house the night before. It didn't take a genius to deduce that someone had been in their bedroom with her: there were two telltale champagne glasses on her bedside table, and several French cigarettes in an ashtray. His wife didn't smoke.
The husband's loyal butler had supplied the names of the ten men who had attended the soiree. The husband had only to discover which of them smoked the damnifying cigs.

The hit man had tracked down nine of the suspects. All were either non-smokers or cigar smokers. He had sat beside number ten on the train, asked him for a cigarette, and gotten just what he had expected — a French smoke that matched those in the wife's ashtray. The man in gray got what was coming to him — no ifs, ands or butts!
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the man in black was a hit man, hired by a jealous husband to kill his wife's lover — a man who had been smoking French cigarettes in the bedroom. The man in gray sealed his fate when he handed a French cigarette to the man in black.

cards.title: The Dying Game
case: Apparently, it was a tragic accident on the golf course. Ben explains that a wild backswing with his one-iron fatally crushed the skull of his wife, Myra. A skeptical detective gets a search warrant for the couple's condo, and Ben is arrested on suspicion of murder.
cards.mystery: On what evidence was Ben arrested for murdering Myra?
clues: Man, was Ben mad at Myra!
Myra's past contained a secret.
story: Ben and Myra were newlyweds who were moving into their new home, a condo near the 16th hole of their favorite golf course. As Ben unpacked a carton of Myra's belongings, his eye fell upon her high school yearbook. Amused and curious, he thumbed through its pages looking for a picture of his beloved.
What first shocked Ben about Myra's senior picture was her very short hair style. Then he saw the sideburns, and finally the name below the picture: Myron!

It took several minutes for Ben to come to grips with the fact that he had married a transsexual who had had a sex change operation. Why had she — he — okay, she — not told him? The totally teed-off Ben then went off to golf with Myra, plotting his revenge. In a remote area of the back nine, Ben delivered the crushing blow. Suspecting foul play, police got a search warrant, discovered Myron's photo, and threw the book at Ben.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Ben had discovered that Myra had once been a man, and killed her by smashing her skull with a golf club.

cards.title: Let's Make a Deal
case: Police in an affluent Manhattan neighborhood question Monty, a local drug pusher. The detective in charge demands to know where Monty and his fellow pushers get their supply.

"I ain't no stoolie!" Monty exclaims, and refuses to tell the police anything. The cops place Monty under surveillance, hoping he will lead them to the drug king pin who services the pushers. Weeks go by and the police are baffled. Finally, an observant officer figures out what's going on and arrests are made.
cards.mystery: How does the drug distributor deliver drugs to Monty and his fellow pushers?
clues: The answer can be found by nosing around.
Monty's best friend is an unknowing helper.
story: Monty, a local drug pusher, lived in an exclusive section of Manhattan and owned an expensive purebred dog. His friendly neighborhood veterinarian, Dr. Sam Smarmy, often dispensed more than medical advice. He was also the illegal drug distributor for the area.

Once a week, Dr. Smarmy mixed up a special batch of dog food which he gave to the local pushers' puppy patients. In reality, the dog chow was an expensive blend of mystery meat and small, undigestible plastic capsules filled with illegal narcotics.

Here's how the plan worked: Like many of his well-to-do neighbors with expensive pets, Monty brought his dog to the vet for weekly grooming and flea baths. Monty's hungry hound was given carefully-measured portions of the special drug-filled dog food. Monty would then pay the doctor and return home with his dog in tow. Later, Monty would give his pet a special treat: liver-flavored laxative tablets! When the pusher's pooch showed an eagerness to go for a walk, Monty brought along his pooper scooper as required by city ordinance. Once the dog did its duty, the cunning crook scooped up his stash and was back in business.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the area's drug distributor was a veterinarian who "treated" his pusher-owned pets to drug-filled dog food, which their owners later scooped!

cards.title: Mummy Dearest
case: After one of her dinner parties, widowed Washington hostess Marcella Stoat dies, seemingly from an Egyptian mummy's curse. Before her son Ernest can be arrested for her murder, he dies.
cards.mystery: How did Marcella and Ernest die?
clues: Marcella was a heavy drinker with sloppy habits.
Ernest was an archaeologist.
story: Drunken, slovenly Marcella Stoat gave a dinner party in honor of her son, Dr. Ernest Stoat, an archaeologist just back from Egypt. By dinnertime she had already drunk six screwdrivers, spilled hors d'oeuvres down her ample front and insulted several guests. Ernest, a fastidious fuddy-duddy, was appalled. Marcella's behavior had embarrassed him all his life. But tonight, he would finally be free of her. Tonight, she would die.

After dinner, Ernest rose and offered a gift to his mom, a large golden goblet from the tomb of Princess Pta. He laughingly mentioned that the goblet was supposedly cursed. Marcella pooh-poohed the notion, poured a screwdriver into the goblet, and drank it down in one swig.

Soon, Marcella was violently ill. "The curse!" cried Ernest as he ran to her. When the doctor arrived, Marcella was fading fast. Ernest threw the goblet into the flames of the fireplace. As the guests left, Ernest sat by the hearth, pretending to mourn.

Marcella died that night. Ernest died the next day. He had coated the inside of the goblet with poison (cadmium), knowing the acid in the orange juice would dissolve it, and that his mother would swallow enough to expire. What he didn't know was that throwing the remaining poison into the fire would cause fumes deadlier than ingestion. Pta-Pta, Ernest!
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Ernest killed his mother by coating her goblet gift with poison, knowing it would dissolve in the orange juice of her screwdriver. The poison fumes from the fireplace later killed Ernest himself.

cards.title: Mayfair Lady
case: On the day before Christmas, cosmetics heiress Countess Mayfair is found stabbed to death in her bedroom. The priceless Mayfair tiara is missing; so is the murder weapon.
cards.mystery: Who killed the Countess, how, and why? And where was the murder weapon?
clues: The Countess was a tyrant.
The Countess thought her tiara had been stolen.
story: The cantankerous Countess had falsely accused her maid of stealing the Mayfair tiara. The innocent maid, fearing for her reputation, visited the Countess in her boudoir to plead her case. But the discussion quickly degenerated into a hysterical confrontation. Impulsively, the maid grabbed the pointed crystal stopper of a bottle of Mayfair Mayhem perfume from the dressing table and plunged it into her employer's throat, killing her instantly.

Aghast at what she had done, the maid attempted to cover up her crime. She washed the stopper and replaced it in the perfume bottle. She then went to her quarters, wrapped the bottle as a gift, and placed it under the Christmas tree.

Thoroughly searching the house for the murder weapon, police unwrapped the presents under the tree. When they discovered that the maid had given the perfume heiress a bottle of her own perfume for Christmas, they smelled a rat. They examined the bottle, found traces of blood on the stopper, and quickly wrapped up the case.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the Countess's maid stabbed her with the stopper from a bottle of the Countess's own perfume, then wrapped up the bottle as a Christmas gift and placed it under the tree.

cards.title: Sayonara
case: A Japanese whaling magnate is the keynote speaker at an industry convention. Throughout his speech he is heckled by a woman in the audience who is a radical animal rights activist. As the magnate closes his speech, the woman stands, draws a gun and fires it five times, killing the magnate instantly.
The assassination is witnessed by the entire audience, yet no one lifts a hand to arrest the woman.
cards.mystery: Why wasn't the woman arrested?
clues: You can't arrest what isn't there.
The shot was followed by a bang.
story: The assassination took place in Hiroshima, Japan, on the morning of August 6, 1945, during World War II. Just a few seconds later, the U.S. dropped the first atom bomb on Japan. (The second was dropped on Nagasaki on August 9.)
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the assassination took place in Hiroshima during World War II, just before an atom bomb was dropped on the city.

cards.title: Yosemite Slim
case: Ratso, a sleazy-looking cowpoke, ambles into the blacksmith's shop and plops down a saddle, announcing it's for sale. The blacksmith pays the price of $50, then rushes to the sheriff's office. The sheriff rustles up Ratso, handcuffs him and says, "You're under arrest for the murder of Yosemite Slim."
cards.mystery: On what grounds was Ratso arrested for murdering Slim?
clues: The blacksmith shared a secret with Yosemite Slim.
Yosemite had been a prospector.
story: Yosemite Slim and the blacksmith were close friends — so close that they shared a secret. Slim was a prospector who had resolved never to be without at least $10,000 as a grubstake.

Because it was dangerous for a prospector to ride around with gold dust, Slim and the blacksmith devised a way to conceal it — in the form of pure gold rivets, rings and other hardware on Slim's saddle. After casting the gold pieces, the blacksmith coated them to disguise them as ordinary brass.

Slim had been missing for many weeks. He couldn't have sold Ratso his saddle, since Ratso was unaware of its value and had only asked $50 for it. Chances were pretty good that Ratso had come into Slim's saddle by some other means. Murder, maybe?
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the blacksmith had cast the hardware on Slim's saddle in gold, and that Slim's saddle was much more valuable than Ratso's asking price, suggesting that Ratso had murdered Slim.

cards.title: Capital Crime
case: If it hadn't been for that beer bottle cap, they would never have figured out that Paul was murdered by his wife, Paula.
cards.mystery: How did she do it?
clues: If Paula had just told Paul to get lost, he'd probably be alive today.
Paula had a magnetic personality.
story: Paul and Paula had a good marriage, until she became an animal rights activist and he an avid bear hunter. Heated arguments eventually gave way to a silent, resentful animosity. Finally, Paula realized she liked animals a lot more than she liked Paul, and decided to spare their lives by ending his.

Paula prepared for Paul's next bear-hunting adventure by sewing powerful little ceramic magnets into the lining of his thick gloves — the gloves which held his compass as he navigated the mountains. Consequently, Paul spent his last hours wandering around in circles on a cloudy day with a wind chill factor of -28 degrees. When rescuers found Paul's frozen body, the magnets were discovered when the cap of his beer remained stuck to his glove. Paula was arrested when identical magnets and thread were found in her home, and the "grizzly" affair was concluded.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Paul froze to death while lost in the woods because Paula had sewn magnets into his gloves, causing his compass to read inaccurately.

cards.title: An Evening with Pat and Mike
case: "The cops will never suspect me," Pat thought as he tiptoed toward the living room, carrying a heavy iron skillet. One whack and his murderous plan would surely pan out! Mike, his brother, would be sitting where he sat every night, in his favorite chair, falling asleep in front of the TV. Killing him would be easy and foolproof.

A week later, alerted by a concerned neighbor, police broke into the apartment and found the bodies. Both men were in the living room: Mike dead in his chair, his head severely dented; Pat in another chair, just as dead. A piece of paper was on the coffee table.
cards.mystery: Why did Pat think he could get away with murder? What really happened that fateful night?
clues: Mike had been very depressed lately.
Pat couldn't see the state his brother was in.
story: Pat was blind. He was living with his bully of a brother who kept a tight rein on his Social Security checks. The resentment built until Pat thought murder was his only way out. Being blind, he figured the police would never suspect him of such a brutal physical attack. Pat would blame it on an intruder.
Meanwhile, Mike had problems of his own. In one week, he had lost his job and his girlfriend, and he felt trapped caring for a whiny brother.

As Pat approached Mike's chair, he had no way of knowing that Mike was sitting there already dead. Mike had written a suicide note, placed it on the coffee table, then poisoned his bourbon and drank several glasses of it.
After Pat swung the skillet, he sat down, and to steady his nerves took several swigs from Mike's bourbon bottle. That was a mistake! Bye-bye, Pat!
cards.specialInformation: Pat did not commit suicide nor did Mike murder him. Pat's death was purely accidental.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Pat was blind and couldn't see that Mike was already dead from suicide and that his suicide note was on the coffee table. Pat died accidentally by swigging some of Mike's poisoned drink.

cards.title: Sink or Swim
case: The drowned body of a young woman is washed up on a foreign shore. She was murdered, but the police think it was an accidental death.
cards.mystery: Who killed her? How and why was she murdered?
clues: The woman was wearing a swimsuit.
The woman was an excellent swimmer.
story: The year is 1956. The place is Bournemouth, England — the home of Judy and Janet Edgerton, identical twins and world-class swimmers. Judy, greedy and needy, always had to have what the sweet and subservient Janet had. This even meant possessing Janet's vain and gullible husband, Giles.

Judy convinced Giles that their affair would progress swimmingly if Janet were deep-sixed. Plotting a daring role reversal at sea, Judy made plans to race in the £5000 Channel Swimming Contest and asked the unsuspecting Janet to be in the boat next to her as she swam. Giles, of course, would accompany Janet.

A well-greased Judy dove in at Dover and swam the difficult waters almost to Calais. Just before landsight, Judy grew tired and came aboard. She and Giles then knocked Janet out, slipped her wedding ring off her finger, greased her up, dressed her in Judy's swimsuit, and threw her overboard to drown.

Judy (now Janet) and Giles reported the accidental drowning to the French authorities just before Janet (now Judy) washed up on shore. The murderous pair then left rather abruptly for a trans-Atlantic cruise. They unfortunately booked passage on the ill-fated Andrea Doria. Bon voyage, Giles and "Janet"!
cards.solution: The investigators must discover that the woman washed up on shore was drowned by her husband and her identical twin (who changed places with her during an English Channel swim).

cards.title: Here, There and Everywhere
case: The suspect has an ironclad alibi. Over a dozen witnesses swear that he was nowhere near the murder scene. The police are finally able to crack the case when they find a small, high quality intercom system stashed in a closet.
cards.mystery: Who was the suspect, who was the victim and what was the alibi?
clues: The killer was a father.
The killer's alibi was a "confession."
story: Father Henderson had a nasty habit of siphoning off money from the church's roof fund to pay his gambling debts. Father Bendix discovered the thievery and threatened to go to the bishop. Father Henderson had to act quickly, even if it meant breaking the fifth commandment: "Thou shalt not kill!"

The parish of St. George had old-fashioned confessionals with small, shadowy grates separating the priest from the parishioner. The priest entered the confessional box from the vestry, out of sight from the main floor of the church. It was often hard to tell if a priest was on duty or not.

On Saturday afternoon, as Father Henderson was hearing confessions, he set up one end of a 2-way intercom in the confessional, and took the other end with him as he sneaked out of the box. He mumbled absolutions as he crept into the rectory where Father Bendix was in bed taking a nap. He picked up a plaster bust and smashed it over the sleeping priest's head, killing him instantly. Five minutes later, he was back in the confessional doing his job. Later, Henderson stashed the intercom in his closet.

A dozen or more parishioners all told the police the same story. While they didn't actually see Father Henderson that afternoon, he was certainly there, right on the other side of the wall, listening to their sins.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that a priest used a 2-way intercom system to establish his presence in a confessional while he sneaked out to murder a fellow priest who was going to turn him in to the police for thievery.

cards.title: A Fatal Attack of Gas
case: "This message was left with my answering service," the millionaire told the police. He then showed them this poem:

Your death will arrive surrounded by pains.
A poisonous gas that no one explains.
The police dismissed the threat, but the millionaire did not. "I'll protect myself if you refuse to!" he shouted.
Within a week, the millionaire was killed just as the message had predicted.
cards.mystery: Who killed the millionaire? How and where was it done?
clues: The "panes" were the glass kind.
He was killed by his own precautions.
story: Lavella Holmsley wanted her husband Ronald dead. She sent him the message — and gave him the idea of how to protect himself. "Since the poem says poisonous gas, dear, why not carry a portable oxygen tank? Then, whenever the attack comes, you can just slip on the oxygen mask."

Days later, when Ronald was leaving his office, Lavella was waiting for him in the lobby wearing a disguise. First, she edged in front of him into the revolving door. Then, as soon as she was out of the door and he was securely in the door, she wedged the door stuck and trapped him inside its glass panes.

Ronald knew immediately this was the "pane" attack predicted by the poem. He slipped on his oxygen mask, and in a second his lungs were filled with poisoned gas. Clever Lavella had switched the tanks the previous night. Ronald ended up poisoning himself!
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the man was trapped inside the panes of a revolving door, and put on an oxygen mask to avoid the poison gas attack. His oxygen tank, however, had secretly been replaced by his wife for one with deadly gas.

cards.title: D.O.A.
case: A man is brought into a hospital emergency room and pronounced dead on arrival by the attending physician, who also signs the death certificate. A week later, the doctor confesses to the crime.
cards.mystery: How did the doctor devise the D.O.A., and what led to his confession?
clues: The doctor and the victim had known each other.
The accident was a suicide.
story: The victim had committed suicide by driving his car at high speed into a bridge abutment. He had hoped to make it look like an accidental death, so that his beloved wife could take advantage of his insurance policy's double indemnity clause.

What he didn't know was that his "beloved wife" was having a torrid affair with the very doctor who would later pronounce him dead at the hospital — the very doctor who had earlier given him a phony diagnosis of terminal brain cancer. The doctor was reasonably certain that his patient would prefer suicide to a painful, lingering death, leaving his wife and the doctor free to marry.

After the man's funeral, the doctor jubilantly (and unwisely) told his lover the details of her deceased husband's demise. The widow, racked with guilt, turned him in to the local police. Under interrogation, the doctor (for whom D.O.A. now meant Doomed on Arrest) confessed to the diabolical deed.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the doctor caused the victim to commit suicide by falsely diagnosing him with terminal cancer; and that his lover (the man's widow) was driven by guilt to report him to the police.

cards.title: Unplugged
case: After several months of wedded bliss, Fred discovers his wife Ethel's well-kept secret: she had been a call girl for years before they married. The next weekend, Ethel takes their deep-sea fishing boat out alone, as she has often done before; but this time, she doesn't return. Her drowned body is later picked up by the Coast Guard, along with the boat, which sank. Although there is no damage to the boat, the bilge plug under the hull has been removed.
A week later, the Police Chief is wandering on the docks when a fisherman shows him a curiosity which turns out to be evidence on which Fred is arrested for Ethel's murder.
cards.mystery: What was the evidence? How did Fred kill Ethel?
clues: Fred got caught by the very thing Ethel had caught.
Unfortunately for Fred, the big one didn't get away.
story: Fred had attached a lure with big game fish bait to the boat's bilge plug. Once Ethel was far out to sea, the bait hooked a fish — a big, fat fish which eventually pulled out the bilge plug. Water rushed in, the boat sank, and Ethel drowned because Fred had made sure no life preservers were aboard.

Fred's plan seemed foolproof, until the same fish got hooked again, this time by a fisherman who discovered the bilge plug still attached — along with Fred's own lure which proudly (and ironically) announced: "Caught by Fred."
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Fred attached a bait-loaded lure to the bilge plug, causing the boat to sink and Ethel to drown when a hooked fish pulled it out. The fisherman later caught the same fish, with the bilge plug and Fred's personalized lure still attached.

cards.title: The Masked Murder
case: Claudia and her roommate Victor spend the evening with Claudia's twin brother, Claude. The next morning, after the tragedy, Claudia tells her story to the police. "Victor and I heard the sound of a fight coming from the library. We walked in just in time to see a man in a mask shoot my brother, then run out the French doors. Victor chased after him."
The maid confirms the last part of this story. "I saw Claude's body. There was blood everywhere. Victor was just running out to the garden. Chasing the burglar, I guess."
The gun was never found. Claudia was eventually arrested for her brother's murder. Her friend Victor, an innocent dupe in the whole sordid mess, was exonerated.
cards.mystery: How was Victor duped into helping Claudia commit murder? What happened to the gun?
clues: The police assume that Victor disposed of the gun.
Victor's full name is Champion Victor Bailey of Jokar.
story: Victor is not only Claudia's best friend — he's also her dog, a Labrador Retriever. Claudia had been planning Claude's murder for some time. Their late father, a rich, chauvinistic landowner, had willed his fortune and the family's huge country estate to the male twin, even though Claudia was older by a full ten minutes.

Claude, a trusting soul, had recently made out a will leaving everything to Claudia. Meanwhile, Claudia was busy teaching Victor a new trick: to take a warm gun from her hand and bury it deep in the woods.
The family estate contains 500 acres. It may be some time before the police find the dog's hiding place.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Victor was Claudia's dog, who was trained to take the gun and bury it in the woods.

cards.title: A Christmas Eve Surprise
case: It was a blue Christmas Eve for Donna Albans. Without any provocation, her husband Richard had walked out on her last week after just three months of marriage. That's why the present that had arrived by mail that morning was such a pleasant surprise. It was unsigned, but the card read "Just so you won't forget me!" Donna was sure it was from Richard — it was his taste.
That night, Donna went to a party and got another surprise — Richard was there. She smiled at him, but he took one look at her and walked out.
Later at home that night, Donna got one more surprise. Richard came knocking at the door. When she let him in, he shot her dead. Then he proceeded to make it look like a botched robbery.
cards.mystery: Why did Richard kill his wife?
clues: Donna wore the present to the party.
The package was addressed to D. Albans.
story: Richard had murdered his girlfriend Shelley exactly one year ago on Christmas Eve. She had been Donna's best friend. To hide his crime, he packed up Shelley's suitcases and buried the body and her luggage together. Then he spread the word that Shelley had made a sudden decision to move to Alaska.

Unfortunately someone knew about the murder, because a few weeks ago Richard started to receive anonymous letters that threatened to turn him in to the police. No wonder Richard was acting erratically!

The present that had arrived at the house was addressed to D. Albans — "D" for Dick. It was more blackmail material. It was the sweater that Richard had given to Shelley last Christmas Eve — and it had been buried with Shelley. Donna mistakenly opened the package thinking it was for her. When Richard saw Donna wearing the sweater at the party, he was convinced that she was the blackmailer and that she had married him only to gather evidence against him. Richard's next victim had to be Donna!
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the present was a sweater implicating Richard in a previous murder, and that it had been sent to Richard, not Donna. When Richard saw Donna wearing the sweater, he mistakenly thought she was the blackmailer and murdered her.

cards.title: The End of DaRode
case: Near an out-of-service country road, at the bottom of a riverbed, a successful business executive is found dead. At first, Edsel DaRode's death is thought to be accidental. But later the police suspect foul play. Found near the body are a map and a card with strange symbols on it.
cards.mystery: Who killed Edsel DaRode, and how was it done?
clues: Edsel was inside his Edsel.
The card was a fortune-teller's tarot card.
story: Marge Brown was a widow who read fortunes to make ends meet. One day, ruthless businessman Edsel DaRode phoned her for an appointment. He didn't know Madame Marge, but she certainly knew him. DaRode had driven her husband out of business and into suicide. Marge plotted revenge!
On the day of his consultation, Marge read Edsel's tarot cards. She turned over the Queen of Cups and warned him not to cross the Main Street bridge. If he did, disaster would befall him.

Horrified, Edsel absentmindedly clutched the card in his hand and ran out. He was already late for an important business appointment and had to cross the river. He took a map out of his glove compartment to look for an alternative route. A tiny wooden bridge on an out-of-service road was his only choice. Marge, of course, had already sawed through the bridge's supports, so when he tried to cross, Edsel in his shiny Edsel went for a swim.
The police traced the distinctive tarot card to Madame Marge. She broke down immediately and confessed to her murderous card play!
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Edsel drove off a bridge sabotaged by a revenge-driven fortune-teller after she had warned him off the safe main bridge.

cards.title: Rip Van Winkle RIP
case: A man wakes up in a private clinic. The doctors inform him that he has been in a coma for three years. As he rehabilitates, the man is amazed by what he's missed: new music, new styles, and political changes like the collapse of Communism.
On the fourth day of his recovery, he is found dead on the garden path below his window.
cards.mystery: How did he die? And what is the story behind his coma?
clues: The man in the clinic was a C.I.A. spy in East Germany.
The year was 1980.
story: It was early 1980. The cold war was still on and Rip Gardner, a C.I.A. spy, was captured by the East Germans. Unable to get any information from Rip, his captors hatched a plan. They drugged him, moved him to a private estate and staffed the place with English-speaking attendants.
