When the drugs wore off and Rip woke up, the "doctors" told him he was in a C.I.A. clinic in the States and that he had been in a coma for three years. They were especially convincing about the fall of Communism and the reunified Germany. Since there was no more reason to keep his secrets secret, Rip gradually felt free to discuss sensitive material with his "doctors."

On the fourth morning, he noticed that a calendar watch on a nurse's wrist said February 29: Leap Day! That date could exist in 1980, but not in 1983! Rip now knew he was never in a coma and was still in East German custody. He also knew that he had betrayed his country by disclosing secrets. Unable to live with his guilt, he leapt to his death!
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that this mystery takes place in the past. The man was a spy and had never been in a coma. He was fooled into believing that the cold war was over so he could discuss his secrets freely. Not being able to live with the guilt, he committed suicide by jumping out of a window.

cards.title: The Root of All Evil
case: Mrs. Bentley Steele, an aging Palm Beach socialite, is found sitting in a chair, dead. Among the evidence incriminating her killer is a sign on the wall next to her.
cards.mystery: Who killed Mrs. Steele? How and why was she murdered?
clues: Mrs. Steele was rich, and had no relatives.
Mrs. Steele was at the beauty salon.
story: The widowed Mrs. Steele had come to regard Monsieur Harold, her hairstylist and sometime escort, as the son she'd never had. In an unguarded moment on the dance floor at The Gator Club, she had told Harold that he was the sole heir to her $11 million fortune. Harold's eyes lit up like a cash register, as he was an inveterate loser at the dog races.

The next week, just before Mrs. Steele visited the salon for her weekly root touch-up, Harold mixed a nicotine rat poison concentrate into her hair color. Within minutes after he rubbed it into her hair, the poison seeped through her scalp and into her bloodstream. Her blood pressure shot up, and she began to perspire and claw at her throat and chest. Harold called 911, but by the time the ambulance arrived, Mrs. Steele was dead.

As Monsieur Harold carried away the remainder of the incriminating hair color, the pungent odor of tobacco from the nicotine pesticide filled his salon. Since there were many NO SMOKING signs on the walls, police immediately smelled a rat.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Mrs. Steele was at a beauty salon, whose owner stood to inherit her fortune. The owner killed her by rubbing nicotine poison into her head during a color treatment. Police became suspicious when they smelled tobacco in spite of the NO SMOKING signs.

cards.title: Good Help is Hard to Find
case: Old Harry Ashton's young wife and the housekeeper are together in the downstairs library. Suddenly they hear a scream from Harry's bathroom upstairs. The housekeeper drops her dust mop and runs up the stairs, followed a second later by the wife. Both run through Harry's bedroom into his adjoining bathroom. Harry is on the tile floor, a fatal wound in his chest. There is no knife in the bathroom or the bedroom.

Later that night, the housekeeper sneaks upstairs and recovers the weapon hidden in a hall closet. The police eventually discover the sequence of events and arrest the housekeeper — but not for murder.
cards.mystery: Who killed Harry? How did the weapon get from the bathroom to the closet? What was the housekeeper's role?
clues: When the housekeeper ran upstairs, her first act was to shut a door.
When the housekeeper recovered the knife, she had to untie it.
story: Harry Ashton was dying, and in financial straits. His insurance policy would inject much-needed cash into his failing business, but the policy would not pay out for death by his disease (a pre-existing condition) or from suicide. What he needed was a suicide that looked like a murder, but one that no one would ever be arrested for.

His plan took nerve, but was simple. He took a lightweight knife, and tied the handle to the retractable cord of a vacuum cleaner in the hall closet. There was an unobstructed path from his bathroom, through the bedroom and out to the closet. After stabbing himself, he let go and the cord retracted, pulling the knife all the way into the closet. His loyal housekeeper was his accomplice: being first on the scene, she closed the closet door, then later recovered the weapon. Ironically, it was the police, not the housekeeper, who noticed the tiny drops of blood leading to the closet.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Harry tied a knife to a vacuum cleaner cord, stabbed himself, then let the cord retract into the hall closet. The housekeeper assisted in his suicide by closing the closet door, then recovering the knife.

cards.title: Brother, Can You Share a Crime?
case: Millionaire Whitney Astorbilt is found dead, bleeding from the neck, in his Park Avenue penthouse. His killer is arrested, based on evidence involving a star.
cards.mystery: Who killed him, how, and why? How was the killer caught?
clues: Blood is thicker than water.
Every Thursday, after dinner, he signed his checks.
story: Maggie Dunham, Astorbilt's private secretary, had a brother who was a real loser, both at gambling and at life. Maggie loved her brother dearly and willingly supported his habits, until he got in over his head and was being blackmailed for $50,000 in casino gambling debts. Maggie asked Astorbilt for a loan to cover her brother's losses, but he flatly turned her down. So Maggie devised a plan to get the money.

During their weekly after-dinner check-signing session at his penthouse, Maggie waited for Astorbilt to sign his last check — a weekly expense check made out to cash for $1,000. Just as he was finishing his signature, Maggie plunged her ballpoint pen into his carotid artery (a trick she learned in a women's self-defense class). She then altered the check to read $51,000.

At the bank the next morning, Maggie was arrested. Unbeknownst to her, Astorbilt had standing instructions to the bank to question any check on which he did not place his trademark star as the dot on the "i" in his last name. Fittingly, Maggie ended up spending time in the pen.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that when Astorbilt refused to lend his private secretary money for her brother, she killed him. As he finished signing a check, she stabbed him in the neck with a pen, then changed the amount on the check. She was caught when the bank noticed the star was missing from his signature.

cards.title: Postage Due
case: John Fitzroy's one-of-a-kind postage stamp was being auctioned in his library. The stamp was first inspected by the world's foremost expert, and then passed around to all of the bidders. When the price soared to a million dollars, one of the bidders, Theo Balbi, asked to inspect it again. Looking through a magnifying glass, he announced, "This isn't the 1867 Z grill. It's an F grill — almost identical, but worth only a hundred bucks!"
The expert agreed. "This isn't the stamp I inspected. A switch has been made!"

Immediately, the security guard left the room and called the police. Everyone was frisked and the room searched thoroughly, but the prized stamp was nowhere to be found. The puzzling crime made headlines!
"I know Theo stole it," John Fitzroy growled. "He's a known thief and forger. A collector will pay a pretty price for it, even if he can never show it off in public."
cards.mystery: What happened to the stamp? And how will the thief profit from his crime?
clues: There was a fire in the fireplace.
The thief was a publicity hound.
story: The thief was Theo Balbi. He knew if he just replaced the Z grill with a forgery, it could be detected as a fake at any time. So he did more. He switched the stamps and hid the rare stamp in the simplest way possible — by dropping it into the fireplace and destroying it. He then cleverly drew attention to the switch.

What Theo wanted was merely the publicity of a theft — and he got it. A week later, Theo made another forgery of the rare stamp and sold it to a collector. The unscrupulous buyer had read the press about the "stolen" stamp and knew that Theo was present when the Z grill vanished. The buyer paid half a million for it, thinking it was the real thing. And since the Z grill was stolen property, the buyer would never be able to have it authenticated. Theo's crime will most likely go undetected since the investigators could never make their accusations stick!
cards.specialInformation: If the Investigators ask if the stamp ever left the room, the answer is "no." If they ask if the stamp is still in the room, the answer is also "no."
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Theo was the thief. He destroyed the real stamp in the fireplace, and called attention to the forgery to create the ruse of a "stolen" stamp. He then was free to peddle a newly-forged stamp as the real thing!

cards.title: The Peeping Tom Murder
case: Tom Youst enjoys using his binoculars to spy on his neighbors. One night, he sees something unexpected in the apartment across the way — the shadowy image of a man shooting a woman. Tom immediately goes into his bathroom, shaves and removes his false teeth. He then packs a suitcase, gets into his car and drives out of the city.
cards.mystery: What did Tom see through his binoculars? Where did he go, and why?
clues: Tom saw someone at his neighbors' who looked like him.
As Tom was shaving, police were receiving phone calls about him.
story: Seven years earlier, Tom's wife had divorced him for another man. Hot-tempered Tom, in a jealous rage, then shot his wife to death at the convenience store where she worked. Knowing he would be Suspect Number One, he hightailed it across the country.

Tom then settled in a small town, where he established a new identity and felt reasonably safe from the law. But while peering through his binoculars at his neighbors watching TV, he was shocked to see a re-enactment of his crime on a Most Wanted program, with an actor who looked like him. Tom "stayed tuned" in horror to see a police drawing of what he might look like today. It could have been a photograph of him taken that day: the details were exact, right down to his hair style, mustache, wrinkles and false teeth!

Certain that someone was bound to recognize him on TV, Tom ran to his bathroom and changed his appearance as best he could on short notice: he shaved his head and mustache and removed his four front false teeth. He then packed a few things and drove off in search of a safer location — a place where they don't watch so much TV!
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Tom had shot his wife to death years earlier. On a Most Wanted program on his neighbors' TV, he saw a re-enactment of his crime, and a police drawing that looked exactly like him. Knowing he would be recognized, he shaved his head and mustache, removed his false teeth and drove to a new location.

cards.title: A Terminal Encounter
case: At an airport luggage carousel, Cathi strikes up a conversation with Liz Perry. Liz tries to avoid Cathi, but Cathi insists on talking. Later, Liz takes a taxi home, while Cathi boards a plane to Paris. A week later, Liz dies at home. On returning to the U.S., Cathi is charged with her murder.
cards.mystery: How did Cathi kill Liz, and why?
clues: Theirs was a five hanky conversation.
Revenge is a dish best served cold.
story: Before their chat at the airport, Cathi and Liz had never met. But they did have a common friend — Liz's husband, Ed. Cathi recently had an affair with Ed, and went crazy when Ed broke it off. The unsuspecting Liz, a frequent traveler on business, figured prominently in Cathi's plan for revenge.

On their final tryst at the Perry house, Cathi sneaked into Liz's bathroom and dropped a dose of strychnine into her cough medicine. That same day Cathi purposely set out to catch a cold. By the time Liz arrived at the airport after a business trip, Cathi was coughing, hacking, and sneezing up a storm. She tracked Liz to the baggage carousel and struck up a conversation with her. Liz tried to avoid the chatty, infectious stranger, but Cathi coughed on her until her bags came down the chute.

The next week, Cathi was in Paris with an alibi while Liz was pouring herself an odd-smelling dose of cough medicine. At first the police suspected Ed — just what Cathi had planned in her double revenge. It was only after Ed had confessed to his affair with the crazed Cathi that police began looking for the person who gave Liz her cold.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Cathi sought revenge after Liz's husband ended their affair. Cathi had secretly poisoned Liz's cough medicine, then caught a cold and gave it to Liz on purpose. Liz died after taking her poisoned cough medicine.

cards.title: Chain Reaction
case: Mac dies in a small room of a large building. Two days later, police visit the home of Brad Thompson with a search warrant. Based on two pieces of evidence found in Brad's basement, the officers arrest him for murder.
cards.mystery: What were the two pieces of evidence? How and why did Brad murder Mac?
clues: There were a criminal killer and a non-criminal killer in this case.
Mac and Brad were both handy with tools.
story: The year is 1948. Ten years earlier, Brad's family had been massacred by Mac Shayne, in a notorious case that came to be called the "Shayne Chain Saw Slayings." After a long trial, Mac was convicted and sentenced to death.

The years Mac spent on death row took their toll in many ways: witnesses' memories faded, public sentiment ebbed, evidence lost its potency. Days before Mac was to die in the gas chamber, his third appeal, on technical grounds, seemed likely to be granted. Brad learned from a confidential informant in the Judicial Department that the appeals court was moving toward reversing the conviction because of certain procedural errors during the trial. In their reluctance to do so, they planned to wait until the last possible moment to call the prison with the order for a stay of execution.

Mac was to be sent to the gas chamber at midnight; Brad learned that the call would come in at 11:55. Vowing that justice would be served, Brad hatched a plan. At 11:45 that night, he used his chain saw to cut down the only telephone pole near the prison. With the pole down, the call didn't make it through to the prison in time to save Mac, who died minutes later in the gas chamber.
Police immediately suspected Brad and obtained a search warrant. What they found in his basement was his chain saw, with sawdust traceable to the telephone pole he cut down.
cards.specialInformation: The killer is Brad Thompson. His offense is criminal homicide. The murder weapon is Brad's chain saw. Although Mac died in the gas chamber, the gas pellets were not the murder weapon, and the state did not commit homicide even though Mac's death was wrongfully carried out.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Mac died in prison in a gas chamber for murdering Brad's family. Brad's crime was murdering Mac: using a chain saw, Brad cut down the only telephone pole near the prison, so that the call ordering Mac's stay of execution could not go through. The two pieces of evidence were Brad's chain saw and the sawdust.

cards.title: Coup de Grass
case: Harry is found dead on the grass in Southern California. His murderers are never found.
cards.mystery: Who killed Harry? How did he die, and what became of his murderers?
clues: The grass was on a field.
The murderers were killed the next morning.
story: It was December, 1941. Ursula Sanders, a famous aviatrix, was in love with her mechanic and wanted to be permanently free of her abusive husband, Harry. She and her lover, Tom, hatched a plan.

Ursula talked Harry into taking flight with her in her Lockheed Vega, a single engine plane that could fly long distances. When Harry arrived at the deserted grass airstrip early the next morning, Ursula was already in the cabin with the engine running. As Harry started to get into the plane, Tom appeared from behind the plane with a gun, and forced Harry to back up — right into the whirling propeller. Tom then climbed into the cabin, and off he flew with Ursula for a Hawaiian vacation.

The next morning, on December 7, 1941, the dastardly duo flew over Pearl Harbor. Unfortunately for them, it was the worst possible moment in history to do so — they were quickly shot down as Japanese fighter planes closed in for a surprise attack. Aloha-ha!
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Harry's wife and her lover killed him by forcing him to back into the propeller of his wife's airplane. When the wife and her lover flew over Pearl Harbor the next morning, on December 7, 1941, they were shot down during the Japanese attack.

cards.title: Polly Want a Lawyer
case: Dottie Fenwick brings her late aunt's African grey parrot to a pet shop to be rehomed. While she fills out the paperwork, the bird keeps squawking the same phrase in a terrified voice. The shop owner listens for a minute, then quietly phones the police. Two days later, Dottie's uncle, Gerald, is arrested for murder.
cards.mystery: What did the parrot say, and why did it lead to Gerald's arrest?
clues: The aunt's death had been ruled an accidental fall.
The only witness had feathers.
story: Gerald pushed his wife down the basement stairs and told police she had tripped while carrying laundry. With no witnesses, the death was ruled an accident. But the couple's parrot, Captain, had been on his perch at the top of the stairs. African greys copy voices perfectly, and Captain had picked up the last thing his owner screamed: "Not the stairs, Gerald! Not the stairs!"

The shop owner recognized the name from the obituary. Police reopened the case and found scuff marks on the railing that matched Gerald's work boots. Gerald learned the hard way that a little bird really can tell.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the parrot had witnessed the murder and was repeating the victim's last words, "Not the stairs, Gerald!", which showed the fall was no accident.

cards.title: Under Cover
case: A blizzard begins at 10 p.m. Just after midnight, someone breaks into Harmon's Jewelry and empties the display cases. Suspicion falls on Vic Dorsey, a former employee with a grudge who lives two miles away. "I've been home since nine o'clock," Vic yawns at his door at 6 a.m. "My car's been sitting right there in the driveway all night."
The officer glances at the car, now buried under a foot of snow, then crouches down to look underneath it. A moment later, Vic is under arrest.
cards.mystery: What did the officer see under Vic's car?
clues: The officer was more interested in the ground than in the car.
Snow can't fall where something is already parked.
story: If Vic's car had been parked in the driveway since nine o'clock — an hour before the snow started — the ground beneath it would have stayed bare and dry: a car-shaped patch of pavement with no snow at all. Instead, the officer found a smooth layer of snow under the car, several inches deep. That meant the car had been parked there long after the blizzard began.

Vic had driven to the jewelry store at midnight, emptied the cases with a key he'd copied before he was fired, and parked back in his driveway at 1 a.m. — right on top of three hours of snowfall. The stolen jewelry was found stuffed in his snow boots in the hall closet. Vic's alibi was a real snow job.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that there was snow underneath Vic's car, proving that he had parked it after the blizzard started — so he had been out during the night when the store was robbed.

cards.title: Wet Paint
case: Sometime on Monday, a small gold statue disappears from the Egyptian Room of the city museum. Museum guard Lenny Pruitt swears he never set foot in the Egyptian Room that day — he was posted at the front entrance from opening to closing. But when the detective notices a smudge on the cuff of Lenny's uniform, she arrests him for the theft.
cards.mystery: What was on Lenny's cuff, and why did it prove he was lying?
clues: The museum was closed on Sunday for a little sprucing up.
Some signs should be taken seriously.
story: On Sunday, while the museum was closed, painters repainted the walls of the Egyptian Room a distinctive shade called "Nile Turquoise" — a color used nowhere else in the building. On Monday morning, "WET PAINT" signs hung in the room, and it was roped off to visitors.

At lunchtime, Lenny slipped under the rope, lifted the statue from its case and hid it in his lunch box. But as he reached past the case, his sleeve brushed the wall. The turquoise smudge on his cuff matched the fresh paint exactly. Lenny hadn't been caught red-handed — he'd been caught turquoise-handed.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the Egyptian Room had just been painted a unique color, and that a smudge of that wet paint on Lenny's cuff proved he had been in the room.

cards.title: Gourd Grief
case: Two days before the county fair, Martha Higgins's giant pumpkin — the odds-on favorite for the blue ribbon — vanishes from her garden overnight. At the fair, her neighbor Clem Puckett wins first prize with a 1,100-pound pumpkin that looks awfully familiar. Clem insists he grew it in his own patch.
The sheriff visits both gardens, then strips Clem of his ribbon and arrests him.
cards.mystery: How did the sheriff prove that the prize pumpkin was Martha's?
clues: Every pumpkin has to be attached to something while it grows.
The pieces fit together like a puzzle.
story: A pumpkin grows on a thick vine, and to harvest it you must saw through its stem. When Clem stole Martha's pumpkin in the dead of night, he left a fresh stump on the vine in her patch.

The sheriff found that stump, still green and newly cut. Then he checked Clem's patch — and found no vine anywhere big enough to have grown a 1,100-pound giant, and no cut stump at all. Finally, he held the stem of the prize pumpkin against Martha's stump. The jagged saw cut matched perfectly. Clem's prize-winning ways had turned out to be nothing but a lot of stem and bluster.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the sheriff matched the cut stem of the prize pumpkin to the freshly sawed stump on the vine in Martha's garden, and that Clem's garden had no vine that could have grown it.

cards.title: Easy Squeezy
case: Eight-year-old Rosie runs a lemonade stand on a hot afternoon. A man in sunglasses buys a cup with a twenty-dollar bill and tells her to keep the change. Rosie is thrilled — until she knocks over a pitcher of lemonade onto her cash box. That evening, her mother takes the twenty to the police station, and three days later the man in sunglasses is arrested.
cards.mystery: Why did Rosie's mother go to the police, and what crime was the man arrested for?
clues: Real money can survive a trip through the washing machine.
Rosie's twenty didn't hold up as well as her one-dollar bills.
story: The man in sunglasses was a counterfeiter who passed his fake bills where nobody was likely to look closely — like a little girl's lemonade stand. Real money is printed with special ink on paper made of cotton and linen, so it doesn't run when it gets wet.

When the lemonade spilled, Rosie's real dollar bills were simply soggy. But the green ink on the twenty smeared and ran into a puddle. Rosie's mom realized the bill was fake and took it to the police, along with Rosie's careful description of "the nice man with the shiny sunglasses and the red convertible." Police found a printing press in his garage. His scheme went sour, but Rosie got a reward — and a much bigger lemonade stand.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the man paid with a counterfeit twenty-dollar bill, and that its ink ran when lemonade spilled on it, which real money's ink does not do.

cards.title: Fudge Factor
case: Overnight, someone breaks into Granny Pearl's Candy Kitchen and steals the week's cash from the register. The thief wore gloves and left no fingerprints, but he couldn't resist a little snack on his way out. Two days later, police arrest Duane Kettle, the delivery driver who brings the shop its sugar.
cards.mystery: What evidence did the thief leave behind, and how did it point to Duane?
clues: The thief had a sweet tooth.
Duane had a very distinctive smile.
story: On his way out, the burglar helped himself to a slab of Granny Pearl's famous peanut butter fudge, took one big bite, and dropped the rest on the counter when a car's headlights swept past the window. Fudge is soft yet firm — perfect for holding a clear bite mark.

The police dentist noticed two unusual things about the bite: a wide gap between the two front teeth and a chipped tooth on the left side. Granny Pearl knew that smile right away. Duane flashed it every Tuesday when he delivered the sugar. A dental impression made it official. Duane learned that crime doesn't pay — and neither does snacking on the job.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the burglar bit into a piece of fudge and left it behind, and that the bite mark matched Duane's gap-toothed, chipped smile.

cards.title: Salt in the Wound
case: Dolores Pembrook has won the Pine County Pie Contest seven years in a row. This year, the judges take one bite of her famous apple pie and spit it out. "It tastes like the Dead Sea!" cries one. Every other pie in the contest tastes just fine — but by the end of the day, one of the other contestants has been disqualified and charged with tampering.
cards.mystery: How was Dolores's pie sabotaged, and how was the culprit caught?
clues: All the bakers used ingredients from the same supply table — except one.
Sugar and salt look a lot alike.
story: Contestants had to bake in the fairground kitchen using ingredients from a shared supply table. Dolores always arrived first, at dawn. Her rival, Bea Crumley, who was in charge of the supply table, swapped the labels on the sugar and salt bins before dawn, then switched them back as soon as Dolores had measured out her two cups of "sugar."

The other bakers arrived later and used the correctly labeled bins. But Bea was afraid of getting mixed up in her own trick, so she secretly baked her pie with sugar she'd brought from home in a jar. When the judges asked why one contestant hadn't used the official supplies like everyone else, Bea had no good answer — and her fingerprints were all over both bin labels. Her bid for the blue ribbon had been a recipe for disaster.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the supply manager swapped the sugar and salt labels just long enough for Dolores to put salt in her pie, and gave herself away by secretly using her own sugar from home.

cards.title: Straw Man
case: Every night for two weeks, ripe peaches have been disappearing from the Calloway family's orchard. Farmer Calloway sits up on his porch with a flashlight and a clear view of the trees, but he never sees a soul come or go. Then, early one morning, he notices that the scarecrow in the middle of the orchard is wearing a brand-new pair of sneakers. He calls the sheriff.
cards.mystery: Who was stealing the peaches, and how did the thief avoid being seen?
clues: The thief was out standing in his field.
Farmer Calloway never looked twice at the orchard's guardian.
story: The thief was Calloway's teenage farmhand, Skeeter Bolt, who was selling the peaches at a roadside stand two towns over. Every evening before dark, Skeeter took the old scarecrow down, hid it in the tall grass, put on its floppy hat and straw-stuffed coat, and took its place on the post.

Farmer Calloway saw only his trusty scarecrow standing in the moonlight. Whenever the farmer dozed off or went inside, Skeeter climbed down and filled his sacks, then climbed back up before Calloway returned. One morning, in a hurry, Skeeter forgot to swap his own sneakers for the scarecrow's old work boots. The sheriff found the real scarecrow in the grass and Skeeter's stash of peaches in the barn. Skeeter's career as a straw man had come to the end of the row.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the farmhand disguised himself as the scarecrow every night, stole peaches whenever the farmer wasn't looking, and gave himself away by forgetting to take off his own new sneakers.

cards.title: Cold Cache
case: On a snowy January morning, thieves smash the window of Glitter & Gold Jewelers and grab a tray of diamond rings. Police catch the getaway car five minutes later, three blocks away, but the two men inside have no rings, no bags, and nothing in their pockets but car keys. Without evidence, police have to let them go. Three weeks later, during a warm spell, both men are arrested again — this time with the rings.
cards.mystery: Where were the rings hidden, and how were they found?
clues: Children in the neighborhood had a busy morning.
The evidence came to light during a thaw.
story: During their getaway, the thieves knew they might be stopped. As they drove past a park where children had built a row of snowmen, they pulled over and stuffed the rings deep inside the biggest snowman's belly, packing fresh snow over the hole. They planned to come back when things quieted down.

But the weather beat them to it. A warm spell melted the snowman into a slushy puddle, and a dog walker noticed diamonds glittering in the slush. Police staked out the park, and the next night the two thieves showed up with flashlights, frantically digging through the slush. They had chosen a hiding place with a very short shelf life.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the thieves hid the rings inside a snowman during their getaway, and were caught when the snowman melted and police watched the spot.

cards.title: Masked Getaway
case: At 4 p.m. on October 31, three robbers in rubber monster masks hold up the First National Bank on Main Street. They run out the front door with bags of cash, and two police cars arrive within a minute. Witnesses say the robbers escaped on foot — yet they seem to have vanished into thin air.
cards.mystery: Where did the robbers go, and how did they get away?
clues: The date is important.
Main Street was very crowded that afternoon.
story: The robbers had carefully chosen the day and time: Halloween afternoon, just as the town's annual costume parade marched down Main Street past the bank. Hundreds of people, children and adults alike, were dressed as monsters, witches and ghosts. The three robbers simply stepped off the bank steps and joined the parade, waving to the crowd, with the bags slung over their shoulders like trick-or-treat sacks. The police were looking for three people in monster masks — and found about sixty.

But the robbers made one mistake. At the end of the parade, the judges handed out a prize for "Best Group Costume," and the three monsters couldn't resist accepting it. Their photo in the next day's paper showed them holding the bank's money bags. It was the trick that came with the treat.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the robbers escaped by joining the town's Halloween costume parade, blending in with hundreds of other people in monster costumes.

cards.title: No Parking
case: On a busy weekday afternoon in the middle of downtown, two men steal a brand-new luxury sports car in front of dozens of witnesses — including a police officer directing traffic at the corner. Nobody tries to stop them. In fact, the officer waves them through the intersection.
cards.mystery: How did the thieves steal the car in plain sight?
clues: The thieves never got inside the car.
The car was parked beside a fire hydrant.
story: The thieves drove a tow truck they had painted to look exactly like the city's official tow trucks, right down to the city seal and the flashing yellow lights. They cruised downtown looking for expensive cars parked illegally. When they spotted the sports car beside a fire hydrant, they hooked it up, tucked a phony ticket under the wiper, and towed it away.

Everyone who saw them thought the owner was simply getting what he deserved. The officer even held up traffic so the "city" tow truck could make its turn. When the owner called the impound lot, they had never heard of his car. Eleven stolen cars later, the thieves were caught when they tried to tow a car belonging to the chief of police — who happened to be sitting in the driver's seat. Their scheme had finally run out of road.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the thieves used a fake city tow truck to haul away an illegally parked car, so onlookers assumed it was being legally towed.

cards.title: Just Right
case: A family returns home from a morning walk to find their front door open. Someone has eaten breakfast from their table, broken a piece of furniture and messed up the beds. The intruder is still in the house, sound asleep upstairs. When the family wakes her, she jumps out of the window and runs away. The family decides not to press charges.
cards.mystery: Who were the victims, and who was the intruder?
clues: The family members came in three sizes.
The intruder was very particular about temperature and comfort.
story: The family was the Three Bears — Papa Bear, Mama Bear and Baby Bear. While their porridge cooled, they went for a walk in the woods. Along came a girl named Goldilocks, who let herself in. She tasted all three bowls of porridge and ate all of Baby Bear's, which was just right. She sat in all three chairs and broke Baby Bear's, which was also just right. Then she tried all three beds and fell asleep in Baby Bear's — which was, of course, just right.
When the Bears found her, she leaped out of the window and ran all the way home. She was never seen in the woods again, and the Bears installed a better lock.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the victims were the Three Bears and the intruder was Goldilocks.

cards.title: A Great Fall
case: A large, round, well-dressed gentleman is found in pieces at the bottom of a wall. The king's entire cavalry and infantry rush to the scene, but none of them can do anything to help.
cards.mystery: Who was the victim, and what happened to him?
clues: The victim had a very thin skin.
He had been sitting on the wall just before the incident.
story: The victim was Humpty Dumpty, a very large egg. He had been sitting on a wall, as he often did, when he lost his balance and had a great fall. All the king's horses and all the king's men rushed to the scene, but they couldn't put Humpty together again.
The royal investigators ruled it an accident — though some suspect he simply cracked under the pressure.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the victim was Humpty Dumpty, who fell off a wall and broke, and that all the king's horses and all the king's men couldn't put him together again.

cards.title: A Gift Horse
case: A great walled city has held out against an enemy army for ten long years. One morning, the citizens wake to find that the enemy has sailed away, leaving behind a single enormous gift outside the city gates. The overjoyed citizens bring the gift inside and celebrate all day. By the next morning, the city has fallen.
cards.mystery: What was the gift, and how did the city fall?
clues: The gift was made of wood and stood on four legs.
It wasn't empty.
story: The city was ancient Troy, and the enemy was the Greek army. Unable to break through Troy's walls, the Greeks built a giant wooden horse, hid a band of their best soldiers inside it, and pretended to sail home. The Trojans dragged the horse into the city as a trophy of victory.

That night, while the city slept off its celebration, the Greek soldiers climbed out, opened the city gates, and let in the rest of the Greek army, which had secretly sailed back under cover of darkness. To this day, people warn, "Beware of Greeks bearing gifts" — and never look a gift horse in the mouth... or anywhere else.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the city was Troy, and that Greek soldiers hidden inside a giant wooden horse sneaked out at night and opened the gates to the Greek army.

cards.title: Remember, Remember
case: Just after midnight, guards searching a cellar beneath a government building find a man in a cloak and a tall hat. He is carrying matches, a lantern and a pocket watch. Beside him are 36 barrels hidden under piles of firewood. He is arrested on the spot. Centuries later, people still celebrate the night of his arrest every year with bonfires and fireworks.
cards.mystery: Who was the man, what was in the barrels, and what was he planning?
clues: The building was in London, and the year was 1605.
He was arrested on the fifth of November.
story: The man was Guy Fawkes, and the barrels were full of gunpowder. Fawkes was part of a group of conspirators who planned to blow up the Houses of Parliament during its grand opening ceremony, killing King James I and much of his government.

One of the plotters sent an anonymous letter warning a friend to stay away from Parliament that day. The letter reached the king's ministers, the cellars were searched, and Fawkes was caught with the matches in his pocket. The British still celebrate Guy Fawkes Night every November 5th with fireworks — the very thing Fawkes never got to set off.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the man was Guy Fawkes, caught guarding barrels of gunpowder he planned to use to blow up the Houses of Parliament and King James I in the Gunpowder Plot of 1605.

cards.title: A Tea Party
case: One cold December night, a band of men disguised as Mohawk warriors board three ships in a harbor. They are quiet and orderly. They harm no one and steal nothing, yet by the time they leave, they have destroyed a fortune in cargo. Most of them are never punished, and some of them later become famous.
cards.mystery: What was the crime, where did it take place, and why was it done?
clues: The year was 1773.
The water in the harbor suddenly became very strong.
story: It was the Boston Tea Party. American colonists, angry that Britain was taxing them without giving them a voice in Parliament, disguised themselves as Mohawk warriors and boarded three British ships in Boston Harbor. They dumped 342 chests of tea into the sea — about 92,000 pounds of it.

"No taxation without representation!" was their rallying cry. The Tea Party helped spark the American Revolution, and several of its participants became heroes of the new nation. It may have been the most expensive pot of tea ever brewed.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the crime was the Boston Tea Party, in which colonists disguised as Mohawk warriors dumped British tea into Boston Harbor to protest taxation without representation.

cards.title: An Apple a Day
case: A beautiful young woman collapses on the floor of a small cottage in the woods. Her seven housemates find her lying perfectly still and fear the worst. Later, she is revived when a stranger on horseback gives her a kiss. Her attacker is never arrested, but she does get what's coming to her.
cards.mystery: Who was the young woman, and who tried to kill her? How was it done?
clues: The attacker was jealous of her looks.
The young woman took a bite of fruit from a kindly old peddler.
story: The young woman was Snow White. Her vain stepmother, the Queen, asked her magic mirror every day who was the fairest of them all. When the mirror finally answered "Snow White," the Queen was furious. Snow White fled into the forest and moved in with seven dwarfs.

The Queen disguised herself as an old peddler woman, found the cottage, and offered Snow White a poisoned apple. One bite, and Snow White fell into a deathlike sleep. The dwarfs watched over her until a prince rode by and woke her with a kiss. As for the Queen, her magic mirror had nothing more to say to her.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the young woman was Snow White, who was poisoned with an apple by her jealous stepmother, the Queen, disguised as an old peddler.

cards.title: Lights On
case: The Ashford family is away on a two-week cruise. To keep burglars away, they've put the lights on timers: every evening, the living room lamp turns on at 7:00 and off at 11:00. Neighbors see the light come on every night, just as if someone were home. Nevertheless, on the fifth night, burglars back a van into the driveway and calmly empty the house.
cards.mystery: How did the burglars know the house was empty?
clues: The burglars watched the house for several nights before the break-in.
Real people aren't that punctual.
story: The burglars made a habit of driving through quiet neighborhoods at dusk, watching for houses that seemed a little too perfect. At the Ashford house, they noticed that the living room lamp clicked on at exactly 7:00 every night and off at exactly 11:00 — never a minute early, never a minute late. No other light in the house ever came on, the curtains never moved, the TV never flickered, and the trash cans never went out to the curb on collection day.

Real families just aren't that predictable. The burglars broke in at 11:01, right after the lamp went off. When the Ashfords came home, they bought smarter timers — and asked a neighbor to put out the trash.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the burglars noticed the lamp went on and off at exactly the same time every night with no other signs of life, and realized the lights were on timers and the family was away.

cards.title: Overdue
case: A gas station in the small town of Maple Falls is held up at gunpoint. A week later, police in a city 200 miles away stop a car that matches the getaway car's description. The driver, Rudy Sloane, insists he has never been to Maple Falls in his life — he doesn't even know where it is. Then an officer looks at the back seat, and Rudy is arrested.
cards.mystery: What did the officer find on the back seat?
clues: Rudy was a reader.
Rudy owed somebody a small fine.
story: While Rudy was watching the gas station in Maple Falls, waiting for the right moment, he killed time in the town's public library, where it was cool and quiet. He liked a mystery novel so much that he got a library card under a fake name and checked it out.

The book was lying on his back seat when he was pulled over — stamped "MAPLE FALLS PUBLIC LIBRARY," with a due-date card in the pocket showing it had been checked out two days before the robbery. Rudy learned that libraries don't just lend books; they also keep very good records. His book, like Rudy, was now seriously overdue.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the officer found a library book from the Maple Falls Public Library, checked out just before the robbery, proving that Rudy had been in the town.

cards.title: Bottled Up
case: A rare golden fish worth $20,000 disappears from its tank at the city aquarium. Guards check every visitor's bags at the exit but find nothing. The only odd thing anyone notices is a man who seems awfully thirsty — yet never takes a sip.
cards.mystery: How was the fish smuggled out of the aquarium?
clues: The thief didn't need a bag.
The fish needed water to survive the trip.
story: The thief was a collector of rare fish who wanted the golden prize for his private tank. He walked into the aquarium carrying a large, clear sports bottle full of water. When the crowd around the tank moved on, he scooped up the small fish with a little net, dropped it into his bottle and screwed the lid back on.

At the exit, the guards checked his pockets and waved him through. After all, who searches a water bottle? But one sharp-eyed guard noticed that the man clutched his bottle all the way to the parking lot without ever taking a drink. She followed him to his car and, through the side of the bottle, saw a flash of gold. The thief was in hot water — and the fish went back into cool water.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the thief smuggled the fish out of the aquarium inside a clear water bottle.

cards.title: Exit Stage Left
case: In the second act of a mystery play at the Royal Theatre, the stage goes black for ten seconds while a gunshot sound effect plays. When the lights come back up, the leading man, Rex Valentine, is gone. The audience applauds what they think is a clever magic trick. But Rex has fallen through an open trapdoor in the stage and broken his neck on the concrete floor below. His understudy, Barry Pinch, is later arrested.
cards.mystery: How did Barry kill Rex?
clues: The trapdoor was only supposed to be opened in Act Three.
Barry had nothing to gain unless Rex left the play for good.
story: Barry had been Rex's understudy for three years and had never once gone on stage. In Act Three of the play, the villain escapes through a trapdoor in the stage floor, so the trapdoor was kept bolted shut for the first two acts. During the blackout in Act Two, Rex always crossed the dark stage to stand by the fireplace — walking right over the trapdoor.

Before the show, Barry crept under the stage and slid the bolt open. In the blackout, the trapdoor gave way beneath Rex. Barry finally got the leading role — for one performance. The stage manager remembered seeing him under the stage before curtain, and the bolt was covered with his fingerprints. It was Barry's final curtain call.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the understudy unbolted the stage trapdoor before the show, so that Rex fell through it in the dark during the Act Two blackout.

cards.title: Glove Story
case: In a championship boxing match, Kid Malone knocks out the defending champion, "Iron" Mike Tully, in the third round. Tully never regains consciousness and dies the next day. At first, it is ruled a tragic accident of the sport. But after the boxing commission examines Malone's gloves, his trainer is charged with murder.
cards.mystery: What was wrong with Malone's gloves, and why was the trainer charged?
clues: The gloves were heavier at the end of the fight than at the beginning.
The trainer wrapped Malone's hands before every fight.
story: Malone's trainer, Sal Grimes, had bet his life savings — and a good deal of borrowed money — on his fighter to win. Before the fight, Sal wrapped Malone's hands with gauze and tape as usual, but this time he had soaked the wraps in plaster of Paris. Between rounds, as he poured water over his fighter's head to "cool him down," he made sure some of the water trickled into the gloves. By the third round, the plaster had hardened into something like a cast. Malone was hitting Tully with fists of stone.
The commission's inspector found the hardened plaster when he cut the gloves open. Malone, who hadn't known what his trainer had done, was cleared. Sal was down for the count.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the trainer soaked Malone's hand wraps in plaster of Paris, which hardened during the fight and turned his punches deadly.

cards.title: Blade Runner
case: Figure skater Tess Navarro is leading the national championship going into her final routine. On her first jump, one of her skate blades twists loose and she crashes to the ice, breaking her wrist. Her rival, Kristen Holm, skates a flawless routine and wins the gold. A week later, Kristen's coach is arrested.
cards.mystery: What happened to Tess's skate, and how was the coach caught?
clues: A skate blade is held on by tiny screws.
The coach borrowed something from the arena's maintenance room.
story: Kristen's coach, Ivan Brisk, knew his skater could never beat Tess on a fair day. While the skaters warmed up, he slipped into the locker room and used a jeweler's screwdriver to loosen the screws holding Tess's left blade to her boot — not enough for her to notice while walking, but enough that the blade would twist loose under the force of a landing.

Arena investigators found fresh scratches on the screw heads. The tiny screwdriver came from the maintenance room, where Ivan had signed it out "to fix a loose skate." Ivan's career went downhill fast. Kristen, who knew nothing of the scheme, gave her gold medal to Tess.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the rival skater's coach loosened the screws on Tess's skate blade so it came off when she landed a jump.

cards.title: Clean Break
case: Two climbers are halfway up a sheer cliff, roped together, when the lower climber, Ned Farris, falls to his death. His partner, Jasper Coyle, tells the park rangers that the rope rubbed against a sharp ledge and frayed through. The rangers recover both ends of the rope, take one look, and arrest Jasper.
cards.mystery: What did the rangers notice about the rope?
clues: Rocks don't make tidy cuts.
Jasper's pocketknife was very sharp.
story: Ned had discovered that Jasper had been stealing from their climbing club's treasury and had promised to tell everyone back at camp. Halfway up the cliff, Jasper cut the rope with his pocketknife and let Ned fall. Then he claimed the rope had frayed against the rock.

But a rope that wears through against a sharp edge leaves a ragged, fuzzy end, with fibers broken at different lengths. Both ends of this rope were sliced cleanly and evenly, every fiber cut at the same point. The rangers found rope fibers caught in the hinge of Jasper's knife. His story had come apart at the seams.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the rope's ends were cut cleanly rather than frayed, proving that Jasper had cut it with his knife.

cards.title: Doggone It
case: Champion show poodle Lady Duchess is stolen from her owner's backyard. The owner, Vivian Prentiss, pays a $10,000 ransom, and the next day the dog is returned unharmed, freshly groomed and wearing her famous pink bows. Vivian is overjoyed — until that evening, when she calls the police again.
cards.mystery: Why did Vivian call the police after her dog was returned?
clues: Lady Duchess knew a dozen tricks.
The dognapper saw Lady Duchess every week.
story: The dognapper was Lady Duchess's groomer, Bonnie Sheers, who saw a chance to make money twice. After collecting the ransom, she kept the real Lady Duchess to breed championship puppies and returned a lookalike poodle she had bought for a few hundred dollars, groomed to look exactly like the champion.

But that evening, when Vivian said, "Dance, Duchess!" the dog just sat there. It didn't roll over, wave or play dead, either. Vivian's vet scanned the dog for the identity microchip implanted in Lady Duchess as a puppy and found nothing. Police traced the pink bows to Bonnie's shop and found the real Lady Duchess in her kennel. Bonnie's scheme had gone to the dogs.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the dog returned was a groomed lookalike, not Lady Duchess; Vivian realized it when the dog didn't know any of Lady Duchess's tricks. The groomer had kept the real dog.

cards.title: Going Underground
case: Over a long holiday weekend, the vault of the Second Street Bank is emptied. The vault door is still locked and the alarm never went off. The only clue is the new shop next door, which opened two months earlier — a wig shop that hardly ever had a single customer.
cards.mystery: How did the robbers get into the vault?
clues: The wig shop's employees carried a lot of heavy boxes out to their truck every evening.
The robbers took the low road.
story: The robbers rented the empty store beside the bank and opened a "wig shop" as a front. Every day, behind a curtain in the back room, they dug a tunnel under the wall toward the bank's vault. Every evening, they carried the dirt out to their truck in boxes labeled "WIGS." Customers who did wander in found the prices so high that they left without buying anything — which suited the robbers just fine.

Over the holiday weekend, they broke up through the vault floor and cleaned out the safe deposit boxes. Police found the tunnel when they noticed that the wig shop had closed for good the same weekend. The crooks were caught when one of them tried to sell a stolen ring to the jeweler across the street — who recognized it as his own.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the robbers opened a fake shop next door to the bank and dug a tunnel to break into the vault from below.

cards.title: Wish You Were Here
case: A valuable painting is stolen from a mansion in Boston. The prime suspect, art dealer Philippe Moreau, says he was on vacation in Paris that week, and he proves it with a postcard he mailed to his sister. It is postmarked Paris on the day of the theft and reads: "Gorgeous sunny weather all week — not a cloud in the sky! Wish you were here." The detective checks one fact and arrests him.
cards.mystery: How did the detective prove the postcard was a fake alibi?
clues: Philippe's friend was in Paris that week.
The detective checked an old newspaper.
story: Philippe wrote the postcard before he ever left Boston, then gave it to a friend who was flying to Paris and asked her to mail it on a particular day. The postmark was genuine, but Philippe had made one mistake: he guessed at the weather.

The detective looked up the weather in Paris for that week and found that it had rained every single day — so much that the river Seine had nearly flooded. The friend admitted mailing the card for him, and the painting was found in Philippe's storage locker in Boston. Philippe's alibi was all wet.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Philippe had a friend mail a pre-written postcard from Paris, but the sunny weather he described was wrong — it had rained in Paris all week.

cards.title: Rolling Getaway
case: At the village fair, a giant wheel of prize-winning cheese worth $5,000 is stolen from the judging tent. Police seal off the fair, but nobody leaves carrying anything big, round or cheese-shaped. That evening, the cheese is found in the back of a pickup truck at the bottom of a steep hill on the edge of town.
cards.mystery: How did the thief get the cheese out of the fair?
clues: Every year, the fair holds a famous race.
Everyone was chasing the cheese, but nobody tried to stop it.
story: The highlight of the fair was the annual cheese-rolling race, in which a wheel of cheese is sent tumbling down a steep hill and dozens of contestants chase after it. The thief, Clive Ruddock, swapped the prize cheese for the plain race cheese while the judges were at lunch.

When the race began, the prize cheese went bouncing down the hill — and two hundred people chased it straight past the police checkpoint. At the bottom, Clive's brother was waiting by the finish line with his pickup truck. In the confusion, he scooped up the cheese and drove off. But the judges soon noticed that the cheese left in their tent tasted a lot plainer than the one they had judged, and the race winners complained they had never received their prize. The brothers' plan was full of holes — like a good Swiss.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the thief swapped the prize cheese for the race cheese, and that it was rolled down the hill during the cheese-rolling race, where an accomplice picked it up at the bottom.

cards.title: Pay and Display
case: For twenty-two years, a friendly man in a uniform collected a parking fee of one pound per car at the entrance to a city zoo's parking lot. Visitors paid him cheerfully every day. One morning, he simply stopped showing up. When the zoo asked the city council to send a replacement, the council said that wasn't its job. The zoo said it wasn't theirs either.
cards.mystery: Who was the parking attendant, and what crime had he committed?
clues: The attendant was never on anybody's payroll.
He retired to a sunny place.
story: The parking attendant didn't work for anybody. He had bought a uniform and a ticket machine, set up a little booth at the entrance to the zoo's parking lot, and started collecting fees. The zoo assumed he worked for the city council. The council assumed he worked for the zoo. Nobody ever asked.

Over twenty-two years, at several hundred pounds a day, he collected a fortune. Then he quietly retired to Spain. The zoo and the council are still arguing about who should have noticed. He had parked himself on top of a gold mine.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the attendant was a con man who set up his own booth and collected parking fees for years, because the zoo and the city council each thought he worked for the other.

cards.title: Bright Idea
case: A burglar breaks into the Kowalski home while the family is out at the movies. He wears gloves inside the house and leaves no fingerprints on the windows, the drawers or the jewelry box. But detectives find a perfect set of his fingerprints on the front porch, and he is arrested.
cards.mystery: Where did the burglar leave his fingerprints?
clues: The porch was dark when the family came home.
The burglar didn't put on his gloves until he got inside.
story: The Kowalskis always left the porch light on when they went out. The burglar, Freddy Finch, didn't want to be seen picking the front door lock under a bright light, so he reached up and unscrewed the porch light bulb with his bare hand. Only then did he pull on his gloves and get to work.

When the family came home to a dark porch, they called the police instead of trying to fix the light. A detective noticed that the bulb wasn't burned out — it had simply been loosened — and dusted it. The glass held two crisp prints from Freddy's thumb and finger. Freddy wasn't the brightest bulb on the porch.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the burglar unscrewed the porch light bulb with his bare hand before putting on his gloves, leaving his fingerprints on the bulb.

cards.title: Web of Lies
case: Overnight, someone steals a box of rare coins from Edgar Thorne's study. Edgar's nephew, Wesley, who is staying in the guest room, says he slept soundly all night. Police find the outside door to the cellar unlocked, and Wesley insists that's how the burglar got in: "Anyone could have come in through the cellar." The detective takes one look at the cellar doorway and arrests Wesley.
cards.mystery: What did the detective see that proved Wesley was lying?
clues: The cellar had a resident who works the night shift.
Its handiwork was perfectly intact.
story: Wesley stole the coins himself to pay off a gambling debt. Then he went down to the cellar and unlocked the outside door to make it look as though a burglar had come in that way.

What he didn't notice in the gloom was a large spider web stretched across the doorway, from the door frame to an old coat hook, glistening with morning dew. Nobody could have walked through that doorway without breaking the web. The burglary had to be an inside job. The detective asked to see Wesley's suitcase, and the coins were wrapped in his socks. Wesley had spun quite a tale, but the spider had spun a better one.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that an unbroken spider web stretched across the cellar doorway, proving that nobody had come through it, so the burglar was someone already inside the house.

cards.title: Keep the Change
case: On Christmas morning, police find two burglars outside a large suburban house. One has a burn shaped like a doorknob on his palm, and the other has a bruise shaped like a paint can on his forehead. Both are covered in feathers and complaining about tarantulas and marbles. The only person who was home at the time was an eight-year-old boy.
cards.mystery: What happened?
clues: The boy's family had flown to Paris for the holidays without him.
The burglars called themselves the "Wet Bandits."
story: This case is the plot of the movie Home Alone. In the rush to the airport, the McCallister family accidentally left their youngest son, Kevin, behind. When two burglars, Harry and Marv, tried to break into the house on Christmas Eve, Kevin defended his home with a series of booby traps — including a red-hot doorknob, paint cans swinging from the staircase, marbles on the floor, a tarantula, and glue and feathers.
The bruised and battered "Wet Bandits" were finally arrested, and Kevin's mother made it home in time for Christmas morning.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that this is the story of Home Alone: a boy accidentally left home alone at Christmas defended his house from two burglars with homemade booby traps.

cards.title: Food Fight
case: For a month, someone at the Dunmore Insurance office has been stealing lunches from the break room refrigerator. Paula Grant has lost four sandwiches and a slice of birthday cake. On Friday, she brings in a special sandwich. That afternoon, she marches into her boss's office and names the thief — even though she never saw anyone take it.
cards.mystery: How did Paula identify the lunch thief?
clues: Paula's sandwich had a little extra kick.
The thief spent a lot of time at the water cooler that afternoon.
story: Paula made a delicious-looking turkey sandwich and loaded it with the hottest pepper sauce she could find — a sauce so hot it came with a warning label. She put it in the fridge with a note: "Paula's lunch — PLEASE don't take!" At lunchtime, it was gone.

Twenty minutes later, Gary from accounting was sitting at his desk, red-faced and sweating, gulping cup after cup of water and refusing to explain why. Paula walked over, set a carton of milk on his desk and said, "That'll help more than water, Gary." He confessed on the spot. Gary had finally bitten off more than he could chew.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Paula laced her sandwich with extremely hot pepper sauce, and the thief gave himself away with a red face and a desperate thirst.

cards.title: Spin Cycle
case: At the 6 p.m. headcount at Stonebridge Prison, inmate Lou "Slick" Malone is missing. The prison is locked down and searched from top to bottom. There is no tunnel, no cut fence and no ladder, and the guards swear no inmate walked past the gates all day. The only vehicle that left the prison that afternoon was a truck that leaves every afternoon.
cards.mystery: How did Slick escape?
clues: Slick worked in the prison laundry.
The truck took the dirty laundry away to be washed.
story: Slick's prison job was folding sheets in the laundry. Every afternoon, a contractor's truck hauled away big canvas carts of dirty sheets and towels to a commercial laundry across town. One afternoon, Slick climbed into a cart and a fellow inmate piled dirty sheets on top of him. The guards waved the truck through as usual.

At the laundry, Slick climbed out, grabbed a uniform off a rack and walked out the front door. He might have gotten clean away — but the uniform he grabbed had "STONEBRIDGE PRISON LAUNDRY" printed across the back. He was picked up an hour later at the bus station. His escape had come out in the wash.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Slick hid in a cart of dirty laundry and was carried out of the prison on the laundry truck.

cards.title: Cat Burglar
case: For months, the residents of Willow Lane have been missing things: socks, gloves, a toy mouse, a pair of underwear and a man's wristwatch. No house has been broken into, and nobody has seen a stranger on the street. Then one morning, Mrs. Abernathy at number 14 opens her back door and finds several of the missing items on her doormat.
cards.mystery: Who was the thief?
clues: The thief came and went through very small openings.
The thief left the loot on the doorstep as a gift for someone it loved.
story: The thief was Mrs. Abernathy's own tabby cat, Mr. Whiskers. Every night, Mr. Whiskers slipped out through the cat flap, prowled the neighborhood, and crept in through other people's cat flaps and open windows. He brought home his prizes — socks, gloves, a watch, and once a pair of underwear from a clothesline — and proudly left them on his owner's doorstep, the way cats leave mice.
Mrs. Abernathy returned everything with an apology and a plate of cookies. Mr. Whiskers was sentenced to house arrest, but he was never truly sorry. He was, after all, a real cat burglar.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the thief was Mrs. Abernathy's cat, who stole things from the neighbors' houses and left them on his owner's doorstep as gifts.

cards.title: Bad Hair Day
case: A department store has been losing jewelry, perfume and watches every week. Store detectives watch every customer closely and check shopping bags, purses and pockets. One customer who visits every Saturday — a sweet elderly woman with an enormous, towering hairdo — never carries a bag and is never stopped.
cards.mystery: How was the jewelry being stolen?
clues: The woman's hairstyle went out of fashion decades ago.
Her hair was not entirely her own.
story: The "sweet little old lady," known to police in three states as Big Hair Harriet, wore a giant beehive wig that rose a full foot above her head. The wig was hollow inside. Every Saturday, she tried on watches and necklaces at the counter, and whenever the clerk looked away, she tucked one up into her hairdo with a quick pat.

One Saturday, a blast from an air conditioning vent tipped her wig slightly sideways, and a gold watch tumbled out onto the counter. The clerk handed it back and said, "I believe this belongs to the store." Harriet's career had come undone.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the woman was hiding stolen goods inside her tall, hollow beehive wig.

cards.title: Off Color
case: A man in a ski mask robs a convenience store at gunpoint. The clerk, too frightened to look at his face, notices only one thing about him: one of his socks was bright red, and the other was bright green. Police have three suspects who were near the store that night. The detective asks each of them a simple question about traffic lights, then arrests one of them.
cards.mystery: What was the detective's question, and why did the answer point to the robber?
clues: The robber didn't realize his socks didn't match.
One of the suspects had once been turned down for a job as a pilot.
story: The detective guessed that anyone who would go out in one red sock and one green sock without noticing might have red-green color blindness — the most common kind. To people with this condition, red and green can look almost the same.

The detective asked each suspect, "What color is the top light on a traffic light?" Two answered "red" right away. The third, Dennis Loomis, hesitated and said, "I go by position — top means stop." Dennis had failed the color vision test when he applied to flight school years earlier. A search of his apartment turned up the stolen cash — and a drawer full of mismatched socks.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the robber was color-blind and couldn't tell red from green, and the detective identified him by his answer about the colors of a traffic light.

cards.title: Get Rich Quick
case: Thousands of people answer a newspaper ad that reads: "LEARN THE SECRET TO MAKING MONEY BY MAIL! Send $5 to P.O. Box 77." Every one of them receives a reply that tells them exactly what the ad promised. Nevertheless, postal inspectors arrest the man who placed the ad for fraud.
cards.mystery: What did the reply say?
clues: The secret worked — for the man who placed the ad.
The reply was very short.
story: Everyone who sent in $5 received a small printed card that said: "Place an ad in the newspaper just like this one." The man had technically revealed the secret to making money by mail — it was exactly what he was doing himself.

After 40,000 replies and $200,000, postal inspectors decided that the "secret" was a swindle and charged him with mail fraud. The judge agreed. His secret to making money by mail ended with a new mailing address — the state penitentiary.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the reply simply told people to place the same ad themselves; the scheme only made money for the man who placed it.

cards.title: Spelling Bee
case: Millionaire Chester Pike receives an anonymous letter: "I know about the favour you did for the mayor. Leave $50,000 in a grey bag at the park bandstand on Friday, or the whole town will find out. Don't try to pay by cheque, and don't involve the police." Chester has four relatives who might know his secret. After reading the letter carefully, the detective narrows it down to one.
cards.mystery: Which relative did the detective suspect, and why?
clues: Chester's nephew Nigel grew up in London.
Look closely at how certain words are spelled.
story: The letter writer gave himself away with British spellings: "favour" instead of "favor," "grey" instead of "gray," and "cheque" instead of "check." Chester's other relatives had all grown up in Ohio. His nephew Nigel had grown up in London and moved to America only two years earlier.

When police searched Nigel's flat — er, apartment — they found a rough draft of the letter. Nigel had been undone by his own vocabulary. Chester agreed not to press charges if Nigel took a very long holiday — er, vacation.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the letter used British spellings — favour, grey and cheque — pointing to the nephew who grew up in London.

cards.title: Left Out
case: Wealthy art collector Walter Brandt is found slumped at his desk with a gun in his right hand and a bullet wound in his right temple. A typed note on the desk says, "I can't go on." His business partner, Carl Dietz, tells the police that Walter had been depressed for months. The detective looks around the study — at the pen on the left side of the desk, the watch on Walter's right wrist and the coffee cup with its handle turned to the left — and arrests Carl for murder.
cards.mystery: Why did the detective decide that it wasn't suicide?
clues: Walter didn't do things the way most people do.
The gun was in the wrong hand.
story: Walter Brandt was left-handed. He kept his pen on the left side of the desk, wore his watch on his right wrist and turned his coffee cup's handle to the left. A left-handed man who shot himself would almost certainly use his left hand.

Carl, who had been stealing from their business, shot Walter and then pressed the gun into his right hand without thinking — because Carl himself was right-handed. Under questioning, Carl admitted he had never noticed which hand his partner used. It was a fatal oversight.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Walter was left-handed, so the gun in his right hand showed that someone else — his right-handed partner — had staged the suicide.

cards.title: Fall Back
case: Art dealer Simone Varga is found strangled in her gallery on a Sunday afternoon. The coroner puts the time of death at 2:30 p.m. Her business partner, Leo, has a perfect alibi: a photo on his camera, stamped 2:30 p.m., shows him at the harvest parade, 40 minutes across town. Even so, the detective arrests Leo after studying the photo for less than a minute.
cards.mystery: How did the detective see through Leo's alibi?
clues: The murder happened the morning after the clocks changed.
The town hall clock was in the background of the photo.
story: Leo wanted Simone's half of the gallery. He knew that daylight saving time had ended at 2 a.m. that Sunday, when the clocks "fell back" one hour, and that his camera never set its own clock. So he went to the parade, made sure a passerby snapped his photo, and drove straight to the gallery.

The camera stamped the picture 2:30, but the real time was only 1:30 — which gave him plenty of time to reach the gallery and kill Simone at 2:30. Unfortunately for Leo, the town hall clock towered over the parade route behind him, plainly reading half past one. His alibi was an hour too good to be true.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Leo's camera hadn't been set back at the end of daylight saving time, so the photo was really taken an hour earlier than its time stamp. The town hall clock in the background showed the true time, leaving Leo enough time to drive to the gallery and kill Simone.

cards.title: Elementary, My Dear
case: Professor Helen Marsh, a chemistry teacher, is found dead in her laboratory, struck on the head with a heavy iron lab stand. Before she lost consciousness, she managed to write something on the chalkboard: the number 47. Police have three suspects — graduate students Robert Gold, Lisa Silver and Andrew Copperfield. After seeing the chalkboard, the detective arrests one of them.
cards.mystery: Which student did the detective arrest, and why?
clues: The professor couldn't write a whole name, but she wrote what she knew best.
Every element has a number.
story: Professor Marsh was a chemist to her very bones. In her last moments, she wrote the atomic number of the element silver: 47. (Gold is 79, and copper is 29.)

The professor had caught Lisa Silver faking her research results and told her she would be expelled. In a panic, Lisa struck her with the lab stand. She assumed the "47" was just part of an old equation. But the detective had taken chemistry, too. Lisa's career in science had come to a solution she hadn't anticipated.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that 47 is the atomic number of silver, so the professor was naming her killer, Lisa Silver.

cards.title: Idle Threat
case: Frank Delaney, a famously heavy sleeper, is found dead in his bed one winter morning. The coroner says he died of carbon monoxide poisoning. Frank's car, in the attached garage, ran for hours during the night with the garage door closed. Frank's wife was visiting her sister 300 miles away that night, but she is charged with murder.
cards.mystery: How did Frank's wife start the car while she was 300 miles away?
clues: Frank's wife had given him a gift for Christmas.
The gift was designed for cold winter mornings.
story: For Christmas, Frank's wife, Lorraine, had a remote car starter installed in his car so he could warm up the engine on cold mornings without leaving the house. Frank loved it.

Lorraine wanted out of the marriage, but Frank had a large life insurance policy, and she decided being a widow would be more profitable. Before leaving to visit her sister, she pulled the batteries from the carbon monoxide detector in the hallway, set the starter so it wouldn't shut itself off, and hid the spare remote in the garage, taped to a cheap electric timer that would press its button at 1 a.m. At 1 a.m., the car started in the closed garage, and the fumes seeped into the house. Police found the timer still taped to the remote, and the receipt for it in Lorraine's purse. Her alibi was 300 miles long, but her plan fell short.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the wife rigged a timer to set off the car's remote starter in the closed garage during the night and disabled the carbon monoxide detector, so Frank was poisoned by exhaust fumes while she was away.

cards.title: Recalculating
case: Late one rainy night, Gordon Pratt drives home from a business dinner in a part of the county he doesn't know well. The next morning, his car is found at the bottom of the lake, just past the end of a boat ramp. Gordon has drowned. His business partner, Ross, who was at a party with forty other people that night, is charged with murder.
cards.mystery: How did Ross arrange Gordon's death?
clues: Gordon trusted a voice in his car.
Ross borrowed Gordon's car the day before.
story: Gordon always relied on his car's navigation system, especially at night in unfamiliar places. He had saved his home address under the button marked "HOME." Ross, who wanted full control of their company, borrowed Gordon's car the day before "to pick up a client" and changed the saved home address to the end of the Lakeside Boat Ramp.

That night, in pouring rain and pitch darkness, Gordon pressed "HOME" and dutifully followed the directions: "In 200 feet, turn right... continue straight." He drove down the ramp and into the lake. Police noticed that the navigation system was set to guide the car to a boat ramp, and its records showed that the address had been changed while Ross had the car. Ross's plan had steered him straight to prison.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Ross changed the "home" address in Gordon's car navigation system to a boat ramp, so Gordon drove into the lake at night following its directions.

cards.title: Field Guide
case: Eleanor Voss, an experienced mushroom hunter, dies after eating a dish of wild mushrooms she picked herself. She was always extremely careful, checking every mushroom against her favorite field guide before cooking it. The book is found open on her kitchen table. Her nephew, who is her only heir, is arrested.
cards.mystery: How did the nephew trick his aunt into eating poisonous mushrooms?
clues: Eleanor trusted her book completely.
One page was a little different from all the others.
story: Eleanor's nephew, Marcus, worked in a print shop. He knew his aunt identified every mushroom using the same well-worn field guide. While visiting, he borrowed the book, took it home and secretly replaced a single page. On the new page, a deadly mushroom was pictured and described as "Pale Meadow Cap — edible, excellent sautéed in butter." He glued the page in so carefully that it was almost impossible to tell.

The next week, Eleanor found a patch of "Pale Meadow Caps," checked them against her trusted guide and cooked them for dinner. Police noticed that the paper of that one page was slightly whiter than the rest and was the only page without a single coffee stain. The printing was traced to Marcus's shop. He hadn't counted on anyone reading between the lines.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the nephew replaced a page in Eleanor's field guide so that a deadly mushroom was described as edible, and she trusted the book and ate them.

cards.title: On the Rocks
case: At a dinner party, two business rivals, Hal and Vincent, agree to settle their differences with a drink. They pour two glasses of punch from the same bowl, both with ice, and toast each other. Hal drains his glass in one gulp and leaves for a meeting. Vincent sips his slowly as he chats with the other guests. An hour later, Vincent collapses and dies of poisoning. Hal is perfectly fine, and the punch bowl shows no trace of poison.
cards.mystery: How was Vincent poisoned when Hal, who drank the same punch, was unharmed?
clues: It took time for the poison to work its way into the drink.
The poison was in the drink, but not in the punch.
story: Hal had frozen poison inside the ice cubes he dropped into both glasses. When Hal gulped his punch down in one go, the ice had barely begun to melt, so he swallowed almost none of the poison. Vincent, as Hal well knew, always sipped his drinks slowly. As the ice melted, the poison was released into his glass, a little more with every sip.
Hal made sure to leave before Vincent collapsed. But police found the rest of the poisoned ice cubes in a bag in Hal's freezer. Hal's plan was cool, but not quite cool enough.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the poison was frozen inside the ice cubes; Hal drank his punch quickly before the ice melted, while Vincent sipped his slowly and drank the poison as the ice melted.

cards.title: Ghost Writer
case: Wealthy recluse Cornelius Bell dies, and his housekeeper produces a handwritten will dated March 3, 1961, leaving her his entire estate. The handwriting and signature look authentic. But a lawyer for Bell's family reads the will closely, points to the address written at the bottom, and the housekeeper is charged with forgery.
cards.mystery: What was wrong with the address on the will?
clues: The address ended with a five-digit number.
