The post office made a big change in 1963.
story: The will left everything to "Mrs. Agnes Pruitt, 22 Elm Street, Riverton, Ohio 45207." But the United States Post Office didn't introduce ZIP codes until July 1963 — more than two years after the will was supposedly written. Nobody writing an address in 1961 would have included one.

The housekeeper had forged the will after Bell's death, carefully copying his handwriting from old letters, but she had added the ZIP code to her address out of habit. Her plan was stamped "Return to Sender."
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the will included a ZIP code, which didn't exist until 1963, proving that the will dated 1961 had been forged later.

cards.title: The Missing Smile
case: On a Monday morning in 1911, the most famous painting in the world vanishes from one of the most famous museums in the world. There is no sign of a break-in. For two years, nobody knows where it is. Then an art dealer in Florence, Italy, receives a letter from a man offering to sell it to him.
cards.mystery: What was the painting, who took it, and how?
clues: The museum was closed on Mondays.
The thief had once worked at the museum, building glass cases for the paintings.
story: The painting was Leonardo da Vinci's Mona Lisa, and the museum was the Louvre in Paris. The thief was Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian handyman who had helped install protective glass cases on the Louvre's paintings. On Sunday, he hid in a storage closet overnight. On Monday morning, when the museum was closed to the public, he came out wearing the white smock that all the workers wore, lifted the painting off the wall, removed its frame and glass, hid it under his smock and walked out.

He kept the painting in a trunk in his room for two years. When he tried to sell it to the dealer in Florence, the dealer called the police. The Mona Lisa went home to Paris — and she's been smiling ever since.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the painting was the Mona Lisa, stolen from the Louvre in 1911 by a former worker who hid overnight and walked out with it under his work smock on a Monday when the museum was closed.

cards.title: Spirited Away
case: Guests at the Lakeview Inn have been checking out in the middle of the night. They complain of eerie music, moaning voices and a woman's ghostly laughter coming from the walls of their rooms. Bookings have dropped to almost nothing. Then the inn's owner discovers a thin wire running up the side of the chimney, and the owner of a rival hotel across the lake is arrested.
cards.mystery: How was the "haunting" done, and why?
clues: The ghost only made itself heard after midnight.
The rival hotel had been nearly empty until the haunting began.
story: Harlan Gage, owner of the Pinecrest Hotel, was losing business to the newly renovated Lakeview Inn across the lake. One night, he climbed onto the Lakeview's roof and hid a small speaker and radio receiver inside the old central chimney, which connected to the fireplaces in all the upstairs rooms.

Every night after midnight, Harlan broadcast recordings of creepy music, moaning and laughter from his office across the lake. The sounds echoed down the chimney into every guest room. Terrified guests checked out — and many of them checked in at the Pinecrest. The inn's owner followed the wire up the chimney, found the receiver and called the police. Harlan's ghost story had finally given up the ghost.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that a rival hotel owner hid a radio speaker in the inn's chimney and broadcast spooky sounds at night to scare away the guests.

cards.title: Grin and Bear It
case: The Hollis family files an insurance claim for $40,000, saying a bear broke into their mountain cabin while they were away. They show photos of torn screens, claw marks on the doors and a wrecked kitchen. But the insurance investigator takes a close look at the claw marks, then at the tool shed behind the cabin, and the claim is denied. The Hollises are charged with fraud.
cards.mystery: How did the investigator know the bear was a fake?
clues: A bear's claws aren't all the same length or evenly spaced.
Something in the shed had sharp prongs.
story: The Hollises had wrecked their own cabin to collect insurance money for a new kitchen. To make the claw marks, they dragged a four-pronged garden claw across the doors and walls.

But a bear's paw has five claws of different lengths, and its scratches are uneven and slightly curved. The marks on the cabin had only four lines, perfectly straight, perfectly parallel and exactly the same distance apart every time. In the shed, the investigator found a four-pronged garden claw whose prongs matched the spacing exactly — with flecks of the cabin door's green paint still on the tips. The Hollises had to grin and bear the consequences.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the "claw marks" were made with a four-pronged garden tool — they were perfectly even and parallel, with only four lines instead of a bear's five uneven claws.

cards.title: Escape Artist
case: The Great Zoltan is the world's most famous escape artist. In front of a sold-out audience, he is handcuffed, locked in a glass tank of water and hidden behind a curtain. He has performed the trick five hundred times and always escapes in under two minutes. This time, after four minutes, his assistant pulls back the curtain, and Zoltan has drowned. His longtime rival is arrested.
cards.mystery: What went wrong with the trick, and how did the rival make it happen?
clues: Every escape artist has a secret.
The rival had once been Zoltan's assistant.
story: The secret to Zoltan's escape was a set of trick handcuffs with a hidden release — a tiny catch that only Zoltan knew how to press. His rival, The Amazing Morello, had been Zoltan's assistant years earlier and knew the secret.

Morello bribed a stagehand to swap Zoltan's trick cuffs for an identical-looking pair of real police handcuffs. Underwater, Zoltan pressed the hidden catch again and again, but nothing happened. Police found the trick cuffs in Morello's dressing room. Morello had made his final appearance — in a courtroom.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the rival switched Zoltan's trick handcuffs for real ones, so Zoltan couldn't free himself underwater and drowned.

cards.title: Pass the Salt
case: At a dinner party for eight, everyone is served the same soup, from the same pot, by the same waiter. The host, Sir Reginald Thorne, dies at the table of poisoning. All the other guests are perfectly fine. The soup pot, the bowls and the spoons show no trace of poison.
cards.mystery: How was Sir Reginald poisoned, and who did it?
clues: Sir Reginald had a well-known habit at the dinner table.
Every other guest found the soup perfectly seasoned.
story: Sir Reginald was famous for shaking salt over every dish before he tasted it — a habit his cook found deeply insulting. His nephew, Basil, who stood to inherit Sir Reginald's fortune, knew this well. Before dinner, Basil filled the silver salt shaker at his uncle's place with salt mixed with poison. The other guests were happy with the cook's seasoning, and nobody else touched that shaker, which sat right beside the host's plate.
Sir Reginald salted his soup generously, as always. Police found the poison in the shaker and Basil's fingerprints on its silver cap. Basil's plan had been seasoned with a little too much confidence.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the nephew poisoned the salt shaker at Sir Reginald's place, knowing his uncle always salted his food before tasting it.

cards.title: Hole Story
case: Avid ice fisherman Leon Petrak walks out onto the frozen lake one January morning to his favorite fishing spot and falls through the ice. He drowns in the freezing water. Everywhere else on the lake, the ice is a foot thick. Leon's fishing buddy, Arnie, is arrested.
cards.mystery: Why was the ice thin in that one spot, and how was the danger hidden?
clues: Arnie had been out on the lake alone the day before.
A fresh layer of snow fell overnight.
story: Leon owed Arnie a lot of money and had refused to pay it back. The day before, Arnie went out to Leon's favorite fishing spot and cut a large hole in the ice with an ice saw. Overnight, the hole froze over with a thin skin of new ice, and a fresh snowfall covered it completely, so it looked exactly like the rest of the lake.

When Leon walked out at dawn, he stepped onto the thin ice and fell through. Police divers noticed that the hole had perfectly straight, square edges — cut by a saw, not cracked by nature. Arnie's ice saw, still wet, was in the back of his truck. Arnie had skated on thin ice for the last time.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Arnie sawed a hole in the ice at Leon's fishing spot the day before; it refroze thinly and was hidden by fresh snow, so Leon fell through.

cards.title: Shadow of a Doubt
case: Mrs. Cora Delacroix is murdered at her home at 7:30 a.m. Her stepson, Lyle, says he was nowhere near — he was at the beach, 50 miles away, from 11 a.m. until sunset. He shows the police a photo of himself on the sunny beach, which he says a stranger took for him at noon. The detective studies the photo and arrests Lyle.
cards.mystery: What did the detective notice in the photo?
clues: The sun was shining brightly.
At noon, the sun is high in the sky.
story: Lyle had gone to the beach at dawn, asked a jogger to take his photo at about 6 a.m., then driven straight to his stepmother's house and killed her at 7:30. He planned to claim the photo was taken at noon.

But in the photo, Lyle's shadow stretched out behind him across the sand — far longer than he was tall. At noon, when the sun is high overhead, shadows are short and stubby. Such a long shadow meant the sun was low in the sky — early morning or late evening. The detective found the jogger, who remembered "the guy who wanted his picture taken at sunrise." Lyle's alibi was only a shadow of the truth.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Lyle's shadow in the photo was very long, which meant the photo was taken early in the morning, not at noon — giving him time to commit the murder.

cards.title: Pollen Count
case: Someone breaks into the greenhouse of famous orchid grower Dame Iris Finch and steals six rare orchids worth $100,000. Her rival, Desmond Pike, claims he hasn't been near her estate in years. But a forensic botanist examines Desmond's coat, and he is arrested.
cards.mystery: What did the botanist find on Desmond's coat?
clues: Some flowers grow in only one place in the whole country.
Flowers leave a trace on anything that brushes against them.
story: Dame Iris's greenhouse contained a rare Brazilian vine with bright orange flowers — the only one in the country. When Desmond squeezed between the plants to reach the orchids, the vine brushed against his coat and left a fine dusting of orange pollen on his sleeve.

Pollen grains are tiny, but under a microscope every type of plant has its own unique shape. The botanist identified the pollen as coming from a plant that grew nowhere but in Dame Iris's greenhouse. The stolen orchids were found in Desmond's own greenhouse with new labels. Desmond had been caught by a flower he never even noticed.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Desmond's coat carried pollen from a rare plant that grew only in Dame Iris's greenhouse, proving he had been there.

cards.title: Read My Lips
case: Two men sit at a corner table in a noisy, crowded diner, talking quietly with their heads close together. Nobody could possibly hear a word they say. Across the room, a woman eating pie alone watches them for a while, then leaves and goes straight to the police. Two nights later, police are waiting when the two men try to break into the jewelry store on Grand Avenue.
cards.mystery: How did the woman learn about the robbery plan?
clues: The woman couldn't hear a thing — and never could.
She didn't need to.
story: The woman, Martha Kemp, had been deaf since childhood and was an expert lip reader. From across the diner, she had a clear view of both men's faces. They thought the clatter of the diner would cover their conversation, but Martha didn't need sound. She read every word as they planned to break into the jewelry store on Grand Avenue at 2 a.m. on Friday by cutting through the roof.
She wrote it all down and took her notes to the police. When the two men dropped through the roof, officers were waiting. The robbers had said far too much without ever raising their voices.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the woman was deaf and could read lips, so she understood the robbers' plan just by watching them talk.

cards.title: Purl Harbor
case: During World War II, a sweet old woman sits at the window of her apartment overlooking a busy railway yard every day, knitting. She knits scarves for "the boys overseas" and mails them every week to a "nephew" in a neutral country. She is arrested as a spy.
cards.mystery: How was she sending military secrets?
clues: She watched the trains carefully while she knitted.
Knitting has two basic stitches — and Morse code has two basic signals.
story: The old woman was an enemy spy. Every time a train full of soldiers or tanks passed through the railway yard, she recorded it in her knitting. Knitting uses two basic stitches, knit and purl, which can stand for the dots and dashes of Morse code or form a simple code for numbers. A row with a certain pattern of purl stitches might mean "troop train," and another pattern might mean "tanks."

Her scarves looked perfectly ordinary, but anyone who knew the code could read them like a letter. A wartime postal censor who happened to be an expert knitter noticed that the scarves had strange, irregular patterns of stitches and showed them to military intelligence. They unraveled her plot, stitch by stitch.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the woman was recording trains carrying troops and equipment in coded patterns of stitches in her knitting, and mailing the scarves abroad.

cards.title: Ribbon Cutting
case: The night before final exams, Professor Hartley types the exam questions on his office typewriter, makes one copy and locks it in his safe. The next morning, the safe hasn't been touched, but a student has sold perfect copies of the questions to half the class. The professor's wastebasket was emptied overnight by the janitor's student helper, Kyle.
cards.mystery: How did Kyle get the exam questions without opening the safe?
clues: The typewriter was an old-fashioned office model.
Kyle found what he needed in the trash.
story: Professor Hartley's typewriter used a single-use plastic film ribbon. Each time a key strikes, it knocks a letter-shaped piece of ink off the ribbon onto the paper — leaving a clear, letter-shaped gap in the ribbon. The used ribbon becomes a perfect record of everything that was typed, one letter after another.

That night, the professor put in a new ribbon and threw the old one in the wastebasket. Kyle, emptying the trash, unspooled it and read the whole exam letter by letter. The professor figured it out when he found his empty ribbon cartridge in Kyle's dorm room. Kyle's scheme had failed the test.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Kyle took the professor's used typewriter ribbon from the trash; the single-use ribbon held an imprint of every letter typed, so he could read the whole exam.

cards.title: Lucky Break
case: Elderly Mr. Fenwick has played the same lottery numbers every week for thirty years. One Monday, he hands his ticket to the clerk at the corner store and asks her to check it. She runs it through the machine and says, "Sorry, Mr. Fenwick, not a winner this time." She tosses it in the trash. A week later, the clerk is arrested.
cards.mystery: What did the clerk do, and how was she caught?
clues: Mr. Fenwick's ticket was worth more than he knew.
Mr. Fenwick never changed his numbers.
story: The ticket was actually a winner worth $250,000. The clerk, Darlene, palmed the real ticket, tossed an old losing ticket into the trash, and later claimed the prize herself.

But Mr. Fenwick's grandson, reading the winning numbers in the newspaper, recognized them as Grandpa's numbers — the family's birthdays, which he had played every week for thirty years. The lottery commission checked its records and found that the winning ticket had been bought at Darlene's store on Saturday, at the exact time Mr. Fenwick always bought his, and cashed in by Darlene. The store's security camera showed her switching the tickets. Darlene's luck had run out.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the clerk told Mr. Fenwick his winning ticket was a loser, kept it and cashed it herself; she was caught because his family knew he always played the same numbers.

cards.title: Sleeper Car
case: On an overnight train, a passenger is found shot dead in his sleeping compartment. His neighbor in the next compartment, Mr. Grey, says he heard nothing at all. Neither did anyone else in the car. Yet the bullet came from a gun in Mr. Grey's luggage.
cards.mystery: How did the killer make sure nobody heard the shot?
clues: Mr. Grey had studied the train's route very carefully.
For about a minute, nobody on the train could hear anything.
story: Mr. Grey had planned the murder of his business rival down to the minute. He knew the train passed through a long mountain tunnel at exactly 2:14 a.m., and that inside the tunnel, the roar of the wheels echoing off the rock walls was deafening. He slipped into his victim's compartment just before the tunnel and fired the shot the moment the train entered it. The noise of the tunnel covered the sound completely.
But Mr. Grey had forgotten to wipe his fingerprints from the compartment's door handle, and the gun was still in his suitcase. He had planned for every sound except the conductor's knock on his door.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the killer fired the shot as the train passed through a long, noisy tunnel, which drowned out the sound of the gunshot.

cards.title: Nothing to Declare
case: A tourist returns home from Europe with a cheap, amateurish watercolor of a sunset that he says he bought at a street market for $20. Customs officers wave it through without a second look. Six months later, the FBI arrests him for smuggling a stolen masterpiece.
cards.mystery: How was the masterpiece smuggled?
clues: The masterpiece was hidden in plain sight.
The sunset washed off easily.
story: A famous oil painting had been stolen from a museum in Italy. To smuggle it out of the country, the thieves had an artist paint a cheap-looking sunset in water-based paint right over the top of the oil painting. Oil paint and water don't mix, so once the painting arrived in America, the sunset could be gently washed away, revealing the masterpiece underneath.

The "tourist" was a courier for an art theft ring. He was caught when the art restorer he hired to clean off the sunset recognized the painting underneath from a list of stolen works and called the FBI. It was the most expensive sunset he'd ever seen.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that a stolen oil masterpiece was hidden under a cheap watercolor painted over it, which could be washed off later.

cards.title: Lemon Aid
case: A prisoner at Graystone Penitentiary writes cheerful letters to his sister every week. The guards read every letter, but they're about nothing but the weather, his health and his sister's lemonade recipe. One day, the warden runs a hot clothes iron over one of the letters, and an escape is stopped in its tracks.
cards.mystery: What was hidden in the letters, and how did the warden find it?
clues: The prisoner had a lot to say about lemons.
Some writing only appears when it's heated.
story: The prisoner and his sister were writing in invisible ink — lemon juice. On paper, lemon juice dries clear and can't be seen. But when it's heated, the juice turns brown and the hidden writing appears.

Between the lines of his ordinary letters, the prisoner wrote secret messages about a plan to escape on laundry day, and his sister wrote back about the getaway car. The warden grew suspicious because the letters kept mentioning lemons — and smelled faintly sour. He ran a hot iron over one, and the whole escape plan appeared in brown letters. When life handed the prisoner lemons, he made a big mistake.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the prisoner and his sister were writing secret messages in lemon juice, an invisible ink that appears when heated, and the warden revealed them with a hot iron.

cards.title: Toll Story
case: For six weeks, drivers on a quiet country road pay a $2 toll at a small booth before crossing an old bridge. The man in the booth wears a reflective vest and hands every driver a receipt. Then a driver who works for the county highway department wonders why she's never heard of the toll and sends someone to check. The booth is gone, and so is the man.
cards.mystery: What was the crime?
clues: The county had never charged a toll on that bridge.
Nobody wanted to argue over two dollars.
story: The toll booth was a fake. A con man named Earl Dibble built it out of plywood, painted it to look official, bought a reflective vest and printed receipts that read "COUNTY BRIDGE TOLL." Drivers grumbled, but they paid. Two dollars wasn't worth an argument, and the booth looked real enough.

Earl collected more than $20,000 before anyone checked. By then, he had loaded the booth onto a trailer and moved on to the next county. He was caught a month later, setting up his booth on a road right in front of a sheriff's station. His crime had finally taken its toll.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that a con man set up his own fake toll booth and collected tolls from drivers who assumed it was official.

cards.title: Under the Covers
case: In the middle of a July heat wave, businessman Kurt Haller is found dead in bed by his housekeeper at 9 a.m. The medical examiner arrives at 10 a.m., notes that the body is still warm, and estimates that Kurt died around 6 a.m. His wife, Lena, has an airtight alibi from 5 a.m. on — she was boarding an early flight to Chicago. But a detective notices something odd in the bedroom, and Lena is charged with murder.
cards.mystery: What did the detective notice, and how did Lena fool the medical examiner?
clues: It was a sweltering night, but Kurt was tucked in very cozily.
A warm body seems to have died more recently.
story: After death, a body slowly cools, and medical examiners use its temperature to estimate the time of death. Lena smothered Kurt with a pillow at midnight, then covered him with an electric blanket turned up to high before she left for the airport. The blanket kept the body warm, so the medical examiner believed Kurt had died hours later than he really had — when Lena was already at the airport.
But the detective noticed that someone had used an electric blanket on the hottest night of the year, and that it was still switched on. Lena's alibi had been unplugged.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Lena killed Kurt at midnight and covered him with a switched-on electric blanket, which kept the body warm and made it seem he had died hours later, after she had left for the airport.

cards.title: Sweet Deception
case: For a month, the Queen's Emerald sits safely in its glass case at the Grandview Museum, watched by guards and cameras 24 hours a day. Then, on a hot summer afternoon, a guard notices a trail of ants marching into the case. The museum director immediately calls the police.
cards.mystery: Why did the ants alarm the museum director?
clues: Ants have no interest in real gemstones.
Someone had made a very sweet copy.
story: A month earlier, during a scheduled cleaning of the display case, the museum's assistant curator, Simon Platt, swapped the real emerald for a fake. The fake was a skillful replica made of green-tinted rock candy — crystallized sugar — which looked just like the gem under the case's lights. Simon sold the real emerald to a private collector.

Nobody noticed the switch until a summer heat wave brought the ants, which found the sugary "emerald" irresistible. Police traced the candy maker's order to Simon. For once, a sweet tooth helped solve a crime.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the emerald had been replaced with a replica made of sugar candy, which attracted ants; the assistant curator had swapped it.

cards.title: Smooth Sailing
case: A luxury yacht is found drifting off the coast with no one on board. The owner, Russell Crane, later turns up on shore and tells his insurance company that a violent storm forced him and his crew to abandon ship, and that the yacht's cargo of rare wines worth $500,000 was swept overboard. But after the Coast Guard examines the yacht, the claim is denied.
cards.mystery: What did the Coast Guard find that proved there had been no storm?
clues: Some things on board were very neatly arranged.
A storm at sea throws everything around.
story: Russell had secretly sold the wine to a buyer and planned to collect the insurance money as well. He set the yacht adrift on a calm night and motored to shore in the dinghy.

But when the Coast Guard came aboard, they found a tall stack of china dinner plates sitting loose on the galley counter, a chess game set up on the cabin table with every piece standing in place, and a vase of flowers upright on a shelf. In a storm violent enough to force the crew to abandon ship, all of them would have crashed to the floor. The buyer of the wine was traced and confessed. Russell's claim sank without a trace.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that loose, fragile objects on the yacht were still neatly in place, proving there had been no storm; the owner had faked the abandonment to collect insurance on cargo he had secretly sold.

cards.title: Punch Line
case: Factory worker Hank Muller is suspected of killing his landlord at 7:15 a.m. on a Tuesday, across town. But Hank's time card shows that he clocked in at the factory at 6:58 a.m. that morning, and the time clock is accurate to the second. The detective examines the time cards of every worker on Hank's shift, then arrests Hank and his friend Joe.
cards.mystery: What did the detective discover about the time cards?
clues: Hank and Joe were best friends.
Two people can't punch in at practically the same moment.
story: Hank gave his time card to Joe, who punched it for him at 6:58 so that Hank would appear to be at work while he was really across town. But the factory's time clock also stamped the seconds. Joe had punched Hank's card and then his own, one right after the other: Hank's card read 6:58:12 and Joe's read 6:58:14.

It's impossible for two different workers to step up to the clock, pull their cards, punch them and put them back in two seconds. The detective realized that one person had punched both cards. Joe admitted that he'd done his friend a favor — without knowing what it was for. Hank's alibi had run out of time.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Hank's friend Joe punched both his own time card and Hank's, which were stamped only seconds apart — too close together for two different people — so Hank wasn't really at work.

cards.title: Inside Job
case: A man in a hooded jacket hands a teller at the Westside Bank a note demanding money, and walks out with $30,000. The teller, Rachel Moore, is badly shaken. But after examining the robber's note, the detective arrests Rachel as well as the robber.
cards.mystery: What about the note proved Rachel was involved?
clues: The note was written on a bank form.
Customers can't reach that form from their side of the counter.
story: Rachel and her boyfriend, Shane, planned a fake "robbery" so that Rachel could simply hand over the money. Shane wrote the demand note ahead of time on a piece of paper Rachel had given him.

But the paper was a special internal bank form — a cash transfer slip used only by tellers and kept in their drawers behind the counter. No ordinary customer could have gotten one. When the detective asked how a robber had gotten hold of a teller's form, Rachel's story fell apart. The happy couple ended up with plenty of time to think things over — in separate prisons.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the robber's note was written on an internal bank form that only tellers could get, proving that the teller had given it to him.

cards.title: Train of Thought
case: A blackmailer orders a wealthy businessman to put $50,000 in a particular brand of gym bag, take the 5:15 train to Riverside, place the bag in the luggage rack above his seat, and get off at the third stop. Police put detectives in every car of the train to watch the bag. Nobody takes it. Yet when the train reaches the end of the line, the bag is empty.
cards.mystery: Who was the blackmailer, and how did he get the money?
clues: The blackmailer could walk up and down the train without anyone noticing.
Nobody suspects someone who is just doing his job.
story: The blackmailer was the train's conductor, Walter Bix, who had learned the businessman's secret by overhearing a phone call on the train. Walter knew the bag would be watched, so he never planned to take it. The brand he demanded had a zippered side pocket facing the aisle.

At each stop, Walter walked down the aisle punching tickets and reached up to "straighten" the luggage in the racks, as he always did. In those few seconds, he unzipped the side pocket and slipped out a stack of bills into his ticket pouch. Nobody notices a conductor straightening luggage. The detectives found the cash in his locker at the end of the line. Walter's career had come to the end of the line, too.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the conductor was the blackmailer; he took the money out of the bag a little at a time while pretending to straighten the luggage rack, which nobody found suspicious.

cards.title: Vested Interest
case: Billionaire Mark Tremont, who has received death threats, always wears a bulletproof vest in public. At a ribbon-cutting ceremony, a gunman fires one shot from the crowd, and the bullet goes straight through the vest and kills him. The gunman is caught, but police also arrest Mark's bodyguard.
cards.mystery: Why was the bodyguard arrested?
clues: The bodyguard was in charge of the vest.
Not every vest is made of the same stuff.
story: Mark's bodyguard, Sergei, was in charge of all of his security equipment. Months earlier, needing money, Sergei had quietly sold Mark's expensive bulletproof vest and replaced it with a cheap costume vest that looked exactly the same but would stop nothing. He never expected anyone to actually shoot his boss.

When the gunman struck, the fake vest was exposed. Investigators found the real vest — with its serial number — for sale on an online auction site, listed by Sergei. Sergei had protected only his own interests.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the bodyguard had secretly sold Mark's real bulletproof vest and replaced it with a fake, so the bullet went straight through it.

cards.title: Sour Grapes
case: At a famous auction, a collector pays $150,000 for a bottle of wine said to have belonged to Thomas Jefferson. The old bottle is engraved with the year 1787 and the initials "Th.J." Years later, an expert examines the engraving under a microscope and declares the bottle a fake.
cards.mystery: What did the expert notice about the engraving?
clues: The engraving was too perfect.
Jefferson's craftsmen didn't have electricity.
story: In the 1700s, glass was engraved by hand with a copper wheel turned by a foot pedal, which left slightly uneven lines of varying depth. Under the microscope, the letters on the "Jefferson" bottle were cut with perfectly even, regular grooves — the unmistakable marks of a modern electric engraving tool, like a dentist's drill.

The bottle and the wine were genuinely old, but the engraving had been added in the 20th century by a forger who hoped to turn an ordinary old bottle into a priceless relic. The collector sued, and the forger's reputation went sour.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the engraving on the bottle was made with a modern electric tool, which didn't exist in Jefferson's time, so the famous initials had been forged.

cards.title: Pop Goes the Weasel
case: All summer long, homes on the east side of town are burglarized in the middle of the afternoon while families are out. Neighbors never see anything suspicious. The only thing the burglaries have in common is that an ice cream truck was nearby every time. But the ice cream man never leaves his truck, and there's never any stolen property in it.
cards.mystery: What role did the ice cream truck play in the burglaries?
clues: The ice cream truck's song changed from time to time.
Everybody heard it, but only two people were really listening.
story: The ice cream man, Benny Fogg, was the lookout for a pair of burglars. As he drove slowly through the neighborhood, he watched for houses where the family had gone out. Normally, his truck played "Turkey in the Straw." When he passed an empty house, he switched to "Pop Goes the Weasel" — the signal to his partners, waiting a street away, that this was the house. If a police car or a returning family came into view, he switched to "Row, Row, Row Your Boat" — the signal to get out.

A retired music teacher on Maple Street noticed that the truck changed songs at odd moments and wrote down which houses it was passing at the time. Her list matched the burglarized houses perfectly. Benny had to change his tune for good.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the ice cream man was the burglars' lookout, using changes in his truck's music to signal which houses were empty and when police were nearby.

cards.title: Rubbing It In
case: Millionaire Otto Brandt changes the combination of his safe, writes the new numbers on a notepad, tears off the page, memorizes the numbers and burns the page in the fireplace. Two days later, the safe is opened and $200,000 in bonds are gone. The safe wasn't forced. The detective asks for a pencil and the notepad, and then arrests the butler.
cards.mystery: How did the thief learn the combination?
clues: Otto always pressed hard when he wrote.
The detective did exactly what the thief had done.
story: Otto wrote the combination with a ballpoint pen, pressing hard as he always did. Even though he burned the top page, the numbers left grooves in the blank page beneath it.

The butler, Hobbs, who had been quietly dusting the study while Otto wrote, took the notepad to the pantry and lightly rubbed a pencil across the blank page. The grooves showed up as white numbers against the gray pencil. When the detective tried the same trick, the numbers appeared again — and he found the same pencil-rubbed page crumpled in the pantry wastebasket. Hobbs had made quite an impression, but not the one he intended.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the butler rubbed a pencil over the page beneath the one Otto wrote on, revealing the indented numbers of the safe combination.

cards.title: Signs of the Times
case: In the final weeks of the baseball season, the home team suddenly starts hitting like champions — but only at home. On the road, they're as bad as ever. At home, their batters seem to know exactly what pitch is coming. Years later, an old groundskeeper confesses his part in the scheme.
cards.mystery: How did the home team know what pitches were coming?
clues: A catcher tells his pitcher what to throw using hand signals.
The home team's clubhouse had a window looking out over center field.
story: The home team's clubhouse sat beyond the center field fence, with a clear view of the visiting catcher's hand signals. A coach sat in the clubhouse with a powerful telescope. When he saw the catcher's signal for a fastball or a curveball, he pressed a buzzer wired to the bullpen, where a player passed the signal on to the batter — by crossing his legs, say, or tossing a ball in the air.

The batters knew what was coming before every pitch. The groundskeeper who had strung the buzzer wire kept the secret for fifty years. It wasn't against the law, but it was certainly against the spirit of the game.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that someone in the home team's clubhouse used a telescope to steal the visiting catcher's signals and relayed them to the batters with a buzzer and signals from the bullpen.

cards.title: Paper Town
case: A small map company sues a giant publisher, claiming that the publisher copied its road maps instead of surveying the roads itself. The publisher insists its maps are completely original. The case is settled the moment the small company's lawyer points to a tiny dot on the publisher's map.
cards.mystery: What was the dot, and why did it prove the map was copied?
clues: Nobody could ever visit the place marked by the dot.
The small company had set a trap on purpose.
story: Mapmakers have long protected their work with "trap towns" — tiny made-up places that exist only on their own maps. The small company had invented a hamlet called Pinwick Hollow and placed it on a lonely country road. Anyone who actually drove that road would know the town didn't exist.

When Pinwick Hollow turned up on the publisher's map, in exactly the same spot, it proved the publisher had copied the small company's work. The publisher paid a large settlement, and Pinwick Hollow became the most famous town that never was.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the dot was a fake town deliberately placed on the small company's map as a trap; when it appeared on the publisher's map, it proved the map had been copied.

cards.title: The Thing on the Wall
case: In 1945, a group of schoolchildren presents the American ambassador in Moscow with a beautiful hand-carved wooden copy of the Great Seal of the United States. The ambassador proudly hangs it in his office. For seven years, conversations in that office somehow keep reaching the Soviets, even though the room is swept for bugs again and again and the carving contains no batteries or wires.
cards.mystery: How were the conversations leaking?
clues: The gift was listening to every word.
It only worked when someone outside was pointing something at it.
story: Hidden inside the carved seal was a tiny listening device with no batteries and no wires. Soviet agents in a building nearby beamed radio waves at the seal. The device used the energy of those radio waves to power itself, and it sent back a signal carrying every word spoken in the room.

When nobody was beaming radio waves at it, the device was completely silent, so the Americans' bug sweeps found nothing. It was finally discovered in 1952 by a technician who happened to pick up the ambassador's conversations on his radio receiver. The Americans nicknamed it "The Thing." The children never knew they had delivered one of the cleverest bugs in history.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the carved seal contained a hidden, battery-free listening device that was powered by radio waves beamed at it from outside the embassy.

cards.title: Special Delivery
case: A bank teller watches a robber run out of the bank and jump into a small white truck parked at the curb. "There was nobody in the driver's seat," she tells police. "He jumped in on the passenger side, and the truck just drove off by itself!" Police check every white truck in town and arrest the robber within a week.
cards.mystery: Why didn't the teller see a driver, and how did police find the robber?
clues: The truck's steering wheel was on the "wrong" side.
The robber's job involved a lot of stopping and starting.
story: The robber was a mail carrier. Mail trucks are built with the steering wheel on the right-hand side, so carriers can reach mailboxes without getting out. To the teller, who saw the robber jump in on what looked like the passenger side, it seemed that nobody was driving. In fact, the robber was the driver.

He robbed the bank on his lunch break, then went right back to his route. Police checked which mail trucks had been near the bank at the time and found the cash stuffed into a mailbag. His crime had been returned to sender.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the getaway truck was a mail truck with its steering wheel on the right, so the robber — a mail carrier — was the driver even though he seemed to get in on the passenger side.

cards.title: Cut and Run
case: Over several years, a rare-book library notices that maps are disappearing from its centuries-old atlases. Nobody has ever been seen tearing out a page, and nobody walks out with a book. Then a guard finds a tiny razor blade on the floor of the reading room, and a well-known map dealer is arrested.
cards.mystery: How were the maps being stolen?
clues: The maps were never torn.
The thief was very good at sitting quietly.
story: The map dealer, Edmund Haverly, was a regular visitor who spent hours quietly studying the library's old atlases. Hidden in his hand was a tiny razor blade. When nobody was looking, he sliced a map neatly from its binding, close to the spine, so that the book still closed normally and the theft went unnoticed until someone went looking for that particular map. He slid the maps into a folder among his own papers and sold them to collectors.

One day he dropped his blade, and a sharp-eyed guard picked it up. The library compared its reading-room sign-in records with the list of missing maps and found that Edmund had studied every one of those atlases. His career was cut short.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that a regular reader used a hidden razor blade to slice maps out of the atlases while studying them, and smuggled them out in his folder.

cards.title: Shortcut
case: An unknown runner wins a big-city marathon with one of the fastest times in history. She crosses the finish line looking fresh and barely sweating. Spectators and other runners can't remember seeing her anywhere along the course. A week later, her victory is taken away.
cards.mystery: How did she "win" the race?
clues: The race wound through the whole city.
She took public transportation.
story: The runner started the race with everyone else but dropped out of the pack early, ducked into a subway station, and rode the train most of the way across the city. Near the end of the course, she slipped out of the crowd of spectators and ran the last mile, crossing the finish line ahead of the real leaders, who were exhausted after 26 miles.

Officials grew suspicious because she wasn't sweating, she didn't seem to know the course, and no photographs showed her anywhere along the route. A subway passenger remembered a runner wearing a race number. The title went to the real winner. Some shortcuts take you nowhere.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the runner rode the subway for most of the race and rejoined it near the finish.

cards.title: Uninvited
case: At a big wedding reception, the gift table is piled high with presents and cards full of cash. When the newlyweds open the cards the next day, nearly all of the cash is gone. Both families are sure that everyone at the reception was a friend or relative. Everyone remembers a friendly woman in a blue dress who chatted with everybody and danced with the groom's grandfather, but nobody knows her name.
cards.mystery: Who was the woman in blue, and how did she get away with it?
clues: The bride's family thought she was a friend of the groom.
The groom's family thought she was a friend of the bride.
story: The woman in blue was a professional wedding crasher. She dressed up, walked into large wedding receptions and acted as if she belonged. The bride's family assumed she was on the groom's side, and the groom's family assumed she was on the bride's side. Nobody ever asked. While everyone was on the dance floor, she slipped the cash out of the gift cards and into her handbag.

The wedding photographer had dozens of pictures of her dancing, and police recognized her from three other weddings. She was finally caught at a fourth reception — where the bride turned out to be a police officer.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the woman was an uninvited wedding crasher who stole cash from the gift cards, because each family assumed she was a guest of the other.

cards.title: Copy That
case: Police are hunting the "Rosebud Killer," who has committed two murders. The newspapers report that he always leaves a single red rose beside his victims. A month later, a third victim, Diane Holt, is found strangled in her home with a red rose beside her. Everyone believes the Rosebud Killer has struck again. But the detective in charge quietly arrests Diane's husband, Gil.
cards.mystery: How did the detective know that Diane wasn't killed by the Rosebud Killer?
clues: The police don't tell the newspapers everything.
Sometimes they tell them something that isn't quite true.
story: To tell the real Rosebud Killer apart from copycats and people who make false confessions, the police had deliberately given the newspapers one wrong detail. The real killer always left a white rose, not a red one. Only the police and the killer himself knew the truth.

Gil Holt wanted his wife's money. He figured that if he copied the Rosebud Killer's style, the police would blame the murder on the serial killer. He read every newspaper article and followed it to the letter — red rose and all. The detective knew at once that Diane's killer had learned everything he knew from the papers. Under questioning, Gil's story fell apart. The real Rosebud Killer was caught months later — with a white rose in his pocket.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the police had deliberately given the newspapers a false detail about the color of the rose; Diane's husband copied the newspaper version, proving that he was a copycat and not the real killer.

cards.title: First on the Scene
case: Inventor Felix Crane's bedroom door is locked from the inside, with the key still in the lock. When he doesn't answer in the morning, his secretary, Owen, and the housekeeper break down the door. Owen rushes in first and kneels over Felix while the housekeeper runs to the hall phone to call for an ambulance. Felix has been stabbed. The windows are locked from the inside, and there is no other way in or out. Owen is arrested.
cards.mystery: How did Owen kill Felix in a locked room?
clues: Felix had a cup of cocoa every night before bed.
When the door was broken down, Felix was still alive.
story: Owen had been stealing Felix's inventions and selling them to a rival company. Felix had found out and planned to call the police in the morning. The night before, Owen stirred a heavy dose of sleeping powder into Felix's evening cocoa. Felix locked his door as usual and fell into a deep, drugged sleep.

In the morning, when Felix didn't answer, Owen raised the alarm, broke down the door with the housekeeper's help, and rushed in first. While the housekeeper turned away to telephone for help, Owen stabbed the sleeping man with a letter opener hidden in his sleeve, then cried out that Felix had been murdered. Everyone assumed the stabbing had happened during the night, inside a locked room. But the medical examiner found that Felix had died only minutes before the ambulance arrived — and the blood on Owen's cuff was still wet.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Felix had been drugged and was asleep, not dead, behind the locked door; Owen stabbed him after they broke the door down, while he was first on the scene and the housekeeper's back was turned.

cards.title: Deep Impression
case: After a heavy overnight snowfall, the body of Harvey Pell, a small, thin man, is found in a garden shed 100 yards from the lodge where he was staying. The only tracks in the fresh snow are a single line of footprints from the lodge to the shed — made by Harvey's own boots. It looks as if he walked out to the shed alone and died there. But the sheriff measures the depth of the footprints and arrests Harvey's brother-in-law, a big, heavy man.
cards.mystery: How was Harvey killed, and what did the footprints reveal?
clues: The footprints were much deeper than they should have been.
The killer got back to the lodge without leaving a single footprint of his own.
story: Harvey's brother-in-law, "Moose" Becker, struck and killed him in the lodge's mudroom during an argument about money. To make it look as if Harvey had walked out to the shed alone and died there, Moose took off his own boots, squeezed his feet into Harvey's, slung the body over his shoulder and carried it to the shed. Then he walked back to the lodge, stepping carefully in the same footprints, so that only one line of prints showed.

But Harvey weighed only 120 pounds, and his footprints should have been shallow. With Harvey on his back, Moose weighed nearly 400 pounds altogether, and the prints were sunk almost to the ground. The sheriff also noticed that Harvey's boots had been stretched out of shape by much bigger feet. Moose's plan had left a deep impression.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the brother-in-law wore Harvey's boots, carried his body to the shed and walked back in the same footprints; the prints were far too deep for a small man walking alone.

cards.title: Whitewash
case: A museum pays $3 million for a newly discovered landscape painting said to be by a famous artist who died in 1870. The museum's own art restorer, Julian Marsh, examined it and declared it genuine. A year later, a laboratory analyzes a tiny speck of paint from the painting's clouds, and both the seller and Julian are arrested.
cards.mystery: What did the lab find, and why was the restorer arrested?
clues: Not every color of paint existed in 1870.
The seller and the restorer had shared a studio in art school.
story: The lab found titanium white in the clouds. Titanium white is a brilliant white pigment that wasn't sold to artists until the 1920s — fifty years after the artist died. The painting had to be a modern forgery.

Julian had painted the forgery himself, copying the artist's style perfectly, and his old classmate posed as a collector who had found it in a grandmother's attic. Then Julian, as the museum's expert, "authenticated" his own work. They planned to split the $3 million. But Julian, so careful with every brushstroke, had reached for the wrong tube of white. Their whole scheme had been a whitewash.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the painting contained titanium white paint, which didn't exist until the 1920s, and that the museum's own restorer had painted the forgery and then authenticated it himself.

cards.title: Unlucky Number
case: Late one night, a woman looking out of her apartment window sees a man struck down in a lighted office across the street. She carefully counts the rows of windows from the street up and tells police the attack happened on the 14th floor. Police search the 14th floor and find nothing — no body, no blood, no sign of a struggle. Two hours later, the detective works out what went wrong, and the killer is caught after all.
cards.mystery: Why was nothing found on the 14th floor, and where did the attack really happen?
clues: Many tall buildings are superstitious.
The witness counted floors, but the police read floor numbers.
story: Like many tall buildings, the office tower across the street had no floor numbered 13. Its floor numbers jumped straight from 12 to 14 to avoid the unlucky number. So when the witness counted fourteen rows of windows up from the street, she was really looking at the floor labeled "15." The police had searched the floor marked 14 — one floor below the real crime scene.

The detective realized the mistake when he stood in the street and counted the windows himself. On the 15th floor, police found a freshly scrubbed carpet and a trash bag full of stained rags. The office manager, who had killed his partner during an argument over stolen company money, was arrested before he could take out the trash. For him, 13 turned out to be unlucky after all.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the building had no floor numbered 13, so the 14th floor the witness counted to was actually labeled the 15th; police had searched the wrong floor.

cards.title: Sealed Fate
case: Old Lord Ashcombe is buried wearing his gold signet ring, which he used all his life to seal his letters with red wax. A month after the funeral, his lawyer produces a sealed letter, dated a week before Lord Ashcombe's death, leaving the whole estate to the lawyer. The family is suspicious, but the wax seal clearly comes from Lord Ashcombe's ring. The detective compares the seal with seals on older letters, then has the grave opened. The lawyer is arrested.
cards.mystery: How did the lawyer forge the letter, and how did the detective know?
clues: The seal on the new letter had a flaw that the old ones didn't.
The ring had been through something rough since the funeral.
story: The lawyer wrote the letter after Lord Ashcombe's death, carefully imitating his handwriting. To seal it, he needed the signet ring — which had been buried on Lord Ashcombe's finger. So one moonless night, the lawyer dug up the grave, pried open the coffin with a crowbar and slipped off the ring, scratching it badly in the process. He sealed the letter, then returned the ring and filled in the grave.

The detective noticed that the seal on the new letter showed a deep scratch across the family crest, while every seal on letters written during Lord Ashcombe's lifetime was perfect. When the grave was opened, the ring bore the same fresh scratch, and the coffin lid showed crowbar marks. The lawyer's plot had been signed, sealed and delivered — straight to the courtroom.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the lawyer dug up the grave to borrow the signet ring to seal his forged letter, scratching the ring in the process; the scratch appeared in the new seal but in none of the seals made while Lord Ashcombe was alive.

cards.title: Upside Down
case: An old man is found badly hurt on the floor of his apartment, in a building where the apartments are numbered from 1 to 99. Before he passes away, he scratches a number into the dust on the floor beside his head. The officers standing in the doorway read it as "89." They arrest the tenant in apartment 89, who has an ironclad alibi and is soon released. The detective lies down on the floor where the old man lay, and arrests someone else.
cards.mystery: Who did the old man really name?
clues: The victim lay on his back with his head toward the door.
Some numbers look different from the other side.
story: The old man had been lying on his back with his head toward the doorway. He wrote the number facing himself — which meant that it was upside down to anyone standing in the doorway. What the officers read as "89" was really "68" when seen from where the old man lay.

The young man in apartment 68 had been stealing the old man's pension checks from his mailbox. When the old man caught him in the act, the young man shoved him, and he struck his head on the radiator. Police found the stolen checks in apartment 68. The detective had simply looked at the evidence from the victim's point of view.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the victim wrote "68" facing himself; from the doorway it looked upside down and read "89," so the culprit lived in apartment 68.

cards.title: Penny Pincher
case: Bank programmer Lyle Fitch never takes a vacation, never asks for a raise and drives a very modest car. Yet over five years, he quietly becomes a millionaire. No customer ever complains of missing money, and the bank's books always balance — very nearly. He is finally caught when the bank's marketing department runs a promotion for its customers.
cards.mystery: How did Lyle steal the money, and how did the promotion expose him?
clues: Lyle took very small amounts from a very large number of accounts.
The promotion rewarded the customers whose names came first and last in the alphabet.
story: When a bank calculates interest, the result often includes fractions of a cent — $14.6238, for example. The bank rounds down, and the leftover fractions of a cent are usually ignored. Lyle programmed the bank's computer to send all those leftover fractions from millions of accounts into a secret account of his own. No customer ever missed a fraction of a penny, but together they added up to more than a million dollars.

To make sure his account would always be processed last, Lyle opened it under the name "Zachary Zzyzx." Then the marketing department decided to reward the customers whose names came first and last in the alphabet — and tried to contact Mr. Zzyzx. There was no such person. Lyle's scheme had come up short.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the programmer diverted the leftover fractions of a cent from interest rounding into a secret account under a fake name designed to come last alphabetically; a promotion for the first and last customers in the alphabet exposed the fake account.

cards.title: Keeper of the Light
case: In 1925, during Prohibition, a smuggler's speedboat smashes onto the rocks below Gull Point Lighthouse on a moonless night. Its captain, Jack Reilly, is killed. The lighthouse was dark that night. The keeper, Silas Gage, says the lamp burned all night as usual, and that Reilly must have been drunk. But a federal agent climbs the tower, checks the lamp and the keeper's log, and arrests Silas for murder.
cards.mystery: Why did the agent believe Silas had put out the light on purpose?
clues: Silas had a secret business on the side.
The lamp's fuel told a different story than the keeper's log.
story: Silas Gage was secretly a rum smuggler himself, working with a rival gang, and Jack Reilly was cutting into his profits. Silas knew Jack would be coming in on a moonless night with a boatload of whiskey, steering by the lighthouse to avoid the rocks. Just before Jack's boat was due, Silas put out the lamp.

The next morning, Silas wrote in the official log that the lamp had been lit at sunset and burned normally until dawn. But every evening, a keeper had to fill the lamp's oil tank, and a full night's burning used up nearly all of it. When the agent checked, the tank was still almost full. The lamp had burned for barely an hour. Federal agents also found Silas's own stash of whiskey hidden under the lighthouse stairs. Silas had kept everyone in the dark — except his oil tank.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the keeper put out the lighthouse lamp so his rival's boat would crash on the rocks; his log said the lamp burned all night, but the nearly full oil tank proved it had barely been lit.

cards.title: Turning Tide
case: Artist Phoebe Lyle lives alone in a cottage on a tiny island, connected to the mainland by a stone causeway. At 10 p.m., she is found dead in her cottage by her sister, who rowed over. The killer had no boat. Phoebe's ex-husband, Rex, says he left the island by the causeway at 6 p.m., when Phoebe was alive, and couldn't have gone back because "the causeway's been underwater all evening." The detective checks a tide table and arrests Rex.
cards.mystery: What did the tide table show?
clues: The causeway disappears and reappears twice a day.
Rex knew the schedule better than anyone.
story: The causeway is covered by the sea at high tide and uncovered at low tide. Rex claimed it was underwater all evening, but the tide table showed that it was covered only from about 6:30 to 8:30 p.m. By about 8:45 p.m., the tide had gone out far enough to walk across again.

Rex walked back to the island at low tide, struck Phoebe during an argument over money she refused to lend him, and walked back to the mainland before the tide came in again. His soaked trouser cuffs and a fresh smear of seaweed on his shoes confirmed it. The tide had turned against Rex.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the tide table showed the causeway was uncovered again later that evening, so Rex could have walked back to the island at low tide, killed Phoebe and returned.

cards.title: Dead Air
case: Late-night radio host Danny Vale is murdered in his apartment at 1:30 a.m. His co-host, Frank Roman, has the perfect alibi: thousands of listeners heard him on the air, live, from midnight to 2 a.m., chatting about the weather, taking callers' questions and reading the news. But the detective listens to a tape of the show and arrests Frank.
cards.mystery: What did the detective hear on the tape?
clues: Frank liked to talk about the weather.
That night, listeners in the city needed umbrellas.
story: Frank recorded the whole show the night before and set the station's equipment to play it at midnight, while he slipped out to kill Danny, who was about to report Frank's gambling debts to the station's owner. To make the show sound live, Frank even had friends phone in during the recording, pretending to be listeners.

But on the recording, Frank cheerfully told his audience, "It's a beautiful clear night out there, folks — not a cloud in the sky." In fact, a thunderstorm had been pounding the city since 11 p.m. on the night of the murder. A host broadcasting live, from a studio with a big window, would certainly have mentioned it. Frank's alibi was nothing but dead air.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the show had been prerecorded; Frank described clear skies while a thunderstorm was raging during the actual broadcast, so he wasn't really in the studio.

cards.title: Smoke Screen
case: A fire destroys the private gallery of wealthy collector Rupert Vance, and with it, ten oil paintings insured for $5 million. The fire seems to have been an accident. But when fire investigators sift through the ashes, they report that something is missing, and Rupert is arrested.
cards.mystery: What was missing from the ashes, and what had Rupert done?
clues: Oil paintings are painted on canvas stretched over a wooden frame.
The canvas is fastened to the frame with dozens of small metal tacks.
story: Rupert had secretly sold his ten paintings to a foreign buyer and replaced them with cheap printed posters in the same frames, under glass. Then he set fire to the gallery to collect the insurance money as well.

Real oil paintings are painted on canvas stretched over wooden frames and fastened with dozens of small tacks. The canvas and wood burn away, but the metal tacks survive the fire. Investigators sifting through the ashes found picture hooks, hanging wire and melted glass, but not a single tack. The "paintings" had never been on canvas at all. Rupert had painted himself into a corner.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that there were no canvas tacks in the ashes, proving the burned "paintings" weren't real canvas paintings; Rupert had sold the originals and burned cheap copies to collect the insurance.

cards.title: Reel Time
case: Leo Kemp is the projectionist at the Bijou movie theater, where reels of film must be changed by hand every 20 minutes. During the 9 p.m. show, his business partner is killed at home, 25 minutes away. The audience saw the movie without a single interruption, and Leo says he never left the projection booth. The detective examines the projector and the film, and Leo is arrested.
cards.mystery: How did Leo leave the booth without the audience noticing, and what gave him away?
clues: A two-hour movie normally comes on six reels.
Leo had been working with tape and scissors.
story: Normally, a projectionist has to switch reels every 20 minutes, so Leo couldn't leave the booth for more than a few minutes at a time. But before the show, Leo spliced three reels together onto one huge reel that would run for an hour without being touched. He started the movie, slipped out the back door, drove home, killed his partner, and was back in time to change to the next reel.

But a projector reel is built to hold only so much film. The detective found the oversized reel on the projector, overloaded so badly that its edges were scraped, with fresh tape at every splice. Leo's alibi had come unspooled.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Leo spliced several reels together into one long reel, so the movie ran for an hour without him, giving him time to commit the murder.

cards.title: Under Pressure
case: A ski cabin high on a mountain is burglarized on a Saturday. The owner's neighbor, Doug Raines, is a suspect, but he says he spent the whole weekend at home in the valley, 6,000 feet lower. "I haven't been up the mountain in months," he insists. The detective looks inside Doug's car, finds a sealed plastic water bottle on the back seat that has been crushed in on all sides, and arrests Doug.
cards.mystery: How did the water bottle prove that Doug had been up the mountain?
clues: The bottle was crushed, but nobody had squeezed it.
The air is thinner at the top of a mountain.
story: Air pressure is much lower high up on a mountain than down in the valley. When Doug drank half a bottle of water at the cabin and screwed the cap back on tightly, the bottle was sealed full of thin mountain air. As he drove back down to the valley, the heavier air outside pressed on the bottle and crushed it inward. A bottle sealed down in the valley would never have collapsed like that.
The detective had seen the same thing happen after his own ski trips. A search of Doug's garage turned up the cabin owner's chainsaw and fishing gear. Doug had cracked under the pressure.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the sealed bottle was crushed because it had been closed at high altitude and brought down to the valley, where higher air pressure squeezed it — proving that Doug had been up the mountain.

cards.title: By the Light of the Moon
case: In 1858, a young man is on trial for murder in Illinois. The star witness swears that he saw the defendant strike the fatal blow at about 11 p.m., from 150 feet away, by the light of the moon. The case looks hopeless — until the defendant's lawyer, a tall, lanky country lawyer, holds up a small, inexpensive book.
cards.mystery: What was the book, what did it prove, and who was the lawyer?
clues: Farmers bought the book every year.
The lawyer later became one of America's most famous presidents.
story: The lawyer was Abraham Lincoln, and his client was Duff Armstrong, the son of an old friend. The book was an almanac — a yearly calendar of information for farmers, including the phases of the moon and when it rose and set.

Lincoln showed the jury that on the night in question, the moon was only about a quarter full and was sitting low in the sky, close to setting. There wasn't nearly enough moonlight for anyone to see clearly from 150 feet away. The witness's story collapsed, and the jury found Armstrong not guilty. The case became famous as the "Almanac Trial."
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the lawyer was Abraham Lincoln, who used an almanac to prove that there wasn't enough moonlight that night for the witness to have seen what he claimed.

cards.title: Patch Job
case: During a dinner party in a country mansion, the lights suddenly go out. In the pitch-black dining room, a shot rings out. When the lights come back on 30 seconds later, the host, Sir Edmund Grey, is dead. All twelve guests swear they couldn't see their own hands in the darkness. Yet the detective is certain that one guest could see perfectly well, and arrests him.
cards.mystery: How could one guest see in the dark?
clues: The guest came to dinner looking a bit like a pirate.
It takes the eyes many minutes to adjust to darkness.
story: When you walk from a bright room into a dark one, your eyes take many minutes to adjust. But an eye that's been kept covered is already adjusted to the dark — a trick sailors are said to have used when going from a sunny deck into a dark ship's hold.

The killer, Colonel Hastings, arrived for dinner wearing a black eye patch, explaining that he had an eye infection. When his accomplice, a footman, cut the power, the Colonel flipped the patch to his other eye. His dark-adjusted eye could make out shapes in the room while everyone else was blind. He shot Sir Edmund and flipped the patch back before the lights came on. But the detective noticed that the patch had been on the Colonel's left eye before dinner and on his right eye afterward. The Colonel had overlooked one small detail.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the killer wore an eye patch to keep one eye adjusted to darkness; when the lights went out, he moved the patch and could see with that eye, and the detective noticed the patch had switched eyes.

cards.title: Background Check
case: Millionaire Henry Blake's prize racehorse, Thunder Road, worth $2 million, is kidnapped from its stable. The kidnapper calls with a ransom demand, and the police record the call. The caller's voice is disguised, and the call can't be traced. But after listening to the recording twenty times, the detective tells police exactly where to find the horse.
cards.mystery: How did the detective figure out where the horse was hidden?
clues: The detective listened to everything except the caller.
Two sounds could be heard: one every half minute, and one at exactly noon.
story: In the background of the recording, the detective heard two sounds. Every 30 seconds came the low moan of a foghorn. And at the very end of the call, which was made at noon, church bells began to play the hymn "Amazing Grace."

Only one lighthouse on that stretch of coast had a foghorn that sounded every 30 seconds, and only one church nearby played "Amazing Grace" on its bells at noon. They were less than a mile apart, at the fishing village of Port Haven. Police searched the barns and boathouses near the lighthouse and found Thunder Road munching hay in an old boathouse. The kidnapper, a disgruntled former stable hand, was arrested when he came to feed the horse. He should have made his call from somewhere quieter.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that the detective identified a foghorn and a church bell tune in the background of the ransom call, which pinpointed where the horse was hidden.

cards.title: Virtual Alibi
case: Software executive Neil Booth is suspected of killing his business partner at 8:30 p.m. But Neil was on a video call with five colleagues from 8:00 to 9:30 p.m. Everyone saw him on screen at his home office desk, nodding, typing and occasionally speaking. After watching a recording of the call, the detective arrests him.
cards.mystery: How did Neil fake his presence on the video call, and what gave him away?
clues: Neil only spoke when someone asked him a direct question.
The detective was more interested in the clock on the wall behind Neil than in Neil.
story: Neil recorded a 10-minute video of himself at his desk, nodding, typing and looking thoughtful, and set his computer to play it over and over as his camera picture on the call. He kept his microphone muted. Whenever someone asked him a question, his teenage son, who was in on the scheme, unmuted the call and played one of several recorded answers: "Sounds good to me," or "Let me check and get back to you." Meanwhile, Neil drove to his partner's house.

But on the wall behind Neil in the video hung a clock. Every ten minutes, its hands jumped from 8:10 back to 8:00 as the video started over. The detective noticed it at once. Neil's alibi kept going around in circles.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Neil played a looping recording of himself on the video call; the clock on the wall behind him kept jumping back in time each time the video restarted.

cards.title: Do Not Disturb
case: Businessman Carl Weston is suspected of killing his rival at 1 a.m., 90 miles away. But Carl was staying at the Grandview Hotel that night. The hotel's electronic door lock shows that his key card opened his room door at 9 p.m. and not again until 8 a.m., when he went down to breakfast. The lobby camera never saw him leave. The detective studies the hotel's records and arrests Carl.
cards.mystery: How did Carl get out of the hotel without using his key card or passing the lobby, and what gave him away?
clues: Carl's room was right next to a fire exit.
The hotel's computer keeps track of more than just guest room doors.
story: Carl's room was on the second floor, right beside the emergency stairway, which led straight outside to the parking lot. At 10 p.m., he propped his room door open with a folded towel so that he wouldn't need his key card to get back in. He slipped down the emergency stairs and wedged the outside door open with a folded hotel napkin so it wouldn't lock behind him. Then he drove 90 miles, killed his rival, drove back, and slipped in the way he had left.

But the emergency door was connected to the hotel's security system, which recorded that it had been held open from 10:04 p.m. until 2:51 a.m. The folded napkin was still wedged in the door frame. Carl had broken the first rule of hotel security: never leave the door open.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Carl propped open his room door and the emergency exit door so he could leave and return by the emergency stairs, but the exit door's alarm sensor recorded that it was held open for hours.

cards.title: Lost at Sea
case: On a Caribbean cruise, Gary Hobbs reports that his wife, Brenda, went out on deck alone at midnight to look at the stars and never came back. A search of the ship and the sea finds no trace of her, and Brenda is declared lost overboard. Gary files a claim on her $2 million life insurance policy. The insurance investigator checks the ship's records, and Gary is arrested — and so is Brenda.
cards.mystery: What happened to Brenda, and what did the ship's records show?
clues: Every passenger's ID card is scanned whenever they get on or off the ship.
The ship docked at an island the next morning.
story: Brenda never fell overboard. The couple had faked her death to collect the insurance money. While Gary reported her missing, Brenda hid in a storage closet. The next morning, when the ship docked at an island, she put on a wig and sunglasses and walked off the ship with the crowd of passengers going ashore for the day, planning to fly home under a false name.

But every passenger must scan an ID card to get on or off the ship, and Brenda had no other way off. Her card was scanned leaving the ship at 9:12 a.m. — nine hours after she had supposedly vanished into the sea. The investigator found her two weeks later, renting a beach cottage under her maiden name. Gary's story was all washed up.
cards.solution: Investigators must discover that Brenda faked falling overboard and secretly left the ship the next morning; her own ID card was scanned when she walked off the ship at the next port.
